#6453. Should Space Data Centers Run on Solar Panels, Nuclear Reactors, or Both?

The last few days weâve been covering a series of papers by Dr. Slava Turyshev of NASAâs Jet Propulsion Laboratory about the constraints surrounding the use of orbital data centers in space. One that has come up repeatedly is weight, and the solar panels used to power these data centers contribute a significant portion of that weight. So why not go with an alternative power source? Nuclear energy in space applications is having a bit of a moment currently â maybe it could provide the power needed for the orbital data center revolution? According to another paper from Dr. Turyshev, released as a preprint on arXiv, it all depends on the mission requirements.

One major problem with using solar panels for orbital data centers is the Sun doesnât always shine in their orbit. During some seasons, each orbital pass will result in the satellite crossing over the Earthâs shadow for up to 21 minutes. And given that the orbits these data centers are on happen around 15 times each day, that means in a 24-hour day, the satellite spends around 5 hours and 13 minutes in the Earth's shadow.

To combat this problem, engineers turn to an obvious solution â batteries. But they are notorious for being heavy, and according to Dr. Turyshevâs calculations, providing enough storage capacity to combat a 21-minute stretch with no power, would require a 1 MW data center cluster to haul 6.46 metric tons of batteries into orbit. Combine that with the needed solar panels and radiators to get rid of waste heat as infrared light, and you end up with a total mass of 43 metric tons for a 1 MW cluster, even before counting any actual computing hardware.

Fraser talks about the potential of a nuclear reactor in space.

A fission reactor would eliminate the need for solar wings, as well as batteries. However, it doesnât really deal well with the other physical constraint on these systems â waste heat. While it eliminates the heat generated by the solar panels themselves, it introduces another engineering problem â getting rid of the heat at two different temperatures.

Running a nuclear fission reactor at 25% efficiency (which is pretty standard for thermal electrical conversion) would produce about 3 megawatts of conversion waste heat for every one megawatt of energy generated, meaning a one-megawatt computing cluster creates nearly four megawatts of ultra-hot waste heat from its power conversion machinery alone. This waste heat would be at around 700 Kelvin â more than double the maximum temperature that processors on the data centers need to be kept below in order not to fry themselves. While this higher-temperature heat can be radiated away with a relatively compact radiator, it would have to be separate from the thermal sinks cooling the processors below their 320 Kelvin ideal temperature. Ultimately, a nuclear-powered cluster would only need around 6% less low temperature radiator area than a fully solar-powered version.

Despite that, after adding all the mass of the reactor, radiation shielding, power converters, and all the other necessary equipment to run a nuclear reactor, fission originally looks like a winner. Compared to todayâs standard solar panels, a compact fission reactor is around ten metric tons lighter per megawatt. And since weight is money in space, that sounds like a win.

Fraser talks about the new nuclear reactor NASA will use for future Mars missions.

However, there are several caveats to that. First, lighter, next-generation solar arrays are coming along quickly, whose increased efficiency could eliminate nuclearâs advantage entirely. Or the engineers could boost the satelliteâs orbit up to 1,450 kilometers, where the Earthâs shadow problem completely goes away and the satellite can consistently bathe in sunlight â admittedly ignoring the potential space debris and trapped radiation problems this causes, as well as the need for higher power communications equipment.

Nuclear suffers from another disadvantage - radiation. Data centers in space already suffer from stray cosmic rays flipping bits unexpectedly. Putting one next to an active nuclear reactor subjects them to random gamma rays and neutrons as well. While this could be lessened a bit by putting the reactor on a long boom â physically separating it from the server racks and placing a dense âshadow shieldâ near the reactor to block radiation from reaching the computers, that would require extra weight in the form of cabling and the boom itself, eliminating more of nuclearâs original weight advantage.

Despite all these trade-offs, there does appear to be a situation where running a hybrid of both solar and nuclear is the best option. If a mission requires a data center to survive a 24-hour failure of its main power system while keeping 20% emergency power active for safe-mode operation, an 80/20 nuclear/solar split weighs in at around 36 metric tons, around a third of the weight of either as a standalone option due to the weight of batteries needed to meet those mission requirements. But to be clear, without that power maintenance constraint, either system in a standalone configuration wins out on weight.

Fraser talks aobut the advantages and disadvantages of orbital data centers.

Ultimately, Dr. Turyshev thinks the financial picture is dependent on the lifespan of the nuclear reactor. Another disadvantage of a nuclear-powered satellite is it canât just burn up in the atmosphere at the end of its life â it has to be boosted to a âgraveyardâ orbit at around 2,000 km, where a spent reactor would stay indefinitely. But, if a reactor lasts ten years, Dr. Turyshev calculates that it would save around $190 per kilowatt-year in launch costs, whereas if it lasts for only two years (as many experimental space-based reactors are designed to), then that flips to a $783 per kilowatt-year deficit.

What the paper doesnât tackle is the social aspect of whether the general public would support putting potentially tens of thousands of small nuclear reactors into orbit. Just this week, NASA and the U.S. Department of Energy locked in the mission architecture for a nuclear-powered reactor known as Space Reactor-1 Freedom to power the propulsion system of a future Mars mission, so thereâs at least some support for it (or at least the government thinks there is). But as more and more data centers are launched, how to power them with the best trade-off of weight vs cost vs safety vs capability will remain an ongoing debate.

S.G. Turyshev - Power-Architecture Crossovers in Orbital Computing: Thermal, Radiation, and Lifetime Constraints

UT - The Physics Wall Facing Orbital AI Data Centers

UT - Robots, Not Astronauts, Will Have to Fix Space Data Centers

UT - NASA Lays Out Ambitious Plans for Moon Base and Nuclear Mars Mission

#6452. Three Ancient Cosmic Collisions May Explain Why the Moon Has Two Faces

Scientists have narrowed down when three massive collisions reshaped the Moon, bringing them closer to understanding why its Earth-facing side looks so different from its far side.

Billions of years ago, a collision powerful enough to melt enormous quantities of lunar rock created the Moon’s largest impact basin. Subsequent collisions broke apart and scattered some of that ancient material across the surface, leaving behind a geological record that scientists are now piecing together.

Located on the Moon’s far side, the South Pole-Aitken (SPA) basin is one of the oldest and largest impact structures in the solar system. Understanding its history could help explain why the Moon’s near and far sides are so different, what lies beneath its surface, and when major collisions occurred during its early evolution.

An international research team led by Professor Guochun Zhao, Mok Sau-King, a professor in the Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences (DEPS) at the University of Hong Kong (HKU), and Dr. Yuqi Qian, the study’s first author, has identified two types of magnesium-rich rocks with remarkably different origins. Published in Science Advances, the research also establishes a clearer timeline of the major impacts that shaped the region.

For decades, the basin remained largely unexplored. That changed in 2019, when Chang’e-4 completed the first successful landing on the Moon’s far side, followed in 2024 by Chang’e-6, which brought the first rock samples from this largely unexplored region back to Earth.

Using Chang’e-6 samples allocated to HKU DEPS and surface measurements from both missions, the researchers obtained the first direct geological evidence from the two landing sites for reconstructing the basin’s impact history. Satellite observations and numerical simulations helped them trace the origins of rocks across the wider basin.

One group of rocks, known as moderately magnesium-rich norites, formed in the aftermath of the original SPA collision. The impact generated a thick sheet of molten rock that gradually cooled, with different minerals crystallizing at different stages. Later collisions exposed these ancient rocks at the central peaks of large craters. Some were eventually blasted toward the Chang’e-4 landing site in Von Kármán crater by the impact that formed Finsen crater.

The second group contained considerably more magnesium and likely formed through a separate process called magnesium-suite magmatism, a type of magma activity associated with the original SPA impact. These rocks were exposed along the western ring of mountain peaks within the Apollo basin before the Chaffee S impact scattered some of them toward the Chang’e-6 landing site.

Earlier research by the HKU-led team had already uncovered evidence of prolonged volcanic activity and previously unrecognized magma activity in the region. Those studies also suggested that underground accumulations of titanium-rich minerals, known as ilmenite-bearing cumulates, helped account for the contrasting volcanic histories of the Moon’s two sides.

The latest findings suggest that the South Pole-Aitken basin formed approximately 4.34 billion years ago. Another major collision created the Apollo basin around 4.2 billion years ago, followed by the formation of the Orientale basin approximately 3.87 billion years ago. Together, these three events reveal how successive collisions reshaped the Moon’s largest impact basin over hundreds of millions of years.

Reference: “Postimpact evolution of the South Pole–Aitken basin revealed by Chang’e-4 and Chang’e-6” by Yuqi Qian, Wenlei Song, James Head, Mingyu Tian, Zhuang Guo, Harald Hiesinger, Carolyn H. van der Bogert, Le Zhang, Jingyou Chen, Wanfeng Zhang, Ziqing Li, Lingzhi Sun, Xiangsong Wang, Wei-Ran Li, Jiacheng Liu, Nicolas Dauphas, Yi-Gang Xu and Guochun Zhao, 18 November 2026, Science Advances. DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aeh9798

#6451. The ESO is Deeply Concerned About Space Data Centers, and the Rest of Us Should Be Too

There's growing concern that AI is polluting our communal spaces. AI is replacing humans online, and we wonder if there's another human being behind what we're reading or viewing. We wonder where this will go, and how it will end.

There's also growing concern that AI, or at least its infrastructure, is taking over physical spaces. Data centers are proliferating, and citizens are concerned about their effects: power usage, water usage, noise, etc. The promise of a few jobs isn't placating concerns about what some say are resource-hogging data centers being forced on communities despite their opposition.

But now AI data centers are about to take their place in the sky, the last frontier of communal space. This is setting off alarm bells for astronomers, who are adamant that the growing cloud of satellites is taking a serious toll on their observations.

The FCC just approved SpaceX's application to launch a staggering one million new satellites in Low-Earth Orbit (LEO). Together, they will be the first orbital AI data center. The system is designed to avoid using energy and resources here on Earth. The satellites will operate in nearly constant sunlight for solar power, and will cool themselves by pumping liquid coolant through radiative panels. The individual satellites would stay in constant contact with each other with lasers.

With Musk/SpaceX's typical hubris, they're calling the system 'Starmind.'

But whatever they're calling it, not everyone is pleased that it's been approved, and many are questioning why the FCC, a purely American body, can be allowed to approve such a project.

There are really two parallel problems. One is the growing number of satellites overall, and the other concerns the proliferation of AI.

This artist's illustration shows the ESO's Extremely Large Telescope in the Atacama Desert in Chile. It's a 39 meter behemoth that will drive astronomical discoveries for decades. But a sky crowded with satellites will make its life difficult. Image Credit: ESO/L. CalÃ§ada

The European Southern Observatory (ESO) has made their thoughts known on the proliferation of satellites and how it affects astronomy. The ESO operates some of the most powerful existing and upcoming telescopes in the world in the Atacama Desert in Chile: The Very Large Telescope (VLT), the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), the ESO 3.6-metre Telescope, and the ESO's upcoming flagship telescope, the Extremely Large Telescope (ELT).

In a new statement, the ESO condemns the Starmind project as a serious detriment to astronomical observations. And, unlike some other opponents, they've analyzed the situation in detail.

âAs approved, this project would not only have profound consequences for astronomy, but also fundamentally alter the night sky for everyone on the planet. We demonstrated these impacts in an extensive technical analysis, and raised them in a response to the US FCC, as did other organisations worldwide. This approval highlights the urgent need for international mechanisms capable of assessing activities whose impacts extend far beyond national borders and affect a global common good,â said Andreas Kaufer, Director General at the European Southern Observatory (ESO).

Their technical analysis is peer-reviewed and was published in Astronomy and Astrophysics in March 2026.

"Large satellite constellations impact astronomy through both visible trails and the generation of diffuse and atmospherically scattered light. Quantification of this cumulative sky-background component is essential to assess the full ramifications of extant and proposed systems," the paper states.

These panels show the effect of one million satellites (V500km = 6), representing the SpaceX Orbital Data Center constellation in slight violation of the V > 7 recommendation. (a) shows the fraction of the Field of View lost for the LSST camera at the Vera Rubin Observatory. (b) shows example positions of individual satellites. The grey dots represent invisible satellites in the Earthâs shadow, whereas the coloured dots represent illuminated satellites. The 1867 orange dots correspond to satellites brighter than V = 7, and the 247 red dots to satellites brighter than V = 5. For comparison, about 3000â4000 stars are this bright. Image Credit: Hainaut 2026. A&A Volume 712, August 2026 A241

"This study evaluates the effect of proposed constellations â ranging from current deployments to mega-constellations and very bright reflector concepts â on direct trail losses, diffuse background, and scattered sky brightness."

Constellations with up to about 60,000 member satellites have a negligible, but not imperceptible, effect on observations. But above that number, things change for the worse. "Conversely, mega-constellations with 106 satellites render trails pervasive, thereby affecting the majority of long exposures," they write. Long exposures are critical in modern astronomy, so the astronomers are taking the issue seriously.

This figure illustrates the effect SpaceXâs one-million-satellite Orbital Data Center constellation on a 300-second exposure with the spectrograph at the Very Large Telescope. Even 1.3 h after the end of astronomical twilight, more than half the sky remains affected by satellite streaks, with an average of more than eight satellite trails per image at zenith. In some observations, more than 20 satellite trails will cross each image. The effect on a 15-second exposure with the 3Â° LSST camera at the Rubin observatory is similar. Image Credit: Hainaut 2026. A&A Volume 712, August 2026 A241

Long exposures are especially important when observing high-redshift objects or other faint objects. High-resolution spectroscopy and deep-time surveys also use long exposures. Astronomical telescopes can take short exposures and stack them to deal with some satellite light-streak pollution, but that has its limits.

"Bright satellites, such as spacecraft analogous to AST SpaceMobile, significantly impact saturating detectors even when their number is moderate. Extremely bright satellites pose a far more severe threat: a 5000-satellite Reflect Orbital-like constellation could elevate the scattered sky background by 20â30%, and a population of 50 000 could increase it by 200â300%," the ESO paper states.

The ESO's technical analysis said there are current proposals to launch 1.7 million new satellites into space, and many of them breach a critical threshold called V550km = 7. That figure indicates a satellite that can't be seen with the naked eye, so breaching that figure means it can be seen with the naked eye. That means that not only will we see them when we gaze upward, but astronomical telescope observations would be inundated with them. The ESO's analysis says dryly that they "would substantially degrade astronomical observations."

"Maintaining satellite brightness below V550km = 7 is important for all instruments but critical for safeguarding saturating instruments, such as the Rubin LSST camera, and for limiting sky-background pollution," the paper states.

Reflect Orbital has something other than AI or communications in mind. They intend to launch large reflecting satellites into orbit. Those satellites would reflect sunlight to customers on the ground. They could illuminate solar panel farms at night, or provide light to allow things like resource extraction to continue past nightfall. But things can always go wrong. Think of hackers or other malicious actors gaining control of an orbiting light source.

But the real problem astronomers face from Reflect Orbital is that their satellites would blow past the V550km = 7 threshold.

This figure shows scattered light as a fraction of the natural dark sky for 37 (a), 5000 (b), and 50 000 (c) extremely bright satellites (V500km = â4), representing the Reflect Orbital constellations envisaged for 2027, 2030, and 2035, respectively, as seen from outside their illuminating beam. Image Credit: Hainaut 2026. A&A Volume 712, August 2026 A241

Reflect Orbital's eventual 2035 constellation of 50,000 bright satellites would be catastrophic for the Vera Rubin and its LSST. "For the saturating LSST Camera, however, the effects of even a single satellite crossing its FoV will be devastating, compromising a very high fraction of the frame affected by that single trail. The 2030 constellation (5000 satellites) would ruin 3% (at zenith) to 12% (at 30Â° elevation) of the LSST FoV one hour after sunset. With the 2035 constellation (50 000 satellites), the losses would be catastrophic, about 30% at zenith to 100% at 30Â°: all LSST images would be entirely unusable," the ESO's paper states.

These panels show the fraction of exposures captured by the LSST that will be unusable because of Reflect Orbital's satellites. (a) is for 36 satellites in 2027, (b) is for 5,000 satellites in 2030, and (c) is for 50,000 satellites in 2035.

"Even under this constraint, the total satellite population should remain below â¼100 000 satellites to ensure that field-of-view losses do not exceed typical technical downtime," they state.

Companies like SpaceX aren't blind to the problem. They're trying to make their satellites less reflective. But their impact on astronomy is just one outcome of the ongoing crowding of LEO. What about the proliferation of space junk? There are efforts to develop ways of mitigating the space junk problem, but they're way behind the massive number of satellites being launched. SpaceX says they have a plan, and the FCC approves it, but the plan is really just disposal by atmospheric re-entry.

Most people aren't too concerned with astronomical observations, except when one makes the news headlines. But some are concerned about reflecting sunlight down onto Earth at night as a business model. For astronomers, it could be catastrophic.

Far more people are concerned with AI intruding where they don't think it belongs. Do we really need AI in space?

Some are saying that Starmind will never be built, that it's part of the SpaceX/Elon Musk hype machine. But those are just some of the opinions out there, and they don't touch on regular citizens' concerns about the encroachment of AI and its infrastrcture into their lives.

Besides, SpaceX isn't the only company contemplating a satellite AI data processing system. Blue Origin is also considering an orbital data center satellite system. It's called Project Sunrise and would have 51,000 satellites.

We've been warned about the growing number of satellites for years now. In a 2021 paper, researchers warned us about the danger associated with "the adoption of a consumer electronic model applied to space assets." Consumer electronics are creating mountains of electronic waste that we're struggling to manage. The proliferation of satellites is adding to our pollution problem.

In the 2021 paper, the authors point out that "satellite re-entries from the Starlink mega-constellation alone could deposit more aluminum into Earthâs upper atmosphere than what is done through meteoroids; they could thus become the dominant source of high-altitude alumina." High-altitude alumina is bad because it may trigger chemical reactions that destroy ozone. And the alumina isn't destroyed itself, so it could drive multiple cycles of ozone destruction.

This image is a 333 second-exposure from the Blanco 4-meter telescope at the Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory. It shows at least 19 streaks created by the second batch of Starlink satellites launched in November 2019. Image Credit: NSFâs National Optical-Infrared Astronomy Research Laboratory/CTIO/AURA/DELVE, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Crowding LEO with more satellites is fraught with problems. But our rapid and widespread adoption of AI in particular could be especially dangerous. AI data centers in space combine both problems into one. Implementing satellite AI systems may end up being a very bad decision, maybe humanity's last big, bad decision.

Who knows where this will go, and who knows if AI is going to destroy humanity. That type of thinking used to sound like an exaggerated science fiction nightmare, or an easily-dismissed, feverish thought experiment. But many AI experts say we're heading for trouble, we're moving too fast, and we're not building in safeguards. The people who build AI can't actually explain how it works. We all know about AI hallucinating and inventing facts, but AI has been caught scheming and deceiving, behaving one way outwardly while hiding its true intentions. That's truly alarming.

There's no denying that AI is a powerful tool. It's powering scientific discoveries and it's helping regular people every day. But that's just one side of it.

From a POTUSA who posted an AI video of himself wrestling a tigerâshortly after a real person was unfortunately killed by oneâto armies of bots spreading political misinformation designed to undermine a nation's sovereignty, to financial scammers with a global reach, AI's presence is proving to be toxic. It ranges from mildly problematic to outright hostile. Bad actors are rapidly adopting this new, powerful tool, and using it to harmful effect.

It's amost impossible to deny that we're on the cusp of something historic. Humanity always struggles with new powerful tools because wisdom lags behind intelligence. It always has and it always will; the only way to acquire wisdom is through experience. Do we have enough wisdom to make careful decisions regarding AI?

At different times in history, angry mobs of citizens have been the only thing standing in the way of terrible ideas and actions. To place AI in space, beyond the reach of the angry mob and its pitchforks, may end up being a terrible mistake.

#6450. The Best Fancy Food Gifts (That We Actually Want for Ourselves)

These Japanese toaster ovens, sleek barware sets, and design-forward coffee grinders will bring a lifetime of (tasty) memories

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

Forgive the Daddy Warbucks-ness of what I’m about to say, but I think it’s important to remember that a splurge and an extravagance aren’t quite the same thing when it comes to gifts. On one end of the spectrum, there are vapid luxury items; on the other, there are the gifts whose steeper price point is tied directly to their artistry, quality, and/or durability. While the former can be fun to window-shop, our hard-earned clams are best spent on the latter.

As a seasoned shopping writer, I ask myself two big questions when mulling over a pricey purchase: What is the story behind this item? Can I picture it in my life for years to come?

Consider the iconic, mid-century modern Moccamaster coffee machine, which first debuted in the 1960s and has been trending on social media lately for its array of colorful, modular designs. I took the cult-fave machine for an extended test run (it’s still my daily driver), and the yellow pepper iteration made me fall in love with drip coffee all over again. The Dutch company behind the appliance, Technivorm, really exercises what it calls its core tenets of “form and function,” and will service any repairs on the machines for up to five years. That is exactly the kind of lore I crave from the splurge-level items on my holiday shopping list (and the kind that will make your own design-savvy, coffee-loving giftee feel special).

If you’re reaching into your budget for gifts that last, impress, and — if you’re giving them to a family member or partner — you might be able to use yourself for years to come, the fancy gifts for food lovers start getting good. There are the big-ticket kitchen titans: a high-tech Mill food recycler, sleek Miele vacuums (post-kitchen-prep cleanup doesn’t stand a chance), and electric pizza ovens that can reach 850 degrees Fahrenheit in just 90 seconds. Sometimes “splurges” are just wise investments, especially with appliances and cookware; your giftee is going to use a well-made cutting board or top-tier kitchen knife for years or decades to come. There are also the gifts with spectacular whimsy: a stationary exercise bike that makes smoothies, a martini-lover’s menorah, a tabletop lighter that’s also an incredible conversation piece.

These gifts may be at higher price points than a classic stocking stuffer, but they’re also extra-special — we’d say, so worth it if you have the dough. If you’re looking to roll out the red carpet with splurge-worthy food and kitchen gifts, look no further.

The casual gift for someone who loves food and loves to host might be nice set of chip and dip bowls, cocktail napkins, or perhaps some beeswax candlesticks. The gift of a whole dry-cured Spanish ham leg, however, is a next-level present for the most passionate entertainer in your family or friend group.

No better way to pull focus at the dining table than with this copper and brass pepper mill, which East Fork says can literally last for “hundreds of years” when cared for properly. The 10-inch tall grinder is made in collaboration with a small, family-run company in Greece, and is actually modeled after the same mills 20th-century Greek soldiers would carry to grind coffee, a fact that finds homage in the Greek lettering inscribed on the mill.

The Eater staff has tested its fare share of toaster ovens, and crowned the Balmuda as one of the best for its minimalist design and ability to not just warm but rehydrate breads and pastries; it uses a steam process to reinvigorate that day-old croissant like a wizard. This Balmuda Pro has an even more powerful heat source, and a setting called Salamander Grill Mode for giving your salmon the restaurant-grade finishing treatment.

The cultural martini discourse has never been stronger, or brinier. Help your giftee celebrate Hanukkah with Susan Alexandra’s dirty martini menorah. As the designer’s site proclaims, “The miracle of Hanukkah was that the olive oil that was enough only for one day of light lasted for eight days. Our favorite way of consuming olives? In a bath of vodka/ gin and a touch of vermouth!”

Behold, a splurge that is also a cooking investment! We’ve all experienced the frustration of chopping special ingredients on a sub-par cutting board, and the moment you level up to a thick, handsome slab is one that can help give you newfound confidence and efficiency as a passionate home cook. Boardsmith’s walnut end grain cutting boards are all made to order out of a sustainably harvested black walnut, resulting in beautiful, checkerboard-like and ombré color variations. Cheese boards have never looked better, folks.

The Chicago-based luxury chocolatier Vosges is known for its intricate, decadent holiday gifts (don’t miss its lodge-inspired advent calendar), and it has curated the perfect assortment of its truffles to go with a bottle of Ceretto Barolo wine. “This is a classic Barolo,” the site explains, “[it’s] light garnet in color with Barolo’s quintessential aromas of roses, tart cherries, and hints of truffles.”

Made in Victor, Idaho, the boutique blades of New West KniveWorks are a departure from the recent fad of making knives extra wide, favoring instead the graceful docility of a light, 8-inch steel blade and a handle made out of a durable resin composite material that will last a lifetime. In the fighting words of New West, “this precision instrument isn’t a club like Mom’s old Wüsthof Trident.” If you’re shopping for a partner who tends to their knife collection like the Crown Jewels, it’s the kind of gift that feels equal parts lifetime cooking investment and personality-forward essential tool.

Gohar World’s elevated kitchen essentials walk the line between Dalí-esque absurdity (remember when Julia Fox wore its kitchen gloves to the Grammys?) and functionality, and this metallic apron is no exception: it lends you a lacy hand (two, actually) while you’re cooking.

I really do think the Moccamaster coffee machine is the Platonic ideal of drip coffee machines; my own yellow pepper model swept me off my feet with its talent for quick, smooth brewing and its modular, chic mid-century modern design. If you love someone who loves coffee — and perhaps already owns the GOATed machine — why not invest in the brand’s powerful burr grinder? It’s certified by the European Coffee Brewing Centre (ECBC), which means it has passed a rigorous testing process for uniform grinding and quality construction.

Imagine casually inviting your beloved over for dinner, and you serve this gorgeous Japanese wagyu ribeye steak along with an Old-Fashioned? Imperia Caviar is best known for its royal osetra, but it’s also where you can find a variety of A5 Japanese wagyu (the highest designation for beef in the country); this grade of wagyu has up to five times more intramuscular fat, which makes for an even richer, buttery flavor.

I always have a few lighters floating around my house for candles and incense, but there’s something so retro-chic about a coffee table lighter. Edie Parker, master of eccentric and surreal lifestyle [puffs chamomile pre-roll] accessories has a line of jelly-inspired tabletop lighters with all kinds of “fillings,” and the olive version is one of the most charming.

Unsurprisingly, we’re picky when it comes to choosing cookware at Eater — that’s why we collaborated with Heritage Steel to make the kind of cookware collection that will last a lifetime. Every frypan, lid, and pot is made out of 5-ply stainless steel, and this robust bundle includes everything you need to embark on all kinds of culinary adventures: two fry pans (8.5- and 10.5-inch), a 2-quart saucier, a 3-quart saucepan, a 4-quart sauté pan, and an 8-quart stock pot ready to simmer your most Strega Nona-worthy stews.

Here’s an idea: Order this massive wheel of Manchego cheese from Flamingo Estate, and ride it to victory at the Cooper’s Hill cheese rolling competition. That, or gift it to someone who can appreciate the fact that it’s sourced, per Flamingo Estate, from one of only ten cheese mongers in Spain that are still making farmstead PDO Manchego Artesano, which results in an even richer and more complex flavor.

You know the big (or rather, full-size) Rocco: a $1,500 high-tech drink fridge, endorsed by Eric Wareheim and seemingly designed by someone who loves Eames chairs. This year, Rocco has launched a miniature version of its posh drink refrigerator, dubbed the Mini Mini Fridge, this 14-inch tall personal fridge fits up to 12 cans of your preferred beverages (or sheet masks; choose your journey). Unlike most mini fridges, the Mini cools down to 39 degrees Fahrenheit (the majority of countertop fridges hit 48 degrees Fahrenheit at their coldest). Kind of the dream set up for your — sorry, your giftee’s — office.

Atelier Sebastião Lobo crafts otherworldly flatware that’s almost too beautiful to use. This set of Calder-esque cutlery has spawned many imitations, because it’s one of the most original designs to come out of the flatware world in recent years, and a prime example of how cutlery and tableware in general got really squiggly and freaky this year.

There is nothing like devoting counter space to yet another coffee machine that requires highly specific capsules, but hey! This one is different — it brews only cold coffee. (Nitro cold brew, cold brew, and cold espresso to be specific.) Sure, it’s definitely a bit of a luxury, but then again, so is spending $7 on an iced cortado from the coffee shop every morning.

N/A drinks were created to be a more inclusive product. Only a rare few can order bottles of bubbly for over $100. The Venn diagram where these two groups overlap is small, but it exists, along with this $119 bottle of booze-free bubbly made with French Chardonnay grapes.

In a way that I cannot quite explain, this feels like it’s targeted at the 1990s kids who grew up with Smart House and Richie Rich. This stationary exercise bike, complete with an orange slice wheel, whips up one of your favorite smoothies courtesy of your own pedaling power. As one reviewer writes, “I am 67 years old, widowed twice, and I have seen enough in this life to know when somebody has finally invented something useful. This bicycle-blender contraption has changed the direction of my spirit. Every morning I put in one banana, some frozen peaches, yogurt, a little honey, and whatever green thing is closest to expiration in my refrigerator. Then I pedal until either the smoothie is done or I start seeing little sparkles. Whichever comes first.”

Khushbu Shah is the former restaurant editor at Food & Wine and the author of the cookbook AMRIKAN: 125 Recipes From the Indian American Diaspora. She lives in Los Angeles and you can follow all of her egg eating adventures on Instagram.

#6449. Experimental Drug Shrinks Tumors in Two of the Hardest-To-Treat Cancers

A single experimental drug designed to block signals from several cancer-driving mutations has shown encouraging early results, raising the possibility of treating multiple hard-to-treat cancers.

When pancreatic or lung cancer continues to grow despite several treatments, doctors can find themselves with few remaining options. In some patients, the difficulty lies in genetic mutations that keep cancer cells growing and have historically been difficult to target with drugs. An experimental cancer drug called ERAS-0015 has shown promising results in an early clinical trial, shrinking tumors in patients who had already undergone other forms of treatment.

The drug targets RAS, a family of genes that provide instructions for making proteins involved in controlling cell growth and division. In healthy cells, RAS proteins act like molecular switches, turning on when cells receive signals to grow and turning off when those signals are no longer needed. Certain genetic mutations can leave these switches stuck in the “on” position, continuously instructing cells to grow and helping sustain cancer.

For years, scientists struggled to develop drugs capable of interfering with these faulty proteins. ERAS-0015 takes an approach known as a pan-RAS molecular glue. It works by bringing proteins together at the molecular level and is designed to bind to RAS while the switch is active, blocking growth signals associated with several different cancer-driving RAS mutations.

“The overall goal of precision oncology is to match a patient’s mutation, or the ‘Achilles Heel’ of a specific individual’s cancer, to a drug that directly targets that mutation. This is what we are attempting to do by studying the effectiveness of ERAS-0015 in patients with RAS alterations,” said Dr. Judy Wang, a medical oncologist at Florida Cancer Specialists and Research Institute in Sarasota, Florida.

Wang presented findings from 148 patients participating in the phase I AURORAS-1 clinical trial on November 19, 2026, at the 38th EORTC-NCI-AACR Symposium on Molecular Targets and Cancer Therapeutics in Barcelona, Spain.

The trial began in June 2025 and is evaluating ERAS-0015 both alone and in combination with other anticancer therapies. Participants include people with pancreatic cancer, colorectal (bowel) cancer, non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) that has spread beyond the original tumor site, and other solid tumors driven by RAS mutations. The results presented at the symposium included 83 patients with pancreatic cancer and 37 with NSCLC. The trial is continuing to enroll patients.

“AURORAS-1 has enrolled patients that have tried a number of other treatments for their cancer. In this context, ERAS-0015 treatment caused a 44% response rate in patients with RAS-mutant pancreatic cancer and a 60% response rate in patients with RAS-mutant lung cancer. A ‘response’ means the patients experienced considerable tumor shrinkage, and these response rates are important as they show clinically meaningful activity from ERAS-0015 treatment in patient groups that have few if any therapeutic options to address their cancer. In addition to this, ERAS-0015 was well tolerated with few severe side effects,” Wang told the symposium.

These response rates came from relatively small groups of patients receiving a 32 mg dose of the drug. Tumors shrank in 11 of 25 patients with pancreatic cancer who had previously received chemotherapy and in three of five patients with lung cancer who had previously been treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors, drugs that help the immune system recognize and attack cancer, or platinum-based chemotherapy.

Researchers gradually increased doses of ERAS-0015 from 2 mg to 40 mg to evaluate how well patients tolerated the drug. After a median follow-up of just over four months, there was no indication that the maximum tolerated dose had been reached.

At doses of 16 to 32 mg, the most common side effects, affecting at least 10% of patients, were rash, diarrhea, nausea, and inflammation of the lining of the mouth. Twelve patients (9.8%) experienced severe treatment-related side effects, classified as grade 3 or higher. No dose-limiting side effects were reported.

“We are encouraged by the preliminary clinical activity and tolerability of ERAS-0015 in patients that have tried a number of other treatments for RAS-driven lung and pancreatic cancer,” said Wang.

“Our goal is to give clinicians new, better options for treating their patients with RAS-driven cancers. Early results suggest ERAS-0015 has the potential to be one of these options.”

Phase I clinical trials involve relatively small numbers of patients and are primarily designed to evaluate safety and determine appropriate doses. Although the tumor shrinkage observed in this trial provides an early indication of the drug’s potential, larger phase II and phase III clinical trials will be necessary to confirm its safety and effectiveness.

“If these early results are confirmed, ERAS-0015 could offer patients with RAS-driven cancers a new option. Clinical development of ERAS-0015 would be impossible without the patients, caregivers, investigators and participating trial centers that put their trust in us to take part in our study. We are deeply grateful for their contribution to AURORAS-1,” Wang concluded.

Professor Elena Garralda, chair of the EORTC-NCI-AACR Symposium and co-director of the Vall d’Hebron Institute of Oncology’s clinical research program, was not involved in the study. She commented: “This is the first presentation of these preliminary results from the AURORAS-1 clinical trial and they have been eagerly awaited. They show that the RAS inhibitor, ERAS-0015, has encouraging anti-tumor activity in cancers that are hard to treat successfully and for which there are few treatment options available. We look forward to further results from larger clinical trials, which are investigating whether ERAS-0015 can help a broader group of patients.

“This is one of several studies being presented at the EORTC-NCI-AACR Symposium that are beginning to show it is possible to design drugs that target cancers driven by RAS mutations, which was not thought possible until recently.”

#6448. Thune will lead Republicans through the minority

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., leaves a meeting in the Capitol on Tuesday, before his election as incoming minority leader later in the day. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Senate Majority Leader John Thune was reelected as the Republican leader on Tuesday and will steer the conference through their time in the minority.

The South Dakotan ran uncontested despite a push from some of his colleagues to delay the leadership elections following Republicans’ stunning defeats last week in the midterms, which saw them lose at least seven seats and the majority.

“Obviously, the election result was not what we hoped for,” Thune told reporters, referring to the midterms. “But I think it’s important that we take the lessons from that and internalize the message the American people were sending to us.”

While he and the rest of the leadership slate sailed through the conference contests by voice vote, it wasn’t without drama.

Before the leadership elections began in the Old Supreme Court Chamber early Tuesday morning, the conference held a meeting at the request of a group of GOP five senators, led by Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis.

The conversation, which several senators described as “frank,” ended up pushing back the leadership elections by a few hours. But they were not postponed to another day as some had hoped.

“This has never been anything against John Thune,” said Johnson, as he made good on his commitment to leave the room early if the conference proceeded with its election. “What I didn’t agree with was holding the election right away, giving nobody an opportunity to really challenge any leadership position.”

“Part of the issue here is who wants the job? God bless him for serving,” Johnson added.

The conference conversation Tuesday morning turned into an “open-mic” with both conservatives and those who lost their elections speaking, according to senators.

Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., told reporters, “To rush into this and to just ratify all the same leadership — I mean, what message does that send?”

But no contender to Thune emerged despite the angst, and a motion to proceed to the election, introduced by Thune’s fellow South Dakotan Sen. Mike Rounds, was accepted.

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., said voters who rejected Republicans last week were reacting to high gas prices, the war in Iran and the cost of living, not to how Senate leaders were running the conference.

“I don’t think anybody in Texas who voted for the Democrat governor was voting against John Thune. If you diagnose that as a problem, you’re misdiagnosing the problem,” Paul said.

Whip John Barrasso, R-Wyo., was reelected to his position, as was the chairman of the Senate Republican Conference, Tom Cotton of Arkansas. Sen. James Lankford of Oklahoma was again selected as vice chair of the conference, while Sen. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia was reelected as Republican Policy Committee chair.

“Our first step is to make sure the American people know that we heard what they said, and the American people’s priorities are our priorities. That’s the way we regain their trust,” Barrasso said afterward.

Sen. Bernie Moreno of Ohio got the nod to chair the National Republican Senatorial Committee, meaning he will helm the campaign arm as the party looks ahead to the uncertain waters of 2028.

Moreno said, “I was in the retail automobile business, so when you don’t listen to your customers, your customers punish you. I think we have to own it, and I think we have to learn from it.”

Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., said on Monday evening, “What we as a conference right now need is honesty. We need focus. We need to try to reach a consensus on what we need to change.”

Kennedy was among those pushing to delay the leadership elections and told reporters on Tuesday he voted present instead of yes on whether to proceed to them.

Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., who ran for GOP leader twice — once in 2022 against Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., and in 2024 against Thune — declined to run again to challenge Thune. But in a Dear Colleague letter on Monday, he detailed what he’d like to see in the lame-duck session before Democrats take power, including confirming every nominee President Donald Trump has sent to the Senate, funding the government without an omnibus, banning stock trading, passing the permitting bill that is advancing this week in the Senate, passing the National Defense Authorization Act, balancing the budget and pushing through a sweeping voter ID bill known as the SAVE America Act.

Senate Republicans on Tuesday also voted on a resolution on their path forward that was spurred by a motion from Scott, aides said.

“It is the sense of the GOP Conference that we will maximize the 54 days we have with congressional majorities, to confirm every judicial nominee and every executive nominee that the conference approves of, to pass our core Republican priorities, and to do everything humanly possible to pass a reconciliation bill before Jan. 3,” the resolution reads in part.

That long list of goals highlights the expectations Thune has faced as leader, where he led one-third of Republicans’ trifecta in Washington. In the next Congress, Democrats will hold the majority in both chambers of Congress after their larger-than-expected wins, while Trump finishes out his term as president.

Thune said he told his conference: “As I look back on the last couple of years, my question is, what would you have me do differently?”

“Given the constraints we had to deal with, all the stuff that was coming at us on a daily basis, a narrow margin in the House, the White House, the Democrats over here who were obstructing two long government shutdowns — I think we came out of it as well as could have been expected, and got a lot of stuff done,” Thune told reporters.

“If you believe the exit polls, it was the war, it was the economy, it was inflation, it was fuel prices,” Thune added. “So no, I wasn’t apologizing for anything that we did. And I think on the political side, I don’t know what else I could have done.”

#6447. All the Gaps We See in Protoplanetary Disks Aren't From Planets

When astronomers look out into the Milky Way at very young stars, they find rings in their protoplanetary disks. It's pretty clear that these rings are where planets are forming. They're carving gaps and rings in the protoplanetary disks, the reservoirs of material around stars that planets form from.

ALMA, the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, has captured images of many of these disks and rings. Those images are part of the effort to understand how planets form, one of the primary questions in contemporary astronomy. But it's not clear if every ring is because of a planet. Protoplanetary disks are complex, and there are many forces at work in them. Some rings could be planets, and some could be caused by other phenomena.

âThese new stars have bright rings and dark gaps patterned in concentric circles resembling the grooves of a vinyl record,â said Masayuki Yamaguchi, a post-Doctoral Fellow from Kyushu Universityâs Faculty of Science. âThese patterns arenât new; what was a mystery was how these grooves were carved. The most popular explanation is that young planets make these gaps as they orbit the star. However, when a disk has many rings, it becomes harder to explain since itâs hard to imagine that multiple planets have already formed.â

Yamaguchi is the lead author of new research in The Astrophysical Journal titled "A Hybrid Origin for the Multiple Ring-gap Structures in the Large Protoplanetary Disk V1094 Sco: A Low-mass Planet and Secular Gravitational Instability" Yamaguchi is a member of a team of Japanese astronomers who studied V1094 Scorpii, a young star about 500 light years away. V1094 Sco has a protoplanetary disk that extends out to 300 astronomical units, with multiple ring-gap pairs at great distances from the star.

This is ALMA's image of V1094 Sco reconstructed with PRIISM. The researchers detected rings and gaps in the disk and were able to determine which were from still-forming planets. Image Credit: By YMasayuki - Own work, CC BY 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/194635370

"High spatial resolution observations reveal that some protoplanetary disks host multiple ringâgap pairs at large stellocentric radii, yet their physical origin remains unsettled," the authors write. The researchers used ALMA images and observations with the Very Large Telescope's SPHERE (Spectro-Polarimetric High-contrast Exoplanet REsearch) instrument to analyze the V1094 Sco disk. "The continuum image shows four narrow dust ringâgap pairs extending to exceptionally large radii (r â¼ 380 au)," they write, and also "trace a spatially extended gas disk (r â¼ 760 au) in Keplerian rotation." Keplerian rotation means that objects further from the star orbit slower than those nearer the star.

Young stars with protoplanetary disks are T-Tauri stars, and among that group, V1094 Sco is known for having a giant disk with multiple rings, making it a rarity. It's the subject of a lot of research and observations. It was first recognized for its extended ring with multiple gaps and rings in a 2018 paper. That paper said, "In this work, the nature of V1094 Sco as a giant, multi-ringed protoplanetary disk is identified for the first time, based on data from the Lupus survey of protoplanetary disks." (The Lupus survey was an ALMA survey of disks in the Lupus star-forming complex.)

Ever since then, astronomers have been trying to understand V1094 and its unusual disk. There's not much doubt that still-forming planets are responsible for some of its features, but can they explain them all?

In an interesting twist, the researchers didn't use new ALMA observing time to study V1094 Sco. They relied on existing data and applied a new open-source super-resolution imaging technique called PRIISM (Python module for Radio Interferometry Imaging with Sparse Modeling.) It was built specifically to reconstruct sharper images with existing ALMA data, and replaces a previous technique called CLEAN. PRIISM proved its value in a 2025 study of 78 disks in the Ophiuchus star-forming region, where it found previously undetectable features in disks, only a few hundred thousand years after the stars formed.

This figure doesn't show V1094 Sco; instead it shows CrA IRS 2, a protostar about 430 light years away. It illustrates how much better PRIISM is at detecting disk structures in existing ALMA data than its predecessor, CLEAN. Image Credit: Ayumu Shoshi et al 2026 ApJ 998 214

PRIISM paid similar dividends in this work.

âWe observed that the disk extends approximately 380 astronomical units (AU)âabout 13 times the distance between the Sun and Neptuneâfrom the center. Within that, we found four narrow rings and gaps between 100â230 AU from the starâs center,â explained Yamaguchi. âWhen we compared the widths and depths of the gaps with the "one planet per gap" model, we could not explain the entire pattern. Instead, the origin appears to differ from place to place."

"The ensemble of gap widths and depths is inconsistent with a simple one-planet-per-gap interpretation," the authors write in their paper.

An exoplanet can explain the innermost gap, according to the results. "At r â 100 au, a double gap and its scattered-light counterpart are consistent with multigap excitation by a single low-mass companion of (55 Â± 35) Mâ," the authors explain.

But further from the disks, the rings were spaced more evenly. "At r â 170â230 au, the outer ring system shows regular spacing and no clear scattered-light counterpart," the authors write. "These outer rings are quantitatively compatible with secular gravitational instability." That means the outer rings aren't associated with exoplanets. Instead, they're dust clumping together under its own gravity, which requires low turbulence.

This is a near-infrared scattered-light image of the V1094 Sco disk obtained with VLT/SPHERE. It's overlain with the locations of dust continuum rings (solid lines) and gaps (dashed lines). The filled white circle indicates the SPHERE coronagraph. Image Credit: Masayuki Yamaguchi et al 2026 ApJ 1006 232

Secular gravitational instability intrinsically produces evenly spaced rings, while exoplanets don't.

"V1094 Sco therefore supports a hybrid pathway in which weak turbulence in an extended disk allows secular gravitational instability to assemble long-lived midplane dust concentrations that can cradle planet formation beyond â¼100 au, alongside planet-driven substructures at intermediate radii," the authors write.

These results don't mean that planets won't eventually form in these features that are at great distances from the star. It just means that there are no planets forming there right now. "In this framework, secular GI does not compete with planet formation; rather, it concentrates solids and establishes disk-wide conditions favorable for subsequent planet growth," the authors write in their conclusion.

ALMA doesn't image planets; that was never its job. But if exoplanets are in V1094 Sco's disk, other telescopes might find them.

âBecause ALMA is a radio telescope, we have not yet directly detected the planet that generates the gap closest to the star. Using other telescopes such as the Subaru Telescope will help us get a clearer picture of this hidden planet,â said Yamaguchi. âAs we analyze more disks, our understanding of the fundamental question of where and how planets form will deepen. Each new finding adds a thread to the tapestry of our knowledge of the universe.â

The brains of people with PTSD bear molecular changes that differ from those in people with other conditions, like depression, a new study finds.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A study of hundreds of brains has revealed molecular differences in people with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) that are not found in individuals without the condition.

These molecular marks also differ from those seen in the brains of people with other conditions, like depression, the research found.

Our environment and experiences influence how our genes work, affecting which genes can be turned on. Rather than changing genes' underlying code, the environment can trigger what are known as epigenetic changes, which include certain chemicals that attach to DNA molecules and change their structure.

One such epigenetic change, called methylation, can work like a "dimmer switch" for genes, or even completely block certain genes from turning on.

"These epigenetic features of the brain are important for shaping the way the brain functions," study co-author Frances Champagne, a psychologist at the University of Texas at Austin, told Live Science. "This can give us some insight into why individuals with PTSD develop PTSD, or how [their brains] are different from a healthy brain."

In the new study, published Friday (Nov. 20) in the journal Cell Reports, scientists took a close look at DNA methylation in 302 brains that had been donated after death. These included 101 brains from individuals diagnosed with PTSD, 101 from people with major depressive disorder and 100 from people without any diagnosed psychiatric disorders. The researchers also had access to these individuals' medical records.

The team zoomed in on three brain regions: the prefrontal cortex, the amygdala and the hippocampus. The prefrontal cortex handles cognitive functions like planning and decision-making, the amygdala is a major hub for emotional processing, and the hippocampus is key for memory and learning.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"The goal of our study was to look at the epigenetics of the PTSD brain and ask how [it] is different from that of an individual who does not have PTSD," Champagne said, "or who comparatively has another diagnosis, like major depressive disorder."

Compared to the brains of people without any disorders, the brains of people with PTSD had different patterns of methylation in the prefrontal cortex, in particular. By contrast, in major depressive disorder, the amygdala stood out as a brain region with distinct methylation.

Additionally, in depression, the observed differences in methylation tended to affect the same set of genes across different regions of the brain. This was not the case in PTSD, which showed more inconsistencies in terms of which specific genes were involved. The methylation patterns in PTSD also appeared to vary depending on other factors, such as patients' sex, ethnicity and age at which they experienced trauma.

The study's results serve as a valuable resource, said Seyma Katrinli, an investigator in the Grady Trauma Project, a large PTSD study, at the Emory University School of Medicine.

Although the findings can't be used to help diagnose PTSD yet, down the line, this area of research could help scientists correlate changes that are measurable in people's blood to changes in the brain, said Katrinli, who was not involved in the new work. Then, blood tests could help guide the diagnosis and treatment of PTSD, she suggested.

That said, the study had limitations. Because the scientists analyzed postmortem brains, they relied on the medical reports rather than assessing the study subjects directly. Additionally, both PTSD and major depressive disorder are associated with substance use, which also causes DNA methylation; this potential confounding factor was not accounted for in the study. .

Finally, at this point, there is no way to tell what triggered the observed differences in DNA methylation. The scientists can't say if the variations are a consequence of PTSD, a risk factor for PTSD, or a downstream effect of other things that co-occur with PTSD.

The research sets the stage to "help us ask better questions," Champagne said. Her team is now looking to investigate factors — such as sex, the timing of traumatic experiences, or history of substance use — that may be driving the variation within PTSD.

"It's a very exciting foray into epigenetic profiling in the brain," she said.

DNA methylation profiling of human brain in posttraumatic stress and major depressive disorders indicate specific molecular features. Cell Reports, 118270. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.celrep.2026.118270

#6445. An Overlooked Metabolic Byproduct Could Help Repair a Damaged Heart

A substance often treated as waste may be vital to the heart during a crisis, offering a potential target for treating heart failure and heart attacks.

The heart has to keep beating whether the body has plenty of energy available or is running low. Maintaining that constant supply of energy is a complicated process, and when it breaks down, it can contribute to serious cardiovascular conditions such as heart failure. Researchers at University of Utah Health have now uncovered an unusual feature of heart muscle cells that helps them stay fueled during periods of stress and could point toward new ways to treat a damaged heart.

Scientists previously knew that the heart could draw energy from two carbohydrate sources at once: glucose, a sugar, and lactate, a substance produced when cells break down glucose. In most human tissues, increasing the use of one fuel makes it harder to use the other. Heart muscle somehow avoids this competition.

In a study published in Nature, researchers discovered that heart muscle cells process these fuels in separate parts of the cell. Glucose is broken down in the cytosol, the fluid that surrounds structures inside the cell, while lactate is used inside mitochondria, which produce much of the cell’s usable energy. Keeping these processes separate allows the heart to draw energy from both sources simultaneously.

The system depends on a molecule called MCT1, which transports lactate into the mitochondria. The researchers found that genetic mutations affecting MCT1 prevented lactate from entering the mitochondria and disrupted the heart’s energy balance. Although the heart could largely function without this pathway under everyday conditions, losing it when the heart was under stress led to heart failure.

“This appears to be a critical backup system for heart function,” says Gregory Ducker, PhD, assistant professor of biochemistry at University of Utah Health and senior author of the study. “In an emergency, we would really, really rely on this.”

The discovery identifies a previously unrecognized role for lactate in sustaining injured heart muscle and gives researchers a potential target for developing treatments that restore its energy supply.

“Our findings help point to new areas in which we could target the heart muscle to benefit and repair itself by allowing it to use lactate better,” Ducker says. “That’s the long-term goal: to help the heart muscle heal.”

Whether enhancing this energy pathway can improve heart function in patients remains to be established, though the researchers see potential applications beyond heart failure.

“Rather than simply releasing lactate into the bloodstream as a waste product, we may be able to enhance the heart’s ability to use it as a valuable source of energy,” says Stavros Drakos, MD, PhD, professor of medicine at University of Utah Health and co-senior author of the study. “By optimizing this process, we could potentially improve heart muscle function in patients suffering from heart failure or heart attacks.”

Reference: “MCT1-dependent mitochondrial lactate import sustains cardiac metabolism” by Ahmad A. Cluntun, Joseph R. Visker, Jesse N. Velasco-Silva, James Carrington, Luis Cedeño-Rosario, Giulia C. #6444. Nuclear Pathfinder Mission To Ceres Would Usher In Era Of Interplanetary Transport

The Dwarf Planet Ceres has long captivated astrobiologists with the tantalizing possibility that it holds the kind of rich chemistry that could have led to ancient microbial life. NASA's Dawn mission which orbited this Main Belt asteroid in 2015 found that Ceres was rife with subsurface water ice, ammonia, nitrogen, and hydrogen.

But a new proposal by two aerospace veterans would capitalize on Ceres's rich chemistry to set up humanity's first interplanetary transport node. That is, a base to use for refueling and as a jumping off point for destinations in the outer solar system or even beyond. The mission would at the same time tackle Ceresâ astrobiological mysteries.

For sixty years every deep-space mission weâve flown has been a one-off: each carries all its own fuel from Earth, heads out, and leaves nothing behind, astrophysicist Pete Worden, co-author of the project proposal, Chairman of the Breakthrough Prize Foundation, and Laureate Professor at the University of Arizona in Tucson, told me via email. We propose replacing this plodding, inefficient approach with a scalable transportation network, and putting its hub at the dwarf planet Ceres, Worden told me.

In a 2026 paper submitted to the Journal of the British Interplanetary Society, Worden and aerospace engineer Fred Kennedy note that their proposed Project CERES (Ceres-Earth Resource Exchange System) has both a lander and an orbiter. Arriving a little over a year after a proposed January 2037 launch, the spacecraft would use nuclear thermal propulsion to fly directly to the dwarf planet.

Project CERESâ first flight would be a Pathfinder mission that surveys Ceres, lands, extracts water and returns samples within five years. The Pathfinder itself is a Dawn-class orbiter plus a lander, a sample capsule and a new engine.

Nuclear Thermal Propulsion (NTP) is the key.

It replaces the combustion chamber of an ordinary rocket with a small fission reactor, says Kennedy. Liquid hydrogen is pumped through the hot reactor core, heated to around 2,700 degrees Kelvin, and expanded through a conventional nozzle, he says.

Because the exhaust is pure hydrogen, it leaves the nozzle at about twice the speed of the best chemical exhaust.

Thus, a trip to Ceres takes a year rather than a decade.

Nuclear thermal rockets operate at two to three times the efficiency of chemical rockets and can make the trip from Earth in a little over a year, says Worden.

Credit: AI image provided by Kennedy/Worden.

Project CERES combines NTP with in-situ production of water, hydrogen, oxygen and ammonia, Worden and Kennedy note in their paper.

A transport node earns its keep by selling propellant to vehicles that pass through, says Worden. That requires something to sell, which at Ceres is water --- burned directly as steam in a nuclear engine, or split into hydrogen and oxygen, or combined with local nitrogen into ammonia, he says.

The nuclear thermal transport technology is mature and ready to deploy.

The reactor physics is sixty years old and was proven on the ground, Aerospace engineer Fred Kennedy, co-author of the project paper; CEO of Dark Fission and former head of the Pentagonâs Space Development Agency, told me via email. Between 1959 and 1972, NASAâs Rover and NERVA programs ran more than twenty reactors and engines at full power in Nevada: an hour at a time at full thrust, with dozens of restarts, he says.

Heat from radioactive decay early in Ceresâ history drove a global subsurface ocean that left behind the hydrated clays, carbonates and ammoniated minerals, before it froze into the ice-rich crust we see today.

The Pathfinder would spend four to five months in orbit mapping volatiles, sounding the depth of the ice table, and choosing a landing site against Dawn's base map, says Kennedy. It then deploys a five metric ton lander to an ice-rich high-latitude site, extracts water from the ground as a demonstration, loads samples, and returns them to the orbiting vehicle, he says.

The vehicle then spends roughly twenty months in an extended survey, before departing in June 2040. The Ceres samples itâs carrying land on Earth in May 2041. They would arrive in a protective capsule, not unlike the Earth return capsule used in NASAâs 2004 Stardust mission to Comet Wild 2.

Credit: AI image provided by Kennedy/Worden.

The Ceres return spacecraft brakes into a cislunar orbit where it becomes available for its next sortie.

A vehicle that refuels at Ceres launches 60 percent less mass per round trip, and on that savings alone the node pays for itself within the life of its first fleet, says Worden.

Ceres also has the added plus of being further out in the solar system. Thus, the next destination is cheaper to reach than from Earth or the Moon. With only a fraction of Earthâs gravity, launching a mission from Ceresâ surface requires much less initial thrust.

What does Ceres offer that our Moon doesnât?

Water, nitrogen and carbon, says Worden; the Moon has essentially none of the last two.

Dawn found water ice at about ten percent by weight within the top meter of Ceresâ regolith at mid-to-high latitudes.

Dawn also found ammoniated clay minerals across the surface, carbonates and organic compounds, and sodium carbonate brine deposits in Ceresâ Occator crater, says Worden.

These are the ingredients for propellant (water, hydrogen, ammonia) and for life support (water, oxygen, nitrogen).

What stays at Ceres is the infrastructure, built up in phases, says Worden. First, thereâs a surface extraction plant and an orbital tank farm, then electrolysis and hydrogen liquefaction with its own power plant, then fabrication, he says.

Ceres' crust is ice-rich; its surface minerals formed in liquid water; and the bright deposits in Occator crater are sodium carbonate salts left by brines that reached the surface within the last few million years, says Worden. The Dawn team interprets this as coming from a deep reservoir of briny liquid that persists beneath the frozen crust, he says.

Whether that water ever hosted anything more than chemistry is a question the Pathfinder's samples can answer, says Worden.

#6443. Hidden Viruses in the Human Gut Offer New Clues to a Disorder Affecting Millions

Many gut viruses were found at lower levels in people with irritable bowel syndrome, offering new clues to a poorly understood condition that affects roughly one in ten people.

Scientists have identified more than 116,000 groups of viruses living in the human gut, over 99% of which had no close match in the largest existing catalog of gut viruses. These largely unexplored microbes could offer new clues to how the digestive system functions and why it changes in people with conditions such as irritable bowel syndrome (IBS).

Research into the gut microbiome has traditionally focused on bacteria, leaving much less understood about bacteriophages, viruses that infect bacteria. Scientists from King’s College London, Helmholtz Munich, and the University of Nottingham are now filling that gap with two studies published on November 17, 2026, in Nature Communications and Gut.

Professor Ana Valdes and Dr. Afroditi Kouraki from the University of Nottingham said, “For a long time the viral part of the gut microbiome has been a kind of dark matter: we knew it was there but couldn’t see it. Advances in sequencing and computational methods mean we can now start to map it properly, and this study shows just how much has been hidden.”

For the Nature Communications study, researchers analyzed genetic material from stool samples collected from more than 1,000 participants in TwinsUK, the largest twin registry in the United Kingdom. Using data on gut bacteria, health measurements, and diet, they examined how populations of viruses and bacteria varied together. Certain viruses were consistently more abundant alongside particular bacteria, while others showed the opposite pattern.

Dr. Panayiotis Louca, a research associate at King’s College London who led the study, said, “Gut viruses are difficult to study, so most of what we found simply isn’t in existing catalogs. What stands out is how closely they track with gut bacteria and with the chemicals those bacteria produce. We can’t yet say whether the viruses are driving that, and testing it is our next step.”

Studying twins also allowed researchers to estimate how much genetics and the environment shape the gut’s viral community. Genetic factors accounted for an estimated 47% of the variation in overall viral diversity, although most individual viral populations appeared to be influenced primarily by environmental factors.

The researchers also discovered a small group of viruses carrying genes linked to harmful bacterial behavior. These viruses were more commonly found alongside bacteria that can sometimes cause infections and less commonly alongside bacteria that break down dietary fiber.

Such relationships could be relevant to IBS, a condition that affects around 10% of the population and can significantly disrupt daily life. Its underlying causes remain poorly understood.

In the second study, published in Gut, researchers used TwinsUK data to identify 50 viral groups associated with IBS, most of which were less abundant in people with the condition. Relationships between bacteria and viruses also differed, with many viruses infecting bacteria previously linked to IBS. This suggests that the condition may involve changes across the wider microbial community rather than in bacteria alone.

Senior author Dr. Cristina Menni, who leads the metabolomics research group at the Department of Twin Research, Ageing and Genomic Epidemiology at King’s College London, said, “Our research highlights that to fully understand the gut microbiome and its links to health and disease, we need to look beyond bacteria and consider the viruses that live alongside them. We reveal a fascinating and largely unexplored dimension of the gut microbiome—discovering that viruses are not only closely associated with bacterial communities, but also with the metabolites that connect the microbiome to our health. This opens exciting new avenues for understanding how the gut ecosystem works.”

Future research will examine whether gut viruses actively influence bacterial metabolism and how these interactions change in health and disease. Understanding these relationships could eventually help researchers develop better biological markers and treatments for IBS, as well as more personalized approaches to gut health.

Dr. Louca added: “The study is observational, so it cannot show that the viruses cause these effects, but it provides greater understanding of a largely unexplored area of the human gut. It would also be beneficial to replicate the study on a more diverse cohort, as participants were mostly older women of European ancestry.”

#6442. BepiColombo Captures Mercury Orbit After 8-Year Trip

The planet Mercury might be one of the least explored planetary bodies in the solar system, but its is arguably the most crucial in helping scientists better understand the formation and evolution of the inner solar system. Its position as the closest planet to the Sun makes it a prime target for how the rocky planets formed and evolved and what this could mean for finding life beyond Earth. However, just traveling to Mercury is a lengthy and time-consuming effort, often taking a spacecraft several years just to achieve orbit. More on that later.

Now, the lauded joint mission between the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) called BepiColombo might have just become the second mission to orbit Mercury. This is because mission leaders recently announced that BepiColombo successfully achieved Mercury orbit insertion (MOI) on November 21 at 18:27 UTC (1:27 pm EST/10:27 am PST). This historic achievement comes 8 years, 1 month, and 1 day since BepiColombo launched on October 20, 2018, and included one Earth flyby, two Venus flybys, and six mercury flybys to achieve orbit just a few days ago.

While MOI is essential for achieving Mercurian orbit, it is not the final orbit BepiColombo will achieve to conduct science operations, which are expected to commence in April 2027. Over the next several months, the team will fire the spacecraftâs thrusters several times to adjust its orbit to achieve a more permanent orbit. The first science operations phase is slated to run from April 2027 to April 2028 with a potential extended mission from April 2028 to December 2029. If the mission is extended until December 2029, the team will then assess the spacecraftâs remaining fuel and determine if continued science operations can be achieved or if it will crash into Mercuryâs surface.

âOur almost 600-strong science team will be delighted to see BepiColombo pass this key milestone and begin revealing more about Mercury, from its interior and surface to the space around it,â said Dr. Geraint Jones, who is the Lead Project Scientist for ESAâs BepiColombo and was previously was a Professor of Planetary Science and Head of the Planetary Science Group at University College London's Mullard Space Science Laboratory (UK).

As noted, BepiColombo just became the second mission to successfully orbit Mercury, with the first being NASAâs MESSENGER (MErcury Surface, Space ENvironment, GEochemistry, and Ranging) spacecraft, which orbited Mercury from March 2011 to April 2015 after initial estimates put the science phase of the mission lasting only one year. During this time, MESSENGER completed more than 4,100 orbits around the innermost planet to the Sun while obtaining almost 300,000 images of the entire Mercurian surface before its fuel was exhausted. Once this happened, the mission team intentionally crashed MESSENGER into the planetâs far side with the team confirming a loss of signal when the spacecraft was scheduled to emerge from the far side.

Unlike MESSENGER, BepiColombo consists of two orbiters, ESAâs Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and JAXAâs Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter ("Mio"), which are currently attached but are slated to separate in early December 2026. Once this happens, MPO will be tasked with studying Mercury surface features and composition while Mio will study Mercuryâs magnetic field and how it interacts with the solar wind.

As noted earlier, traveling to Mercury is a lengthy and time-consuming effort. This is because as an object travels closer to the Sun, our starâs immense gravity becomes greater, thus increasing the speed of the object. In the case of a spacecraft, this means it has to slow down enough to enter orbit around Mercury. However, this would require an insane amount of fuel, which adds weight to the spacecraft, and the financial and logistical costs spiral from there. This is why spacecraft like BepiColombo and MESSENGER conducted several planetary flybys to slow down, with MESSENGER performing three less mercury flybys compared to BepiColomboâs six Mercury flybys.

What new insights about Mercury will BepiColombo teach scientists in the coming years and decades? Only time will tell, and this is why we science!
