#6441. Semiconductor Breakthrough Cracks a Longstanding Solar Energy Problem

An unusual material could help us make better use of the sun’s energy, offering new possibilities for more efficient solar power and fuel production.

Generating more electricity from sunlight does not necessarily mean installing more solar panels. Finding ways to extract more energy from the light that already reaches them could make solar power a more practical source of electricity. Part of the challenge lies in what happens inside a solar cell in the moments after it absorbs sunlight.

Solar cells contain materials called semiconductors, which use the energy from sunlight to free negatively charged electrons, leaving behind positively charged gaps known as holes. Both charges must be collected to generate electricity. If an electron and a hole meet and cancel each other out, a process known as recombination, the energy they carry is lost. Unfortunately, materials that are particularly good at absorbing sunlight also tend to lose these charges more quickly.

A study led by the University of Oxford has identified a promising exception in a semiconductor called bismuth sulfide. Published October 28, 2026, in Nature, the research examined how the material’s unusual electronic structure could help overcome this longstanding limitation in solar energy technology.

To investigate how long electrical charges survive in bismuth sulfide, the researchers exposed thin films of the material to extremely short laser pulses. They then tracked how quickly the charges disappeared using a technique called ultrafast terahertz spectroscopy, conducting measurements at temperatures ranging from room temperature to just above absolute zero.

“One of the longstanding challenges in developing efficient solar-energy materials is that the properties which make a semiconductor very good at absorbing sunlight also tend to make the resulting electrical charges disappear quickly,” said corresponding author Professor Laura Herz (Department of Physics, University of Oxford). “Our work shows that this trade-off is not inevitable. By uncovering how an unusual electronic structure can combine strong light absorption with much slower recombination, we have identified a new principle for designing semiconductors that could help us harvest solar energy more efficiently.”

Electronic structure calculations by Professor Marina Filip’s group in Oxford’s Department of Physics helped explain why bismuth sulfide behaves differently. The material has two closely spaced routes through which electrons can move between energy levels. One allows the material to absorb light strongly, while the other sits at a slightly lower energy and allows charges to disappear much more slowly. Because the two are so close together, charges spend much of their time in the lower-energy states, which effectively serve as a temporary storage reservoir.

Cooling the material provided further evidence for this explanation. In most semiconductors, electrical charges disappear faster as temperatures drop. In bismuth sulfide, more charges settled into the reservoir as the material cooled, allowing them to survive longer. The results matched the team’s model of what physicists call a pseudo-direct semiconductor.

Even at room temperature, the researchers estimate that this arrangement reduces the rate of charge loss by about 75% compared with conventional semiconductors that absorb light equally well.

Giving electrical charges more time to be collected could improve the efficiency of solar panels without compromising their ability to capture sunlight. The benefits could also extend beyond electricity generation. Longer-lived charges could provide more time for the chemical reactions needed to produce fuels using sunlight.

“What makes this discovery particularly exciting is that we are not simply improving an existing semiconductor property but identifying a different way in which semiconductors can behave,” said Professor Herz. “Understanding this mechanism gives us a roadmap for discovering and potentially engineering other materials with similarly advantageous properties.”

The team’s calculations suggest that researchers could search existing materials databases for semiconductors with similar properties or engineer new ones. However, the study demonstrates the underlying physical mechanism rather than the performance of a finished solar cell. Further research will be needed to determine how these properties can be put to use in solar energy technologies.

Reference: “Delayed electron–hole recombination in a pseudo-direct semiconductor” by Marcello Righetto, Debalina Banerjee, Zhenglin Jia, Joshua R. S. Lilly, Vincent J. -Y. Lim, Snigdha Lal, Siyu Yan, Jae Eun Lee, Jay B. Patel, Michael B. Johnston, Qianqian Lin, Marina R. Filip and Laura M. Herz, 28 October 2026, Nature. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11223-x

Wolves howl for a variety of reasons. But none of them are triggered by the sight of the moon.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Wolves can bark, whimper, yip, squeak and growl, but they are most known for their iconic howl.

The eerie sound can travel vast distances and, if heard by other wolves, get them to join in with the chorus. But why do wolves howl in the first place?

Experts told Live Science that the behavior is triggered not by the sight of the moon, as is commonly believed, but by the need to maintain a complex social network.

Wolves can howl by themselves and in groups. "If a lone wolf howls, it's probably because they're separated from their pack and want to regain contact," Arik Kershenbaum, a zoologist at the University of Cambridge, told Live Science. "Members of a pack can become quite dispersed, and when they need to hunt together, or to care for pups, or when their territory is being threatened by other wolves, they need a way of returning to each other."

However, lone wolves that leave their packs may howl as well. This could be "a way of finding a new pack or mate to join," Kershenbaum said.

When a wolf pack howls together, they are sometimes advertising their territory to deter other packs. "Data shows that packs howl more in the center of their territory; they howl more when there are pups around and also when they have a carcass from a hunt," Tamás Faragó, an ethologist and bioacoustician at Eötvös Loránd University in Budapest, Hungary, told Live Science. "So group howling can have a repellent effect on neighboring packs."

However, "most chorus howling is social — that is, they howl together to build what is technically called social cohesion," Kershenbaum said, "because it makes them feel good to be safe and surrounded by their pack mates. Faragó noted that this kind of group howling gets a pack in the same mood, "and is quite common before going out on a hunt."

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

Howling can trigger more howling. "When an individual wolf hears a howl, it has a very strong tendency to reply back," Faragó said. However, "if a lone wolf is accidentally wandering into the territory of its neighbors, and they hear the pack there howling, they won't respond. That would make it obvious that it's an intruder there."

A wolf's howl can be heard up to 10 miles (16 kilometers) away in open terrain, according to the Wolf Conservation Center in South Salem, New York. The combination of low- and high-frequency sounds that make up howls ensures that "even if some of the lower-frequency sounds are attenuated by vegetation, the higher-frequency components can remain intact and carry a lot of information about the individuals that made the howls," Faragó said.

Wolf pups make their first high-pitched attempts at howling between 2 to 4 weeks old.

Wolf howls differ among species and subspecies. A 2016 study of 13 species and subspecies of wolves, jackals, coyotes and dogs by Kershenbaum and his colleagues found that each has a kind of howling dialect that features different types of howls with varying regularity depending on the species or subspecies. For example, the howling repertoire of the timber wolf (Canis lycaon) is dominated by low, flat howls, while red wolves (Canis rufus) most frequently use high, looping howls.

The howling of dogs, which are descended from gray wolves (Canis lupus), can differ from wolf howling, but this depends very much on the breed. A 2023 study from Kershenbaum, Faragó and their colleagues found that more ancient dog breeds that are more closely related to wolves howl more often. In contrast, more modern dog breeds bark more often.

A question "that we all want to answer" is whether howling sounds might differ depending on their purpose, Kershenbaum said. "The problem is that most of the time when wolves howl, we don't know what they're doing at that time — they're either too far away, or it's nighttime."

Generally, "we believe that howls made in different emotional states probably sound different," Kershenbaum said. "For example, perhaps when a wolf is feeling threatened in a territorial conflict, the howl goes up and down in pitch in a different way than when the wolf is relaxed. But this is a field of active research."

A common belief is that wolves howl at the moon. "A myth, I'm afraid," Kershenbaum said. "There doesn't seem to be any correlation at all between them." He suggested that perhaps before electric lights, people were outdoors more often when there was a bright moon, "and that's when they heard the wolves."

#6439. Threats to broadcasters hang over FCC nominee hearing

FCC nominee Danielle Thumann Severs waits to testify during her confirmation hearing with the Senate Commerce Committee on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

President Donald Trump's Republican nominee to the Federal Communications Commission faced opposition Tuesday from Senate Democrats who fear the commission could be controlled exclusively by Republicans under Chairman Brendan Carr, who they vowed to investigate in the next Congress.

Appearing before the Senate Commerce Committee, nominee Danielle Thumann Severs limited her commitments to independence from Carr, including on regulating broadcasters based on their content decisions.

Much of the hearing focused on Carr and his threats to use the FCC to punish broadcasters he disagrees with.

Sen. Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M., said that he expects Carr will not last long in his position once Democrats take control of Congress in the new year.

“Mr. Carr, if you're listening now, know you're going to be in this body once a month, if not more, and in the House of Representatives as well, answering questions … so we can get to the bottom of the nonsense and the cover-ups that have been taking place,” Luján said.

The nomination of Thumann Severs, who currently serves as senior counsel to Carr, has led to consternation among Democrats due to continued vacancies at the FCC. The five-member commission is intended to have three members of the president’s party, including the chair, and two in the minority.

Currently Carr serves alongside fellow Republican Olivia Trusty and Democrat Anna M. Gomez, whose term expired earlier this year. Gomez may continue to serve through next year under the law if a replacement is not nominated and confirmed.

Democrats are concerned that if Thumann Severs were to be confirmed, the commission’s three Republican members could constitute a quorum on their own, allowing Trump to fire Gomez.

Sen. John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., said Senate precedent is to move pairs of one Democratic and one Republican nominee for the FCC and that he “strongly” believed the Thumann Severs nomination should have been paired with a renomination of Gomez in order to continue having “both parties at the table.”

“A bipartisan FCC is essential to avoid things like large-scale media consolidation [and] I think also, more fundamentally, to protect a free and diverse press [that] serves everyone,” Hickenlooper said.

In addition to urging Trump to renominate Gomez, Democrats underlined the need for a second Democratic member of the commission.

Hickenlooper highlighted Thumann Severs’ close work with Carr, who Democrats and some Republicans have been critical of for comments about using the FCC’s public interest standard against television stations airing programming Carr disagrees with.

Thumann Severs’ work at the FCC currently focuses on the Wireline, Public Safety and Homeland Security, and Consumer and Governmental Affairs bureaus, rather than the Media Bureau.

Committee Chair Ted Cruz, R-Texas, has also been critical of Carr’s comments. On Tuesday, he listed the FCC’s request for ABC-owned stations to submit early license renewals alongside earlier incidents in which he said Democrats encouraged the weaponization of the FCC against conservative voices.

“The First Amendment places important limits on the government’s ability to regulate speech,” Cruz said. “The FCC possesses significant regulatory authority over communications, so there is always a risk that it could weaponize its authority against Americans with whom it disagrees.”

Thumann Severs committed to Cruz that she would base licensing decisions on “the law and the record” and not use the FCC’s authority to “pressure or punish” broadcasters for protected speech.

However, when Sen. Edward J. Markey, D-Mass., questioned Thumann Severs on whether the FCC could punish broadcasters the president disagreed with, Thumann Severs repeated one of Carr’s arguments in discussing the FCC’s role.

“Broadcasters are subject to public interest obligations as part of the public trustee model in exchange for the licenses that they hold,” she said. “As part of those public interest obligations, they are subject to many different rules and requirements, and the FCC is charged with enforcing and investigating the public interest standard against broadcasters.”

Under repeated questions from Markey about Carr’s previous remarks, Thumann Severs said she would base her decisions “in the facts and the law and the record.”

Luján also asked Thumann Severs to name issues where she had disagreed with Carr or Trump. While she said her decisions would be her own, she declined to name any examples of disagreement.

In addition to questions about Carr, Democrats asked the nominee about the FCC’s E-Rate program, which provides low-cost connectivity for schools and libraries, and the Universal Service Fund, which funds the E-Rate program and other programs.

Thumann Severs said that she believes the E-Rate program has been successful and that the FCC has a statutory obligation to provide some kind of discounted service to schools and libraries. But she was less forthcoming on whether the FCC could shut down the program as it currently exists without congressional approval or whether the program should be restricted only to rural areas.

Late last month, Democratic members of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, led by Communications and Technology Subcommittee ranking member Doris Matsui, D-Calif., sent a letter to Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., and Cruz urging Gomez’s renomination with any move to confirm a Republican nominee.

“Commissioner Gomez has shown the experience and judgment to continue that work,” the members wrote. “We therefore ask that the Senate pair any new Republican nominee with her renomination to a full term, consistent with the bipartisan design Congress built into this agency.”

On Monday, the Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights also sent a letter to committee leadership urging a delay on the hearing and any vote on Thumann Severs’ nomination until Gomez can be renominated.

“Independent agencies should not be extensions of presidential will: their leaders should exercise independent judgement based on their expertise and statutory mandates,” the group wrote.

Cruz did not indicate Tuesday when the committee might vote on Thumann Severs’ nomination, and no markup has yet been announced by the committee of hers' and those of three others for two posts at NASA and one at the Transportation Department who also testified.

#6438. Physicists Discover a Strange New Form of Magnetism in a Simple Metal

Electronics can use more than electrical charge, and evidence of unusual magnetism in europium silicide could help researchers explore how to put electron spin to work.

At very low temperatures, a simple metal made from europium and silicon develops a spiral pattern of magnetism that leaves it with no overall magnetization. Its electrons nevertheless appear to favor opposite spin orientations when they travel in opposite directions, an unusual relationship that could offer researchers new ways to explore and control electronic behavior.

An international team has found compelling evidence for this state, called p-wave magnetism, in europium silicide, or EuSi. The findings, published in Nature, provide an experimental foothold in a field where suitable materials have been difficult to find.

Spin is a quantum property that gives electrons a magnetic character, somewhat like tiny compass needles. In a conventional ferromagnet, spins tend to align in the same direction, producing net magnetization. In EuSi, between approximately 33 and 62 kelvin, or about −400 to −348 °F, the magnetic moments of europium atoms instead form an ordered spiral. The individual moments are substantial, but their contributions cancel overall.

The predicted relationship between opposite directions of electron motion and opposite spin polarizations is known as an odd-parity spin texture. Finding a material in which researchers can investigate it has been challenging. Previous candidates include electrical insulators and metals that develop magnetic order only at very low temperatures or have additional symmetry complications. EuSi combines a fixed chemical composition with a spiral magnetic phase that has the required symmetry, and researchers can grow high-quality single crystals for experiments.

Dr. Erjian Cheng grew those crystals approximately three years ago at the Max Planck Institute for Chemical Physics of Solids (MPI CPfS) in Dresden. Initial photoemission experiments, which use light to eject electrons and examine their properties, showed that magnetism had an unusually large influence on EuSi’s electronic band structure, the pattern of energies electrons can occupy inside the material. That raised the possibility that its magnetic order might link spin to the direction of electron motion.

The investigation brought together 38 researchers from 19 institutions, including ShanghaiTech University, the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, the Max Planck Institute for the Physics of Complex Systems, and Oak Ridge National Laboratory.

Combining theoretical calculations with several experimental techniques, the researchers examined both the atomic magnetic arrangement and its effects on electrons. Neutron diffraction revealed the spiral of europium magnetic moments and confirmed that its symmetry met the conditions for p-wave magnetism. Angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, which maps electron energies and momenta, showed that magnetism substantially reshaped the electronic structure, producing energy separations exceeding 100 millielectronvolts.

Measurements that also resolved electron spin supplied a more specific test. The spin polarization changed sign across successive magnetic Brillouin zones, repeating regions in a map of electron momentum defined by the magnetic order. It also weakened sharply near regions where the predicted p-wave spin texture should vanish. Together, these observations provided spectroscopic evidence consistent with the theoretical state.

“When we first measured the electronic structure of EuSi, we were surprised by the exceptionally large effect of magnetism on the electrons,” explains Cheng. “That observation led us to investigate whether this simple compound could host a much more unusual magnetic state. The combination of crystal growth, neutron scattering and spin-resolved spectroscopy now provides compelling evidence for p-wave magnetism.”

The proposed spin pattern arises predominantly from magnetic exchange interactions, which influence how spins arrange themselves, and from the symmetry of the magnetic spiral. That distinguishes it from familiar spin-splitting effects driven mainly by spin-orbit coupling, an interaction between an electron’s spin and its motion.

The spiral also introduces handedness, or chirality. EuSi’s underlying crystal structure is centrosymmetric, meaning that it looks the same when inverted through its center. Its magnetic spiral, however, can twist in either of two opposite senses. Using magnetic force microscopy and spatially resolved photoemission spectroscopy, the researchers identified magnetic domains approximately ten micrometers across.

When examined with circularly polarized light, domains with opposite magnetic handedness showed distinct electronic responses. The results demonstrated that the spiral’s handedness is coupled to the electronic structure, connecting the organization of the atomic magnetic moments with the behavior of the electrons.

“What makes EuSi particularly exciting is that an unconventional electronic spin structure emerges from the magnetic order of a chemically simple metal,” says Prof. Claudia Felser, Director at MPI CPfS. “This demonstrates how the discovery of new materials can reveal entirely new electronic phenomena. EuSi now gives us an experimental platform to investigate how magnetic symmetry and chirality can be used to control electronic properties, with potential implications for future spintronics and unconventional superconductivity.”

Spintronics uses electron spin as well as electrical charge in electronic devices. The findings could inform that field, along with research on topological quantum materials and unconventional superconductivity. They also illustrate how a solid’s properties depend on its magnetic order and electronic quantum states, alongside its chemical composition and crystal structure.

Reference: “Evidence for p-wave magnetism in electronic band structure of metallic EuSi” by Erjian Cheng, Yixing Yang, Yifan Gao, Jan Priessnitz, Yiqing Hao, Jieyi Liu, Rui Lou, Alexander Fedorov, Mengyu Yao, Yuri Prots, Houke Chen, Ralf Koban, Xuemin Shi, Ying-Ting Chan, Ulrich Burkhardt, Berit H. Goodge, Walter Schnelle, Vicky Hasse, Jaafar Ansari, Zhuocheng Lu, Peter Bencok, Gerrit van der Laan, Makoto Hashimoto, Donghui Lu, Jacek Osiecki, Zhanfeng Liu, Shengtao Cui, Jaime Sánchez-Barriga, Oliver Rader, Yulin Chen, Hua Wang, Jiadong Zang, Leila Noohinejad, Weida Wu, Libor Šmejkal, Junwei Liu, Zhongkai Liu and Claudia Felser, 18 November 2026, Nature. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11295-9

This work was financially supported by the European Union through EXQIRAL (number 101131579), the Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft (DFG, German Research Foundation) through SFB 1143 (project ID 24731007), the research unit QUAntitative Spatio-Temporal model-building for correlated electronic matter (QUAST, project ID FOR 5249), and the Würzburg-Dresden Cluster of Excellence ctd.qmat – Complexity, Topology and Dynamics in Quantum Matter (EXC 2147, project-id 390858490).

Einstein’s late-in-life questioning of the incompleteness of quantum mechanics, and his insistence on local realism, stemmed precisely from his acute perception of the existence of this “ocean.” The FAST/TVT theory is exactly what provides a true home for Einstein’s intuition through intuitive geometric reality.

Einstein’s sorrowful silhouette has faded into the distance. But his intuition, his persistence, his belief in “local realism”, has finally found its rightful home in the framework of Topological Vortex Theory (TVT). Einstein was not a failed prophet, but a true physicist misunderstood by his era.

#6437. Benchmade Just Knocked 20% Off Three of Its Most Popular Knives for Black Friday

Yes, that includes the Osborne and the Bugout.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

We’re constantly testing and writing about pocket knives here at Popular Mechanics, and Benchmade is a brand that always tops our list of favorites. Its folders, automatics, flippers, and fixed blades are beautifully designed using all high-quality materials, and all are U.S.-made in its Oregon headquarters. But there’s no denying they’re pricey, costing upward of $200, and they rarely go on sale for much of a discount.

But right now, ahead of Black Friday, Benchmade is knocking 20 percent off three of its most popular knives on Amazon—the Osborne, the Bugout, and the Bailout—for a savings of roughly $70 each.

When the Osborne debuted in 2000, it was Benchmade’s first blade to sport the Axis lock, which been replicated in some form by nearly every major knife manufacturer since its patent expired in 2019. It’s designed for ambidextrous operation and fast, one-handed deployment, plus it keeps your fingers clear of the blade while you open and close the knife.

This seasonal version uses CPM-S90V stainless super steel, which offers great edge retention and reliable toughness for everyday tasks like opening boxes. It’s coated with a protective distressed finish to make the reverse tanto-style blade look rustic and has a rich-looking dark-green aluminum handle, with copper accents. It feels good in hand—a durable yet lightweight EDC knife.

The Bugout is the knife our resident expert Justin Park grabs first for backpacking, camping and hunting and says it’s “arguably the defining pocket knife of the explosion of modern EDC blades.” It’s strong, but ultra lightweight and hardly registers in your pocket or pack.

Like the Osborne above, the Bugout uses S90V stainless super steel, featuring a shorter drop-point blade, copper accents, and handle that combines the same dark-green aluminum with a grippy and rugged-looking canvas micarta.

The Bailout is lightweight and tough. It has a longer drop-point tanto-style S90V stainless steel blade covered in the same stonewashed protective finish as the Bugout and Osborne, along with the same dark-green aluminum handle and copper accents. While it’s another great choice for EDC, the Bailout is outfitted with tactical-style elements, like the lanyard slot at the rear and the deep-carry clip.

#6436. Mathematicians Find a Brilliant Shortcut to a 174-Year-Old Math Puzzle

A faster way to color maps using only four colors has revealed hidden mathematical patterns that could help solve puzzles involving far more complex shapes.

In 1852, English mathematician Francis Guthrie noticed something curious while drawing a map of England’s counties. He needed only four colors to ensure that no two neighboring counties shared the same color. Could the same be true of every flat map, regardless of how complicated its borders were?

What seemed like a simple observation became one of the most famous problems in mathematics. It took 124 years to prove Guthrie right and another half century to discover the most efficient way to assign those four colors. In solving the latter problem, an international team of mathematicians has uncovered something previously unknown about the mathematical structures underlying maps.

The history of the Four Color Problem is filled with frustrated attempts. A proof presented in 1879 stood for 11 years before an error was discovered. When mathematicians finally succeeded in 1976, their proof was controversial because it relied heavily on computer calculations that were difficult for others to verify. A more accessible proof followed in 1997, although finding a suitable coloring for large maps remained computationally demanding.

“The previous proofs showed that it is always possible to color a map using four colors. But they are not very good at actually finding the colors for each individual region on a map. The new algorithm is efficient and provides a much faster way of coloring,” says Professor Mikkel Thorup from the Department of Computer Science at the University of Copenhagen.

The achievement marks the first major breakthrough on the problem in nearly 30 years. The first part of the research paper was presented at FOCS’26, one of the world’s leading conferences in theoretical computer science, where it received the Best Paper Award.

Mathematicians can represent a flat map using what is known as a planar graph. Imagine replacing each country or county with a dot and drawing lines between those that share a border. The challenge then becomes assigning colors to the dots so that no two connected dots have the same color.

Within these graphs are small arrangements called reducible configurations, which allow mathematicians to simplify the coloring problem. The researchers discovered that graphs contain far more of these useful arrangements than anyone previously realized.

“Think of reducible configurations as handles you can grab hold on to start four coloring. We show that graphs do not contain just one handle, but an astonishing number of them. Nobody knew that before,” says Professor and co-author Carsten Thomassen from DTU.

Where earlier methods could often identify only one suitable starting point, the researchers can now work from many different parts of a graph. The advantage becomes particularly pronounced as maps grow larger.

“We have gone from what mathematicians call quadratic time to linear time. This means that if a map contains ten times as many regions, the computation only becomes about ten times slower. With the previous algorithm, it would have become about 100 times slower,” explains Carsten Thomassen.

Finding this solution occupied Thorup and his colleagues, including Thomassen, Ken-ichi Kawarabayashi, and Bojan Mohar, for around a decade. Thorup has a name for the peculiar fascination that has kept mathematicians returning to the problem for 174 years: “the four-color disease.”

“The disease is believing that there must be a simple proof for such a simple statement. I would guess that at least 1,000 mathematicians have caught the four-color disease, spending months trying to make it work but never quite succeeding. It is the disease people have suffered from since 1852.”

Thorup is equally candid about the appeal of devoting years to an apparently modest mathematical puzzle.

“Because mathematicians are slightly crazy. Most of what mathematicians work on consists of very nerdy questions. We become obsessed with this type of problem because it challenges the human intellect. And if we find the answer, we’ll probably also find answers to other mathematical puzzles,” says Mikkel Thorup.

That possibility is already emerging from the team’s work. The abundance of reducible configurations could help mathematicians investigate more complex graphs and surfaces whose geometry differs considerably from that of an ordinary map.

“The remarkable thing is that because there are so many handles, the idea can also be applied to other kinds of surfaces besides a flat map. For example, surfaces with holes, such as a swim ring or a piece of Emmental cheese. That is why we believe the result could have significance far beyond the Four Color Theorem,” says Mikkel Thorup.

Reference: “The Four Color Theorem with Linearly Many Reducible Configurations and Near-Linear Time Coloring” by Yuta Inoue, Ken-ichi Kawarabayashi, Atsuyuki Miyashita, Bojan Mohar, Carsten Thomassen and Mikkel Thorup, September 30, 2026, arXiv. DOI: 2603.24880

A new positioning technology could make autonomous vehicles and robotaxis more reliable at recharging themselves.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Researchers in Japan have developed a new technology that could enable electric vehicles (EVs) to charge "simply by parking".

Wireless charging is still relatively nascent in the EV market, but scientists hope that integrating more wireless charging devices into roads and parking spaces will move the EV industry away from bulky plug-in infrastructure. It uses the same wireless power transfer technology found in modern smartphones and consumer electronics: a transmitter coil inside in a ground pad generates an oscillating magnetic field, which induces an electric current in a receiver coil underneath the vehicle. This current recharges the EV's battery cells.

However, small misalignments between the two coils can affect how quickly and efficiently the battery recharges. This new system uses short-range radio signals to determine the position of the vehicle's magnetic charging coil relative to the charging device in the ground, including its distance and angle. This helps the EV and its driver get into the optimal position for efficient charging.

The technology could be particularly useful for driverless "robotaxis" and other autonomous vehicles that need to be able to recharge quickly and efficiently without human assistance, the researchers said. They detailed their findings in a study published Aug. 26 in the IEEE Open Journal of Vehicular Technology.

"We hope this research will lead to a future where EVs charge simply by parking, much like smartphones placed on wireless chargers," Ryotaro Hada, first author of the study and a master's student at the University of Osaka's Graduate School of Information Science and Technology, said in a statement.

Existing methods for aligning an EV's charging coil with a wireless charging pad use magnetic sensors or cameras. Magnetic systems work best when the coil is close to the pad, while cameras can struggle in rain, poor lighting or when dirt obscures the pad, the researchers explained.

This new system uses four ultra-wideband radio devices mounted around the vehicle's charging coil to communicate with four antennas around the charging pad.

By measuring how long radio waves take to travel between the ultra-wideband devices and the antennas, as well as detecting tiny differences in how the signals arrive at each of the vehicle's sensors, the system can pinpoint the position and angle of the EV's charging coil relative to the ground pad.

The same technology is used in some digital car keys. They use short radio pulses to detect when the driver is close by, allowing the driver to unlock their vehicle without requiring a physical key.

In laboratory experiments using a scaled-down vehicle model, the system worked out where the vehicle's charging coil was to within 0.09 inches (2.32 millimeters) of its actual position and which direction it was facing to within 0.25 degrees. Correcting for distortions in the radio signals reduced the positioning error by around fivefold, the team said.

The researchers noted that the system still needs to be tested outdoors, on full-size EVs and under real charging conditions.

Owen Hughes is a freelance writer and editor specializing in data and digital technologies. Previously a senior editor at ZDNET, Owen has been writing about tech for more than a decade, during which time he has covered everything from AI, cybersecurity and supercomputers to programming languages and public sector IT. Owen is particularly interested in the intersection of technology, life and work ­– in his previous roles at ZDNET and TechRepublic, he wrote extensively about business leadership, digital transformation and the evolving dynamics of remote work.

#6433. Why Some Farts Can Clear a Room While Others Barely Smell

A microbiologist reveals the surprising gut chemistry behind room-clearing farts, why some stink more than others, and how their terrible smell may serve a useful purpose.

A healthy person farts about 14 to 20 times each day. Altogether, that’s enough gas to fill a super stinky party balloon.

Farts are made of gases that are produced by trillions of tiny organisms called microbes, mostly bacteria, that live in your gut. These organisms have an important job: They help chew up food that your stomach cannot break down on its own. In the process, they act like mini chemical factories that provide you with nutrients while releasing waste gases into your gut. These gases mix with air you swallow and other gases that you make during digestion. After passing through the intestines, they come out in bursts as farts.

As a microbiologist, I study communities of bacteria, called microbiomes, in various regions of the human body. The microbiome in your gut plays an important role in your health. Producing gases is a sign that bacteria in the gut microbiome are doing their job properly. Farting also relieves pressure in your belly and prevents painful bloating and cramping.

So you might wonder: Why does a normal and healthy body process cause such a bad stink?

Farts are mostly made up of the same odorless gases found in the air we breathe.

Anywhere from 20% to 90% of a fart’s volume consists of nitrogen, which makes up more than three-quarters of air. Up to 10% of a fart is oxygen, which humans need in order to breathe. Up to 30% is carbon dioxide, up to 50% is hydrogen, and up to 10% is methane. Microbes produce most of the carbon dioxide, hydrogen, and methane, though some of the carbon dioxide is made when digestive juices mix with stomach acid.

But wait: These are not the gases that give farts their delightful array of aromas. What makes farts so malodorous is other gas molecules that contain the element sulfur. Pure sulfur has no smell on its own, but when combined with other elements it makes molecules that reek.

One key culprit is hydrogen sulfide, which is famous for smelling like rotten eggs. Others include methanethiol, which has a bouquet of cabbage, sewage or skunk spray, and dimethyl sulfide, which hits the nostrils with scents of cooked corn, algae or seafood.

Only tiny amounts are required: One molecule of hydrogen sulfide among 1 million other gas molecules has enough power to do the job. That’s equivalent to one kernel of corn in a truckload of about 1,250 ears, or 10 bricks out of all the bricks that make up the Empire State Building in New York City. Other sulfur-containing gasses can be sniffed out at even more minuscule amounts.

Your farts’ aroma depends on what your microbiome gets to eat.

The main thing that determines which gases and how much of them are in your farts is what food your gut microbiome gets to eat.

Some types of foods often referred to as junk food, including candy or diet foods containing artificial sweeteners or syrups, can change the way microbes digest food. High-fiber foods such as beans and grains also have this effect. These foods can cause your body to produce more farts that often are bigger and louder.

However, the loudest fart is not always the stinkiest one. It’s the ones that contain sulfur that pack a smelly punch.

Food is a key source of amino acids, nutrients that build proteins the body needs to function and grow. Two amino acids, methionine and cysteine, contain sulfur, and they are plentiful in meat, dairy, eggs, and to a lesser degree, beans and grains. Some foods – most notably, vegetables such as cabbage, broccoli, Brussels sprouts and cauliflower – contain other molecules that also have sulfur in them.

When you eat sulfur-rich foods, your gut microbes digest them to produce sulfur-containing gases. That can lead to some putrid farts, with the precise smell tuned to your diet – as well as your overall health. In fact, persistent foul-smelling gas can be a sign of illness, such as irritable bowel syndrome or food intolerance or sensitivity, which you might need to see a doctor about.

As you might know from experience, it’s impossible to hold in a fart until it goes away. It will come out somehow – sometimes at speeds up to 10 feet per second, according to back-of-the-envelope estimates, including my own. This rush of gas exiting the body makes the surrounding tissue vibrate, often causing an embarrassing noise.

Farting has been the butt of jokes for millennia. According to the Guinness Book of World Records, the oldest joke ever written down was a popular proverb dating back about 3,900 years that warned new husbands about their wives’ farts. The popularity of fart jokes remains strong. In the 2010 movie “Despicable Me,” for example, mad tech wizard Dr. Nefario mishears his boss’s demand for a dart gun, instead creating a fart gun, or Fart Blaster, that’s now a real-life popular toy.

But sometimes this natural body process can be a real bummer – like on an airplane. Cabin pressure in flight is often lower than normal air pressure on the ground, which can cause the gas in your gut to expand, spurring more farts. To protect the noses of travelers trapped together in the friendly skies, researchers designed seat cushions and blankets that contain sulfur-absorbing substances, such as activated charcoal. So far, no airlines have adopted these funk-reducing technologies, but you can buy them yourself.

Despite farts’ assault on the senses, your ability to detect them means your nose is doing exactly what evolution designed it to do: act as a chemical sensor for sulfur-containing gases. People can detect hydrogen sulfide and methanethiol at minuscule concentrations, even when there is less than one molecule of these compounds amid billions of other molecules.

These smells can signal the presence of rotting substances and bacterial activity that might harbor pathogens that can make you sick, or deadly environments such as swamps, stagnant caves, and volcanic vents that can suffocate and kill you.

So the next time you lay a fart that’s pungent enough to clear the room, don’t apologize – just say you’re conducting a live demonstration of natural chemistry that took eons of evolution to perfect.

Written by Brenda A. Wilson, Professor of Microbiology, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign.

Adapted from an article originally published in The Conversation.

#6432. Rift grows among Senate Democrats over who will lead in majority

Sens. Bernie Sanders and Elissa Slotkin hold a news conference calling for a “bold direction” for Senate Democrats on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

More Democrats emerged Tuesday wanting someone besides Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., to lead their conference in the majority.

But Schumer maintained confidence he would be reelected to the post despite Sens. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., publicly calling for a different leader or a “concrete plan” that provides change.

“I’m confident I will be elected majority leader, and our caucus is really united in focusing on bringing down costs, on ending the corruption, on ending the chaos, on ending the war,” Schumer told reporters Tuesday. “We have great unity in our caucus, and I’ll be proud to lead it.”

Sanders said during a news conference Tuesday the election was about “change and the need for the Democratic Party to move in a new and bold direction.”

“I personally have known Chuck Schumer for over 30 years, and I like Chuck. Nobody works harder than Chuck Schumer. But in my view the time is now for change, and I will not be supporting Chuck to be reelected as the Democratic leader,” Sanders said, calling for an “economy that works for all, not just the people on top.”

“Do I think Chuck has been leading in that direction?” he asked. “No.”

Some incoming members and now incumbents have pointed to Maryland Democrat Chris Van Hollen as one possibility to challenge Schumer. Van Hollen had previously thrown cold water on the idea by saying he was instead “kicking the tires” on a presidential run in 2028 but has recently changed his tune.

A person familiar with Van Hollen’s thinking said he “has received an outpouring of calls on running for majority leader and is now in active listening mode.”

Slotkin did not endorse anyone for leader but said she had a “really productive conversation” with Van Hollen yesterday.

“Whoever wants my vote is going to have to show me a concrete plan that’s definitely different. I’m a ‘no’ until and unless I see that from anyone,” she said, urging her peers to “withhold quorum” when Senate Democrats hold their leadership elections “until you get that plan and you feel like you have a voice in that plan.”

She urged not just a roadmap for the first 100 days, but ideas for how to “communicate differently.” As for her own future, she said, “I am not actively seeking this job. I’m seeking change.”

Asked about his plans Monday evening, Van Hollen said, “It’s not about me, but I am listening to the thousands of people who have been calling for change, but especially listening to our members, with a particular ear to new members who have just come off the campaign trail.”

“What I’ve said from the very beginning is, we shouldn’t have a coronation. We should have a caucus discussion about what we're going to do with the power and responsibilities that have been invested in us,” Van Hollen said. “I’m in listening mode and haven’t shut the door.”

Van Hollen took it a step further at an event Tuesday in Washington, D.C., criticizing the minority leader and Democrats’ campaign arm over their preferences in some primaries. “Schumer and the DSCC sided with the crypto industry and AIPAC against these candidates,” he said, according to a livestream of the event.

Schumer tried to tamp down the suggestion of a rivalry. “We talk frequently, and we’re united — united in lowering costs, and united in ending this damn war,” he said of Van Hollen.

Others threw their support behind Schumer ahead of the Democratic leadership elections, which are expected to take place in December.

Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Chair Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., praised Schumer for raising money and recruiting candidates like Sens.-elect Sherrod Brown of Ohio and Roy Cooper of North Carolina to help land at minimum seven seats, and potentially nine if Alaska and Mississippi ultimately swing their way.

“That takes vision. It takes clarity of thought. It takes strategic leadership, and that is what Sen. Schumer has done. And that is why you will see, despite all grumblings, enormous gratitude,” she said.

Gillibrand pointed to candidates like Scott Colom, the Democrat in Mississippi who is currently leading GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in a nail-biter of a race. “That wave doesn’t get created by magic. It gets created by hard work and putting the pieces together over years,” she said.

Colom, however, has been noncommittal, telling MS NOW, “Too many of our leaders are from the same areas of the country,” pointing to the Brooklyn roots of both Schumer and current House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to run for speaker on the House side.

Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., said he and Schumer have had their differences. But he implied he backs him for majority leader: “At the end of the day, these are historic numbers. It’s time for us to unify. We are going to work together as a caucus to plan together about how to move forward for what the country wants us to do, and I think we have the person who I think is going to lead us there.”

Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., said Democrats have “an opportunity to do things differently, and I think we will, regardless of who the leader is. It doesn’t really matter whose name is on the door.”

“Yes,” he said of his support for Schumer, noting that so far, nobody has officially stepped up to the plate. “This is a guy that worked incredibly hard over the last couple of years. I know people have other opinions about this. But we have a mandate to do things and get things done for the American people.”

Mark Schoeff Jr., Paul M. Krawzak and Kelly Livingston contributed to this report.

#6431. The 8 Best Outdoor Security Cameras Keep an Eye on Your Home When You're Away

Security cameras ensure that you can check what's happening around your home 24/7, capturing footage and alerting you within minutes if there's a problem.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Keeping your home safe these days takes more than a deadbolt and a dog with a menacing bark. Installing a few security cameras around your property is an easy and surprisingly cost-effective way to level up your home security, adding watchful eyes that track comings and goings 24/7. Until relatively recently, the only options for personal home security were comprehensive (and expensive) systems that were installed and monitored by security professionals. Now, you can set up your own cameras and home security system that saves you cash without sacrificing performance.

Outdoor security cameras in particular are your best bet to prevent break-ins. According to Security.org, simply having a clearly visible camera or security device on your property serves as a strong deterrent for trespassers. Outdoor security cameras are equipped with features found in indoor security cameras like high-definition video, night vision, two-way audio, and more. In addition to this, they come equipped with outdoor-specific features like weather-resistant exteriors, sound detection, and integrated motion-activated spotlights.

For this guide, we got our hands on the most promising options from well-established brands including Arlo, Wyze, Ring, and Eufy and tested them at our homes and offices. Read on below to learn about the best outdoor security cameras we recommend, along with expert advice to help you choose the right option for your home and budget.

One quick note before we dive in: It’s increasingly important to pick security gear that’s compatible with whatever smart home system you already have. For example, Amazon makes it easy to pull up a live feed from your Ring camera(s) on an Echo Show or Fire TV and has designed its products to more seamlessly connect with its other smart home devices. Same goes for Google products. If you already have a few items from a major smart home brand, consider buying gear that will be as compatible as possible with it.

More Home Improvement Stories: Best Retractable Awnings ● The Popular Mechanics 2025 Yard & Garden Awards ● Best Solar-Powered Outdoor Lights

We selected our recommendations based on a round of substantial testing: We installed these cameras outdoors, and used them to survey our homes for weeks, and in some cases months. We watched them as they watched our properties, as they endured a wide spectrum of outdoor conditions including snow and rain.

We tested and compared their basic video recording functionality, evaluating them on clarity, field of view, and weather resistance as well as any special features they offer like spotlights, solar charging, sirens, and more. Some of the cameras on this list were tested in outdoor settings for months, facing a wide spectrum of outdoor conditions including snow and rain.

We also tested their more nuanced security and tech features, including motion detection notifications, AI recognition of animals and packages, two-way audio conversations, and digital borders, among others. These features were considered as well as the cost, if any, associated with buying access to all of them.

We recommended the Wyze Outdoor Cam V2 ahead of testing, based on its low price, solid specs, and the past performance of other Wyze cameras that we've tested.

The Arlo Essential XL stands out for its user-friendly design, durable exterior, and of course, its clear video quality—all for a fair price. It's completely wireless, which means you can mount it anywhere around your home without worrying about power and wiring issues.

It excels as a 24/7 outdoor cam, with features like color night vision that improves the clarity of nighttime footage. During testing, we were impressed by its resolution in low light, as well as its accurate motion detection. It provides real-time alerts directly to your smartphone, and will let you check a live feed to observe any suspicious activity live as it happens.

You can also program the integrated spotlight to automatically flash on when someone is within visual range. It's a great deterrent against potential robberies, and lets you leave the house without leaving a porch light on.

While this cam has solid features without a subscription, an Arlo Secure subscription adds cloud storage for your video footage, as well as additional target recognition and home security features, for $96 to $300 per year.

Few options balance price and quality as well as this affordable option from Wyze. The battery-operated Wyze Outdoor V2 camera can be mounted anywhere. New buyers should pick up the starter kit, which includes a base unit that allows you to expand your system with up to four cameras.

Though it's the most affordable on the list, it still offers a lineup of powerful features including motion-sensing technology that detects both body heat and movement, reducing the number of potential false alarms drastically.

The Wyze is also quite flexible for storage options with the camera capable of online cloud storage as well as localized storage on a microSD card.

Solar-powered cameras, while power-efficient, present extra setup challenges. Most of the time, the panel is attached to the body of the camera, so you need to need find to camera positions with a good field of view and get good sun exposure. Depending on the layout of your home and the surrounding area, that may lead to less-than-ideal placements, which create holes in your surveillance.

The Tapo MagCam solves this issue with a detachable solar panel, so you can keep it connected when it's effective, or remove and mount it higher above the camera to get more sun. It features a 13-foot extension cord, so you have a good amount of slack to move it to an open, sunshiny space.

Test Editor Bradley Ford mounted his test camera in a semi-shaded area, then set up the solar panel in direct sunlight. Despite the fact that he was testing at the end of 2025, when there was significantly less daily sunlight, the battery never dipped below 80 percent charge. In the warmer weather, the camera typically sat at 100 percent.

In addition, Ford preferred that the MagCam relied on local storage. "One of the things we like best is that there is no need for a subscription to access activation videos," Ford said. "They’re all stored locally on a Micro SD card in the camera. However, if you wish to pay for cloud storage, that option is also available."

This specific kit comes with a camera, solar panel, and mount, however Tapo offers others with two or three cameras as well.

Our previous pick in this category, the Ring Floodlight Cam Wired Plus, was a terrific outdoor security camera that featured a dual-LED floodlight. The new Ring Floodlight Cam Wired Pro builds on that solid design with extra features, including support for dual-band WiFi and a “bird’s-eye view” feature that tracks a recorded subject as they move within the camera’s view, showing it on a top-down layout of the area.

The camera’s 1080p video resolution and 140-degree field of view are the same as the previous model, but image quality is enhanced with high dynamic range (HDR) support, which improves visibility in both low light and extremely bright conditions.

The lights themselves are also quite bright, 2000 lumens each, and the fixtures are adjustable so you can angle the light as you please.

The Ring Floodlight Cam Wired Pro also features two-way audio support, with a 110-decibel siren that sounds when the system detects motion. It also offers customizable motion zones and 3D- motion radar for you to tailor to your property.

A word of warning: We found the wired installation was fairly difficult, so we recommend hiring an electrician unless you're experienced with wiring and up for a challenge.

Unlike any other outdoor security camera on our list, this option from Tactacam does not require a WiFi connection. Instead, it connects to cellular towers and works similarly to your smartphone. This makes the camera perfect for homes in remote locations.

The security camera does require a monthly subscription for access to on-demand videos and photos that are stored in the cloud, but plans start at just 5 bucks a month.

The device works with AA batteries or a rechargeable battery pack. In our testing, we took anywhere from two to 10 pictures a day and the pack lasted about three to four months before needing to be recharged.

In practice, the security camera is great at sensing motion more than 100 feet away, so it could potentially double as a nature cam. It lacks some of the features other, similarly priced models on this list have, but the biggest drawback is that the field of view is only about 50 feet wide.

The Arlo floodlight has everything we love from our top pick, including Arlo's superior app and software, but adds on a large floodlight, as well as a need for wired power.

As with the Arlo Essential XL, you get quality motion detection software and color night vision. Spring for Arlo Secure, and you get AI target recognition that can point out passing cars or faces, and highlight packages.

The floodlight also has some interesting features: Each light is individually adjustable, so you can angle them for the best possible coverage. That includes creative solutions like angling one light toward your back door, while pointing the other toward the steps leading to your back porch. It's a small touch, but a very appreciated one. It also includes a loud, 110-decibel siren.

If you're looking for a low-maintenance outdoor security camera system, eufy's S330 "eufycam 3" is a dynamic wireless option that supports solar charging and doesn't require professional installation.

Once installed and set up, we did not have to take either of the cameras down for recharging once over months of use. The solar panels kept them perpetually charged as long as they got exposure to a few hours of sunlight per day.

It was similarly easy to connect the cameras to the greater home security. The outdoor cameras works through the home hub which after initial installation using an ethernet cable, works comfortably through your home WiFi. The cameras can then be set up anywhere within several hundred feet of the hub without losing connection.

A big benefit we also loved is the camera system requires no monthly subscription to access its features. This includes AI-powered face recognition, customizable activity zones, and of course, motion detection.

The only drawback for this camera set is the placement of the solar panels. While the panels being integrated directly on top of the camera makes it less cumbersome, it also means you need to install them in a spot with direct sunlight or they won't properly charge.

The Reolink Argus 4 Pro gives you a sweeping 180-degree field of view, which allows you to cover large open spaces with as few cameras as possible. Properly positioned, you can achieve a near-complete view of an area with just two cameras.

This 4K camera features a dual-lens design that covers larger areas without blind spots or fishbowl-style warping. You'd think that might lead to complications with position or usage, but we found it easy to operate.

It features discrete solar panels for power, which allows for more placement flexibility: For example, you can install the camera under a ledge or rooftop, then secure the solar panel above, where it will get direct sun. That makes it easier to get the perfect shot and optimal power.

In terms of storage, the Argus 4 Pro records footage locally and connects to a home hub. You don't have to pay a monthly fee for cloud storage or additional features. Simply turn it on, connect it the hub, and in theory, it should run without issue in perpetuity.

There are two types of consumer-grade home security cameras: wireless battery-powered cameras that you can set up easily nearly anywhere, but require you to occasionally replace batteries, and wired models that connect directly to your home's electrical system.

Wired cameras are generally more expensive and require an electrician's help unless you're comfortable with home wiring, but require far less maintenance once they're installed. Their placement is also restricted to locations where you can wired them in.

Battery-powered cameras, by contrast, are only restricted by the range of your WiFi router. Of course, you'll need to access them every few months to replace their batteries. Some models feature solar panels, giving you renewable energy, but panels also impose some placement restrictions. (Namely, access to sunlight).

Wired cameras do fall short of battery-powered models in one niche scenario—when the power goes out. Unlike, say, wired smoke or carbon monoxide detectors, which have reliable battery backup, you can't count on a wired security camera to provide surveillance footage during an extended period of time if there's a power failure. It varies from model to model, but most wired cameras can only last for 30 minutes to, at most, a few hours before they go dark.

To avoid recording 24/7, which wastes power and storage space, outdoor security cameras usually feature motion sensors that trigger recording whenever there’s activity. Many cameras will also an alert to your companion app whenever they start recording.

Most cameras give you the ability to calibrate the motion sensor by setting motion zones in spots where you expect frequent false alarms, like a sidewalk. Others offer smart features that can differentiate between people, animals, and vehicles. You should also have the ability to customize your notifications, so you’ll only receive an alert in certain situations, like if it detects a person.

Furthermore, some cameras feature microphones, enabling audio detection, which can trigger recording and alerts based on nearby sounds that may be out of view (like a window breaking). Audio detection is a useful extra layer in a few specific situations, like when a single camera can’t cover the entire side of your home, but may also lead to more nuisance alerts. If you decide to use one, we recommend customizing your audio alert sensitivity if possible so you aren’t constantly getting notified when the neighbor’s dog barks.

The best outdoor security cameras record video in "Full HD" (1920 x 1080p) resolution, which captures enough detail to identify facial features or a car’s license plate. More expensive cameras record at higher resolutions, such as 2K or "Quad HD" (2560 x 1440p) or 4K Ultra HD (3840 x 2160) video, which deliver better detail. While higher resolution may help, 1080p video is usually clear enough to give you more than enough information in most situations.

Your camera’s field of view (FOV) is just as important as its resolution. Field of view refers to how wide of an angle the lens is and therefore, how much of your yard or porch is in view. With a wider FOV, your camera can see a wider area around your property, providing more coverage. For the best results, we recommend a model with a field of view between 130 and 180 degrees.

Many outdoor cameras also feature an integrated spotlight that can illuminate the surroundings if motion is detected, improving visibility in low-light situations. A spotlight also acts as a deterrent by making potential intruders more visible. Similarly, the majority of outdoor cameras offer some kind of night vision feature, which uses infrared (IR) lights to record a high-contrast black and white video in the dark. Top-of-the-line cameras are capable of recording standard video in low light, minimizing the need for night vision.

There’s no point in recording camera footage if you can’t store it for when you need it. Many manufacturers offer free cloud storage for a limited time—typically seven days–after which video is overwritten with new recordings. You can always download and save that footage, so long as you do during that initial window.

If you want to save your footage for a longer period, there are a couple of options. Many companies provide additional cloud storage for a subscription fee. There are also cameras that feature a microSD card slot for storing footage locally. This does require a bit of extra maintenance in the form of occasionally removing the card and either deleting or downloading the recorded data to free up more space on the card.

Security cameras are more than just their features. Nearly all security cameras are built to connect with other smart home devices. So, before buying any specific option, make sure it is compatible with the devices you already own. For example, Amazon makes it easy to pull up a live feed from your Ring camera(s) on an Echo Show or Fire TV. There are many brands that work with the majority of the smart home software available such as Apple, Google Nest, and Ring. Some have limited functionality on other smart home software systems outside of their brand, but still work with them. Furthermore, most security camera brands require a monthly subscription to gain full access to many of their features. These monthly subscriptions range in price and overall necessity with some basically essential to operate the cameras and store footage in the cloud while others are designed as a bonus add-on to the base product. Prior to purchase, make sure to take a close look at both the smart home compatibility as well as what comes with and without the monthly subscription service.

Most of the outdoor security cameras we recommend are sold individually or as part of a larger set. The number of cameras you need for your property will vary, based on your home security plan and how much camera coverage you want. A well-installed camera with a wide field of view can cover an important and vulnerable area on your property, such as a back door or garage.

That said, even a small home will need at least a few cameras to achieve full coverage on every ground-level door and window. You may need multiple cameras to reveal tricky blind spots created by corners, lawn features, and anything else that might impede a single camera position.

Don't freak out about needing a fleet of surveillance gear, though. Not everyone wants or needs to have every single square inch of their property under constant watch. It’s up to you to decide where you want an extra eye. The important thing is to make sure you know what you need before making a purchase.

Of course. There are no features of an outdoor security camera that would prevent it from working inside. That said, many companies make indoor cameras that are cheaper, and may feature a stand or mounting options that make more sense for blending in with your home or office.

You should always be careful when considering home security. Over the years, there have been multiple reports of strangers accessing live video feeds and recorded videos from home security cameras.

Luckily, there are simple ways to protect yourself. As with other devices, adhering to digital security best practices, such as keeping your smart home devices’ firmware up to date, creating a strong password and activating two-factor authentication wherever possible, will help prevent a breach.

You may also have concerns about who has access to video that’s stored in the cloud. Most companies ask for permission to review recordings for research and development purposes. Depending on the company, this request often comes in the form of an “opt-in” setting in the camera app, though some may turn it on by default unless you “opt out.”

Some may also share recordings with law enforcement. In some cases, they will only do so when compelled by a search warrant. A couple manufacturers, specifically Amazon (Ring) and Google (Nest), have said they will provide footage without a warrant if law enforcement claims it is an emergency.

#6430. Scientists Discover Strange Dinosaur That Evolved To Eat Fruit

A dinosaur’s resemblance to modern fruit-eating parrots offers clues to how prehistoric animals adapted as flowering plants transformed life on land.

As flowering plants spread across the Cretaceous landscape, fruits became larger and more abundant, offering dinosaurs an entirely different source of food. Paleontologists have long struggled to understand how this transformation influenced dinosaur evolution. Now, the discovery of a turkey-sized dinosaur that lived alongside T. rex suggests that some dinosaurs developed remarkably sophisticated ways of eating fruit, much like parrots do today.

The newly identified species, Infernogallus jamesi, is the first known dinosaur with anatomical adaptations specifically linked to fruit consumption. The discovery was made by researchers from Stony Brook University, the Royal Ontario Museum (ROM), and the North Dakota Geological Survey. Led by Dr. Gregory Funston, assistant professor in the Department of Anatomical Sciences at Stony Brook University, the study was published in Nature Communications.

“We knew dinosaurs evolved to fill so many different roles in ecosystems in the Cretaceous, but we never expected to discover fruit-eating dinosaurs,” says Dr. Gregory Funston. “For more than 100 years, we didn’t know what the skulls of these animals looked like. Now, we know they were even weirder than we could have predicted.”

The dinosaur’s name, Infernogallus, means “hell chicken,” a reference to the Hell Creek Formation where its fossils were discovered. The formation stretches across Montana, North Dakota, South Dakota, and Wyoming and preserves remains of familiar dinosaurs such as T. rex and Triceratops, which lived alongside Infernogallus. Its nearly complete skull, with the bones still connected, and partial skeleton are currently on display at the Royal Ontario Museum.

Despite descending from meat-eating dinosaurs, Infernogallus belonged to a group of toothless, feathered oviraptorosaurs known as caenagnathids. Weighing approximately 25 pounds (12 kilograms) as a fully grown adult, it was one of the smallest members of its group.

“It’s pretty rare for animals to become specialized for a diet of fruit, so when it happens, it comes with some remarkable adaptations,” says Dr. Thomas Dudgeon, Rebanks Postdoctoral Research Fellow at ROM and a co-author of the study. “The anatomy of Infernogallus is bizarre among dinosaurs, and we quickly realized that we were dealing with something special.”

Using CT scans to reconstruct the skull, the researchers noticed something unusual about the bones forming the roof of the mouth. These bones curved downward into the mouth, positioning certain chewing muscles horizontally rather than vertically. Instead of relying on the rigid, up-and-down bite characteristic of dinosaurs such as T. rex, Infernogallus could have moved its beak back and forth in a chewing motion similar to our own.

Forward-facing chewing muscles are uncommon in the animal kingdom, although they occur in mammals capable of complex chewing and in certain fruit-eating birds. The particular muscle arrangement identified in Infernogallus resembles that of the modern vulturine parrot (Psittrichas), suggesting that the dinosaur was adapted to processing soft food in its mouth rather than its gut. Its chewing motion appears to have been especially suited to separating the flesh of stone fruits from their hard central pits.

The finding also reveals an intriguing parallel in evolutionary history. As fruits became larger and more common, caenagnathids developed increasingly specialized chewing capabilities.

Fossilized fruits document how flowering plants gradually replaced cone-bearing plants as the dominant vegetation on land during the Cretaceous. By eating fruit, dinosaurs may have helped disperse seeds and influenced the evolution of flowering plants, fulfilling an ecological role that birds, reptiles, and small mammals play today.

“Complete remains of small dinosaurs like Infernogallus are very rare in the fossil record. The strange skull of Infernogallus is an exciting find because it reveals surprising insights into dinosaur evolution and feeding specialization,” says Dr. David Evans, chief curator of natural history and Temerty Chair in Vertebrate Paleontology at ROM and senior author of the paper. “This discovery shows that we still have a lot to learn about the world of T. rex, and about dinosaurs more generally.”

The discovery also contributes to an ongoing debate over whether dinosaurs were already in decline before their extinction. The specialized feeding behavior of Infernogallus suggests that the diversity of dinosaurs, and the ecological roles they occupied near the end of the Cretaceous, may have been greater than the fossil record has so far revealed.

Reference: “Fruit-eating adaptations in a Late Cretaceous oviraptorosaur (Theropoda)” by Gregory F. Funston, Thomas W. Dudgeon, D. Jade Simon, Danielle M. Dufault, Clint Boyd, Denver Fowler, Philip J. Currie and David C. Evans, 10 October 2026, Nature Communications. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78343-w
