#6408. I’ve Tested Vacuums for Years. These Are the 6 Best Cordless Stick Vacs Under $300, Ranked.

Clean hardwood, carpet, pet hair, and everything in between for less.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

The most powerful cordless stick vacuums will easily run you $500 or more, but in my experience, there are plenty of capable cleaners under $300. They may not rival the suction power, battery life, or features of their higher-priced counterparts, but many are perfectly capable of keeping up with typical household messes on hardwood, carpet, and every surface in between.

I’ve spent years testing vacuums for Popular Mechanics, and that experience informs a lot of my recommendations below. Some of these models have been through my own series of hands-on tests, while others made the cut based on my familiarity with their brands and product lines, along with research into their features and real-world performance. From budget-friendly everyday cleaners to options for pet owners, these are the best cordless vacuums that deliver the most for under $300.

The Shark PowerDetect is a feature-packed option for anyone who wants a cordless stick vacuum that does a lot of the thinking for them. The Detect mode automatically adjusts suction based on floor type and amount of debris, and a dual-roller floor head tackles tough messes on hardwood and carpet.

The hinged wand is great for cleaning under furniture and makes it a lot easier to reach hidden areas without having to bend down at all kinds of weird angles. It’s on the heavier side, and the long recharge time is a drawback, but strong pickup and smart features make it a good pick for whole-home cleaning.

Don’t let the price fool you: The Bissell PowerClean FurFinder is a strong and versatile cordless vacuum. It isn’t too heavy to carry between rooms, and the self-standing design means you don’t have to remount it or lay it flat any time you need to pause during your cleaning session.

It has a tangle-free brush roll that does a great job picking up pet hair (as well as your own stray strands around the house). I also like the LED headlights that show hidden dirt, dust, and debris on floors and furniture. The attachments are great for above-floor cleaning, too. Battery life drops considerably when you crank up the suction power, so it’s best for maintenance cleaning.

The LVAC-300 packs cleaning power and everyday convenience into a lightweight machine. It’s easy to maneuver, and it transitions between hard floors, rugs, and low- to medium-pile carpet without scattering debris all over the floor. The tangle-resistant brush roll is a major pro for homes with pets or long hair, and five-stage filtration and washable filters are valuable additions.

It converts to a handheld vacuum cleaner with attachments for upholstery, stairs, and car interiors, and it uses a pleated mechanical HEPA filter with a dense arrangement of fibers to capture even the tiniest dust particles. The smaller dustbin and shorter runtime on max power might negatively impact your overall experience using this vacuum, but still, it’s versatile enough to take care of a variety of common household messes.

The Tineco Pure One Station 5 is the sibling to the Station 5 Pro that I’ve tested and still use to this day. And luckily, this more affordable model doesn’t cut key features that I love, such as the self-emptying and self-cleaning bagless docking station and green laser light for dust detection.

This model also has HEPA filtration and smart features. Internal sensors detect dust and adjust suction accordingly, and the anti-tangle brush roll helps prevent hair buildup. You get a shorter runtime with this model than you do with the Pro (estimated 70 minutes compared to the Pro’s 100), but the automated cleaning capability is hard to beat.

The Dyson V8 is right at the edge of our $300 budget, but it’s a powerful option for homes with lots of carpeting or area rugs. I haven’t tried this specific model yet, but the motorbar floor cleaner is the same design that comes with other Dyson vacuums I’ve tried, such as the Dyson V15 Detect. It works well for hard floors, but I’ve found it particularly useful for dislodging embedded hair and debris from carpet fibers.

The V8 comes with three attachments and converts into a handheld vacuum if you need more portability. Runtime is on the lower end for Dyson, but if you’re looking for a premium design without the premium price tag, the V8 is it.

The Eureka ReactiSense 440 offers a number of features that make vacuuming less of a chore. It has dust detection sensors, automatic suction adjustment, floor head lights, and an anti-tangle brush roll with fins and a comb strip to prevent hair from getting wrapped around it.

I like that this model uses HEPA filtration to capture up to 99.7 percent of airborne particles and odors (which is great if you’re a pet owner). This model is lightweight and portable, converts to a handheld, and provides up to 60 minutes of runtime. Battery life will likely vary if you’re regularly cleaning at high power levels, but I’d reach for this vacuum for daily maintenance cleaning and quick pickups.

Amber is a Reviews Editor with bylines on Popular Mechanics, Runner’s World, Bicycling, and Best Products sites. Specializing in kitchen gadgets, small appliances, lifestyle, and consumer tech, she brings hands-on testing and a detail-oriented approach to every review. In her free time you can likely find her trading trinkets at an EDM festival, searching for hidden gems at thrift stores, or cuddling with her two cats.

#6407. New Technology Could Help Astronauts Make Their Own Oxygen on the Moon

Astronauts on the Moon could one day breathe oxygen pulled from lunar soil using a technique borrowed from chipmaking.

Computer chip manufacturing and lunar exploration seem like completely different worlds. Yet our latest research suggests the two may be more closely connected than expected.

Using technology widely employed in semiconductor manufacturing, we have shown that it is possible to extract oxygen and products containing oxygen from material designed to mimic lunar soil.

This matters because oxygen is one of the most valuable resources for future space exploration. Astronauts need it to breathe, and it is also a major component of rocket propellant.

But transporting large quantities from Earth would be enormously expensive, so space agencies are investigating ways to obtain it directly on the Moon instead.

The challenge is that lunar oxygen does not exist as a readily available gas. Instead, it is chemically bound within minerals that make up the Moon’s surface layer. And although that layer contains a large amount of oxygen by weight, extracting it requires breaking strong chemical bonds within lunar minerals.

Many of the complex techniques that could potentially achieve this extraction would require large amounts of energy.

So our team decided to explore an alternative, lower-temperature approach inspired by a well-established industrial technology called “plasma-processing.”

Plasma is often called the fourth state of matter (after solid, liquid, and gas). It forms when sufficient energy is supplied to a gas, creating a mixture of charged particles, electrons, and highly reactive chemical species.

In semiconductor fabrication, plasma interacts with silicon dioxide in a process that underpins the production of billions of electronic devices every year.

We asked a simple question: if plasmas are highly effective at reacting with compounds containing oxygen in semiconductor processing, could a similar approach be applied to the oxygen-based compounds in lunar soil?

To investigate, we exposed artificial moon soil (known as lunar regolith simulants) to plasmas generated using gases that are commonly employed in semiconductor manufacturing.

The results were encouraging. During plasma treatment of the lunar regolith simulants, we detected oxygen and oxygen-containing gaseous products being released.

Further analyses confirmed that the plasma was chemically modifying oxygen-bearing minerals within the material, with some lunar minerals reacting more readily than others.

Understanding these underlying mechanisms is important for enhancing the efficiency of the process and identifying opportunities to improve future systems. But oxygen yields would need to increase substantially before any practical lunar system becomes possible.

One reason this approach is attractive is that it builds on decades of experience developed by the semiconductor industry. Space engineering often requires entirely new technologies, but there are advantages in adapting systems that already exist, are well-understood, and have been refined for years on Earth.

The semiconductor industry has spent decades studying how fluorine plasmas interact with materials containing oxygen. Rather than starting from scratch, future researchers can draw on that extensive knowledge base.

There are practical benefits too. Plasma processing is a dry process, avoiding some of the challenges associated with transporting and handling liquid reagents (chemicals added to the process to make a reaction occur) in space. The operating temperatures of plasma processing can also be significantly lower than those required by some conventional oxygen extraction methods.

The implications may extend beyond using oxygen for life support on lunar bases. Lunar soil contains useful elements, including silicon, aluminum, and iron. While our current work focused on oxygen-bearing reactions, future studies may explore whether plasma-based processes could contribute more broadly to the use of other lunar resources.

Much more research is needed to understand the chemistry, to improve yields, and to determine whether the process can be scaled economically.

But the plasma technology that enables the manufacture of billions of transistors may also help humanity tackle one of the biggest challenges of space exploration: learning how to live off the land on another world.

Reference: “Impact of oxygen extraction from lunar regolith simulant using fluorinated plasma processes” by Aneeta Jaggernauth, Sean Kelly, Brian K. Tanner, Robert O’Connor, Aidan Cowley and Rajani K. Vijayaraghavan, 2 September 2026, Scientific Reports. DOI: 10.1038/s41598-026-67891-2

Adapted from an article originally published in The Conversation.

At a cliff site in Texas, archaeologists discovered hundreds of bison bones, stone tools and arrowheads, suggesting Indigenous people used "bison jumps" to hunt.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists have uncovered an extremely rare example of a "bison jump" in the Texas Panhandle, where a natural geological formation allowed Indigenous people to hunt North America's largest living land mammal for 3,000 years. The discovery confirms that the prehistoric hunting technique ‪—‬ which involved channeling a herd of bison into a stampede off a cliff, akin to "walking the plank" ‪—‬ was not limited to the northern Plains like experts previously thought.

"Bison jumping is an iconic, uniquely North American hunting technique that yielded some of the most productive food-getting events in the history of human hunting," researchers wrote in a study published online Nov. 9 in the journal American Antiquity.

Although jump sites are well known throughout the northern Plains, only one such site had ever been found in the southern Plains. But a second bison jump called Nighthawk has now been identified in Caprock Canyons State Park in the Texas Panhandle, and researchers found that Indigenous people used the Nighthawk bison jump for millennia.

"Returning to the same place over and over again over 3,000 years shows that people had a significant connection to the Nighthawk hunting facility," study first author Gus Costa, an archaeologist at Rice University in Houston, said in a statement.

Nighthawk was found when bison remains began eroding from a bone bed (a place where bones naturally accumulate) underneath a roughly 65-foot-tall (20 meters) cliff spur. Archaeologists investigated and found chipped stone tools near the bones, as well as a few arrowheads. Several of the bison bones had cut marks from stone tools consistent with prehistoric butchery practices. These discoveries added up to a possible bison jump.

Archaeologists found hundreds of bison bones at the Nighthawk bison jump site in Texas.

"The only way bison can arrive at the site is by falling from above, as the site surface is sandwiched between two cliffs," the researchers wrote. Indigenous hunters likely used the cliff's natural spur shape to herd the bison to their deaths. "Instead of a stampede toward a surprise fall, Nighthawk could have operated more like 'walking the plank,'" according to the researchers.

Even more surprising than the discovery of a bison jump site in the southern Plains was the length of time the jump was used.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

A series of radiocarbon dates revealed that there were at least seven mass bison kills at Nighthawk over a span of three millennia, between roughly 1550 B.C. and A.D. 1550. One of these events, which the researcher named Kill 3, was responsible for most of the bison bones. That enormously successful hunt most likely took place around A.D. 300 to 400 and would have required an immense labor force and precise coordination.

Archaeologists excavating a bison jump site called Nighthawk in Caprock Canyons State Park in the Texas Panhandle.

"Bison jumping is a complicated community effort," Costa said. "Large scale bison harvests (like jumps) are exciting because they require a large group of people working together to be successful."

It is not entirely clear what the Indigenous hunters were doing with the bison killed in the hunt. In the northern Plains, archaeologists have long assumed that bison jumps were generally performed in the fall and used to provision the community for winter. Bison in the North were used to make pemmican, a shelf-stable mix of dried meat and rendered fat.

But although pemmican was an extremely useful foodstuff and trade good in the North, it was likely too warm in Texas for bison fat to last more than a few weeks, the researchers wrote. This may mean that the southern Plains bison hunts were more useful for displaying power and building alliances.

All of the kill events at Nighthawk were at least a century apart, with an average of 500 years between each bison jump. That points to an infrequent use of the jump but also a clear memory of its utility.

"The simplest explanation for long-lived jump facilities is that these techniques were passed down over long time spans rather than revived again and again," the researchers wrote.

Costa, A. G., Houk, B. A., Lyle, A. S., Bement, L., Lintz, C., Lawrence, K. L., Frederick, C. D., & Culleton, B. J. (2026). The Nighthawk bison jump: New evidence for recurrent Late Holocene bison jumping in the Southern Plains. American Antiquity, 1–28. https://doi.org/10.1017/aaq.2026.10229

Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

#6404. White House warns Democrats against aggressive oversight

Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., is expected to lead the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo)

The Trump administration signaled it would respond aggressively to a Democratic-led Congress with a letter this week threatening to prosecute lawmakers for oversight efforts.

The letter from White House Counsel Will Scharf sent Monday to House Oversight and Government Reform ranking member Robert Garcia, D-Calif., argued that members of Congress have limited authority to conduct oversight of a presidential administration and that some of the threats to issue subpoenas “may cross the line into blatant criminality.”

The letter, obtained from a White House official, marks the latest escalation from the Trump administration ahead of Democrats taking control of both chambers of Congress next year. It also dovetails with years of Trump’s threats to prosecute his critics.

“We are monitoring the abusive and capricious threats that are now proliferating from Democrat legislators who seek to abuse the legislative process to intimidate and to interfere with the lawful functioning of government,” the letter says.

Garcia, the likely committee chair next Congress, pushed back on the threat in a statement Wednesday, accusing the administration of having “something to hide” and that Congress has wide authority to investigate the executive branch.

“The American people voted overwhelmingly for us to pass laws to root out corruption and abuse," Garcia said. "The Trump Administration continues to weaponize the government with threats of unconstitutional attacks on Congress. We are a co-equal branch of government and will not be deterred by baseless threats from a weaponized DOJ or from the President’s lawyers.”

The letter came after Attorney General Todd Blanche previously refused to rule out criminal charges against members of Congress in response to investigations.

"It depends on what the crime is and what they have done,” Blanche told CNN over the weekend.

Last week, President Donald Trump himself said that threats of investigations and impeachment were “extortion at the highest level” and called for the Justice Department to “look into this criminal act, immediately!”

He also singled out Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., calling for her to be imprisoned. The administration previously unsuccessfully attempted to indict Slotkin and other Democrats over a video she published calling for soldiers to disobey illegal orders.

And Trump last year publicly called for longtime critic Sen. Adam B. Schiff, D-Calif., to face unspecified charges in a post on Truth Social addressed to then-Attorney General Pam Bondi that also called for the prosecution of former FBI Director James Comey and New York Attorney General Letitia James. Both have faced criminal charges, pleaded not guilty and fought them in court as political attacks.

Garcia and other Democrats have signaled they intend to pursue oversight aggressively in the new Congress. After Democrats won the House majority last week, Garcia put out an all-caps statement urging administration officials to “LAWYER UP” ahead of the new year.

Garcia, as well as other likely incoming chairs such as House Judiciary ranking member Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md.; Homeland Security ranking member Rep. Bennie Thompson, D-Miss.; and Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., have hinted at broad inquiries ranging from the handling of files related to deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein to immigration enforcement and more.

Raskin told reporters last week that he thought Democratic oversight efforts could dovetail with the party’s broader effort to address affordability issues, including by addressing the Iran war, allegations of corruption within the Trump administration and more.

“We're going to get all the information that we need in order to restore the rule of law in American constitutional democracy,” Raskin said.

The letter also echoes a previous fight the administration pitched with the House in the first Trump administration, where officials resisted in court allowing former White House Counsel Don McGahn to testify to the House Judiciary Committee for years.

#6402. Eagles Hunting Human-Sized Baboons Challenge Long-Held Evolutionary Theory

Evidence of eagles hunting adult baboons suggests that aerial predators may have helped shape how early humans learned to communicate and protect one another.

In the middle of the Sahara, researchers have found evidence that eagles are killing primates as large as some of our early ancestors. One of the apparent victims, an adult male baboon, was estimated to have weighed more than 26 kilograms (57 pounds), challenging a long-held assumption about the dangers early humans faced.

Eagles have hunted primates for millions of years, yet no primate weighing more than 13 kilograms (29 pounds) had previously been confirmed to have been killed by a bird of prey. Scientists believed that humans and their ancestors had escaped this threat for roughly the past 2.5 million years because they were too heavy for even the giant eagles of the past to lift.

The discovery comes from the Ennedi Plateau in northern Chad, where an isolated population of baboons lives in the Sahara Desert. Researchers from the University of St Andrews traveled to the region with colleagues from Dartmouth College, the University of Konstanz, the Max Planck Institute of Animal Behavior, and African Parks.

Lead author Professor Catherine Hobaiter, from the School of Psychology and Neuroscience at the University of St Andrews, said, “This was such an extraordinary expedition, any primatologists dream! Some of the baboons there are so remote they rarely, if ever, see people, and so after a couple of days they ended up following us around—we were probably the most interesting thing they’d seen for a while!”

She added: “We saw the eagles while we were searching for the baboons, but we never imagined that they might be a threat to them. Then we found the first skull with a puncture mark, and then another, and another.”

In a new study published in the American Journal of Biological Anthropology, the researchers describe finding the remains of adult male baboons with telltale signs of eagle predation, including talon punctures in their skulls and distinctive scrapes and rake marks on their shoulder bones.

Senior author Professor Nathaniel Dominy from Dartmouth College said, “At first, the idea of eagles hunting adult male baboons seemed to exist on the thin edge of possibility, until it didn’t. Our skepticism slowly gave way to acceptance. The evidence was convincing.”

The behavior of the living baboons offered another clue.

Professor Hobaiter explained, “One of the most exciting observations was seeing the baboons respond when a pair of Verreaux’s eagles swept overhead—primates are very specific about only responding to eagles that are a genuine threat. We’d seen them very relaxed around other big birds of prey, but as soon as the Verreaux came into view they alarm called and dropped down to safety.”

For scientists studying human evolution, the possibility of attacks from above is particularly interesting. Primates defend themselves differently against eagles than they do against predators such as big cats and crocodiles. One strategy, known as mobbing, involves primates, particularly larger adult males, charging an attacker to drive it away. If our ancestors faced similar threats, eagles may have helped shape the evolution of communication and group cooperation.

Many primates living in areas where eagles hunt also travel in large groups alongside other primate species. For much of our evolutionary history, our ancestors shared their surroundings with other early human species and primates. Although these relationships are often viewed in terms of competition, protection from predators may have given them a reason to stay together.

Dr. Gisela Kopp, from the University of Konstanz and the Max Planck Institute of Animal Behavior, said, “Primatology often focuses on regions with a high diversity of primates, but shifting our attention to a place where no primatological data has ever been collected before, proved to be extremely rewarding.”

Dr. Jean Didier Akpona, from African Parks, said, “Having worked in this region for about three years, I had the opportunity to visit these gueltas (pockets of water that form within rock formations) and often observed Verreaux’s eagles. I had never imagined that these predators would target primates of this size until the research team stumbled upon evidence. This discovery leads us to explore further the mystery that surrounds the gueltas of the Sahara Desert.”

The researchers are eager to continue studying the isolated baboon population, whose unusual lifestyle is already challenging several assumptions about the species.

Professor Hobaiter added, “Baboons are some of the best studied monkeys in Africa, but our very first observations from Ennedi upended all sorts of notions about what these baboons should be doing—from their diet to their social lives, I can’t wait to see what new ‘rules’ they’ll break next!”

Reference: “Signs of Eagle Predation on a 22-kg Adult Primate” by Catherine Hobaiter, Tewogbade J. D. Akpona, Gisela H. Kopp and Nathaniel J. Dominy, 18 November 2026, American Journal of Biological Anthropology. DOI: 10.1002/ajpa.70377

This work was supported by the University of St Andrews (Global Partnerships Travel Grant), the Scottish Funding Council (International Science Partnership Fund), the Dartmouth College (Harris Distinguished Visiting Professorship program), the Marion and Jasper Whiting Foundation (Fellowship for Higher Education), the Rust Family Foundation; the Hector Stiftung II (Hector Pioneer Fellowship), and the Zukunftskolleg, University of Konstanz (ZENiT Fellowship, through the Federal Ministry of Education and Research (BMBF), and the Baden-Württemberg Ministry of Science as part of the Excellence Strategy of the German Federal and State Governments).

#6401. Glaciers Are Melting at Alarmingly Different Rates and Climate Alone Can’t Explain Why

Where a glacier ends can influence how quickly it disappears, with implications for communities that depend on mountain meltwater or face the threat of flooding.

Between 2000 and 2020, the number of lakes in direct contact with glaciers worldwide grew by about 35 percent. Their expansion has consequences for the ice that remains. Lake water can melt glaciers from underneath, while chunks of ice can break away and fall into the water. Until recently, scientists had struggled to determine how much these processes contribute to glacier loss worldwide.

An international research team, including Tobias Bolch from the Institute of Geodesy at Graz University of Technology (TU Graz), used artificial intelligence to map glacial lakes from satellite images taken in 2000 and 2020. The researchers manually checked the results, distinguishing lakes that touched glaciers from those already separated from the ice. Their findings were published in Nature Climate Change.

Over the 20-year period, glaciers ending in lakes lost an average of 66 centimeters (26 inches) of water equivalent annually, meaning the lost ice would produce a layer of water that deep. By comparison, glaciers ending on land lost 40 centimeters (16 inches), and those ending in the sea lost 36 centimeters (14 inches).

“Our research has shown that contact with a lake further accelerates the loss of ice from a glacier,” says Tobias Bolch. “While the climate and the topography of the glacier are the most significant factors influencing glacial mass loss, lakes significantly exacerbate it.”

The number of lakes touching glaciers increased by more than 3,500, with particularly pronounced expansion in Alaska and the southern Andes. Their combined area grew by around 600 square kilometers (232 square miles). They also gained an estimated 66 cubic kilometers of water, enough to submerge the entire city of Vienna under approximately 160 meters (525 feet) of water

Using machine learning models, the researchers found that glacier characteristics such as elevation and slope accounted for 46 percent of the explained influence on ice gains and losses. Temperature, precipitation, and other climatic factors accounted for around 43 percent, while glacial lakes contributed approximately 11 percent.

“The findings from this study will help us to estimate future changes to the glaciers more accurately,” says Tobias Bolch. “This is particularly important for mountainous regions and their forelands, where meltwater is a significant source of water. Such findings are also relevant when assessing the risks posed by glacial lakes in the event of potential outbursts.”

Reference: “Climate and glacier geometry dominate global glacier–lake interactions” by Shaochun Zhao, Guoqing Zhang, Matthias Huss, Georg Veh, Jonathan L. Carrivick, Tobias Bolch, David R. Rounce, Qian Tang, Yifan Bu, Yan Song, Menger Peng, Xue Wang, Xinhai Zeng, Danni Huang, Mengjie Zhu, Tao Zhou and Jie Cheng, 20 November 2026, Nature Climate Change. DOI: 10.1038/s41558-026-02808-5

This work was supported by grants from the Basic Excellent Research Group for Tibetan Plateau Earth System, National Natural Science Foundation of China (NSFC ERGTPES project no. 42588201), the National Key Research and Development Project of China (2024YFF0809104), the National Natural Science Foundation of China (grant no. 42571153), the Second Tibetan Plateau Scientific Expedition and Research Program (STEP, 2024QZKK0301), the Department of Science and Technology of the Tibet Autonomous Region (XZ202502JD0025, XZ202403ZY0028) and the High-Level Talent Program of Xizang University (XZDXDR202501).

“Ice-contact lakes explain 11 ± 7% of the mass loss of lake-terminating glaciers globally, whereas climate forcing (43 ± 10%) and glacier geometry (46 ± 10%) are more relevant predictors for ice loss.”

So just what does all of this mean? What do we conclude from climate forcing only accounting for 43% of the mass loss of lake-terminating glaciers?

#6399. A Train Carrying Deadly Materials Was on Fire for Nearly an Hour as It Barreled Toward a Small Town. Why Didn’t Anyone Stop It?

A small sensor failed to do its job—leading to one of the worst train wrecks in American history.

Editor’s note: In July 2024, after this story was published, the National Transportation Safety Board released its final analysis on the Norfolk Southern freight train derailment in East Palestine, Ohio. It also released a companion illustrated digest of the incident. The analysis determined that the train derailed after an overheated wheel bearing caused an axel to “burn off.” The punctured DOT-111 tank car leaked butyl acrylates, which are flammable and likely started the post-derailment fires. Further, the decision to intentionally “vent and burn” vinyl chloride tank cars was likely unnecessary and based on incomplete or misleading information, according to the report. The NTSB issued 34 new safety recommendations covering several needs, including defect detection systems, tank car standards, hazardous materials, and emergency response procedures.

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:

On the frigid evening of Friday, February 3, 2023, at around 8:50 p.m., a Norfolk Southern freight train measuring more than a mile and three quarters long snaked its way through the town of East Palestine, Ohio. The train consisted of 149 cars, pulled by three locomotives—two at the front, one in the middle—and traveled just under 50 miles per hour. Of those 149 cars, 20 were tankers labeled with hazardous-materials placards. Several of the tankers contained liquefied vinyl chloride gas, the combustible and carcinogenic precursor material for PVC pipe; others contained ethylene glycol, a toxic ingredient in antifreeze. Driving the lead locomotive was Tony Faison, the train’s engineer; with him were the train’s conductor and a trainee.

Engineers chart their progress by designated mile markers along the track. About 20 minutes earlier, the train had crossed mile marker 69.0, just east of Salem, Ohio. While crossing that spot, an infrared sensor built into the track called a “hotbox detector” had reported elevated temperatures on one of the front axles of the 23rd railcar. The ambient temperature that night was 10 degrees Fahrenheit. The bearings on the axle had reached an abnormally hot temperature of 103. The car, a hopper designed to hold commodities like grain, wasn’t carrying hazardous materials, but the hotbox detector relayed an alert to Norfolk Southern’s Atlanta command center all the same. No further action was taken.

As the train left East Palestine, it approached Ohio’s border with Pennsylvania, passing within a few hundred feet of the State Line Tavern, a local watering hole. There, at 8:55 p.m., it crossed mile marker 49.8. As the twenty-third car crossed the next hotbox detector, the infrared sensors revealed that the temperature of the axle’s bearings had risen sharply, to over 250 degrees. Faison immediately received an audio message from the locomotive’s onboard computer to stop the train. He reacted quickly to apply the brakes, but it was too late. He didn’t know it, but for the previous 40 minutes, his train had been on fire.

The train took more than a thousand feet to come to a stop. As it did, the compromised axle gave way. The left-side journal box, which held the axle in place, broke off and landed on one side of the track; the wheelset, consisting of the axle with two steel wheels mounted at both ends, ended up on the other. The twenty-third car jumped the rail, and the cars behind it followed suit, creating a tremendous series of crashes that could be heard throughout town. Thirty-eight railcars piled up, including 11 of the hazmat tankers.

Faison leaped from the locomotive to inspect the damage. From his standpoint at the front of the train, he could see flames rising into the night. He immediately contacted 911. So did many of the town’s residents, reporting both the train crash and the fire. One thought a gas station had exploded.

In the next few hours, the toxic flames would force an evacuation of the town. The specter of chemical poisoning lingered over East Palestine for months. And even today, the question of how a system of detectors—expressly designed to prevent this kind of derailment—failed to notice a dangerously overheated train axle remains unanswered.

In the minutes after the derailment, first responders rushed to the blaze, but they were initially underequipped. Serving a town of fewer than five thousand people, the East Palestine fire department was a mostly volunteer force. The sole professional on staff was Chief Keith Drabick, who on that night was almost three hundred miles away, driving through Pennsylvania on vacation. Informed of the crash at 9 p.m., Drabick turned his car around and drove straight back to East Palestine, but he didn’t arrive until five hours later. For the first few minutes, volunteers had to fight the blaze alone. Meanwhile, following protocol, Faison cut the first two locomotives from the train and moved them a mile down the track. In the confusion that followed, some firefighters seemed unaware they were responding to a hazmat site and reported to residents that the burning train cars were carrying only malt liquor.

Some of the train cars were carrying malt liquor, but others contained stronger stuff. As the scope of the disaster slowly became clear, the volunteers were joined by professional firefighting crews from nearby counties, including a special hazmat squad. At 9:45 p.m., concerned about the risks of a vinyl chloride explosion as well as the toxic cocktail of flaming chemicals escaping into the night, officials began evacuating nearby homes. Meanwhile, some of the contents of the leaking tankers began seeping into nearby Sulphur Run, a stream that flowed directly from the crash site through the center of town.

Even before the official order, citizens had started to evacuate. East Palestine resident Jami Wallace had learned of the train wreck from her mother. Wallace, a human resources manager in her forties, had recently gotten engaged. She called her fiancé, who was with a friend at the State Line Tavern. Driving past the burning crash site, he raced home to collect Wallace and their three-year-old daughter. “Grabbed her a couple of changes of clothes and out the door we went,” she told me. “We didn’t even know where we were going. It was the middle of winter and the heater was broken in the car.”

After an hour and a half of firefighting, the Ohio State Police expanded the evacuation zone to one mile surrounding the derailment site. Around midnight, still fearing an explosion, the firefighters retreated. They then began to survey the crash site with aerial drones, in an attempt to determine which specific chemicals were leaking. The survey was challenging: The site was, well, a train wreck, and some of the plastic hazardous-materials placards had melted in the fire.

Eventually, responders determined that three hazmat cars had been physically breached. One contained ethylene glycol, the antifreeze ingredient, which can be lethal in concentrated doses. The other two contained acrylates, used as base ingredients in adhesives and paint. All three materials were burning off, releasing volatile organic compounds into the air. The fire was additionally fueled by nonhazardous but flammable railcar cargo, including several tankers loaded with petroleum lubricants. For days to come, an ominous toxic cloud hung suspended over the site. “You know how smoke, like, moves through the sky? Yeah, this wasn’t moving anywhere,” Wallace said. “It was almost like a green cloud that was, like, hovering.”

Initially, none of the vinyl chloride tankers were breached. (If they had been, a series of explosions might have occurred, and the cancer-causing chemical could have rained down on the town.) Still, five vinyl chloride tankers, containing more than 115,000 gallons of vinyl chloride in total, had piled up in the burn zone. Each tanker had an emergency pressure release valve designed to vent gas into the atmosphere. Over the next few days, as temperatures rose inside the tanks, these valves automatically opened and closed, periodically releasing excess vinyl chloride gas into the air—where it immediately caught fire. In one extraordinary display on the evening of Saturday, February 4, one of the tanker valves vented for 70 continuous minutes, creating a spectacular flamethrower.

With the crash site cordoned off and the tankers burping flames, officials deliberated on what to do. One worry was that the release valves on the tankers were starting to suffer thermal damage. Another was that the vinyl chloride inside the tanks might “polymerize,” forming into chains of PVC, which might cause the valves to stick, sealing the pressure in and causing the tankers to blow.

From the outside, the hazmat experts couldn’t be sure if polymerization was occurring. Eventually they settled on two options. One option was to deliberately puncture the tanks and conduct a controlled burn of the vinyl chloride gas. The other option was to wait it out and hope the tanks cooled down enough so they wouldn’t explode. Chief Drabick was presented with this devil’s bargain: Wait, and potentially watch the exploding tanks rain shrapnel and poisonous chemicals on his town, or release mass quantities of vinyl chloride—a known Group A carcinogen—into the atmosphere. “I was given 13 minutes to make a decision,” Drabick told investigators from the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB), the federal agency responsible for investigating the wreck.

After consulting with his chief officers, Drabick chose to vent and burn. Following an expanded evacuation order, specialists attached explosive charges to the exteriors of five damaged tanker cars. At 4:37 p.m. on February 6, the charges were detonated, sending twin columns of flaming vinyl chloride gas high into the air and obscuring the setting sun with thick, black smoke. The burn continued through the following day; it was not until February 8, five days after the axle on train car 23 had first started to burn, that the fire was fully put out.

East Palestine soon found itself host to another kind of toxic cocktail, one consisting of corporate communications specialists, blustering public officials, government bureaucrats, and enterprising class-action attorneys. Complementing this splendid company were the more respectable representatives of the NTSB. Leading the agency’s efforts was Ruben Payan, an NTSB veteran with a heavy build, a thick mustache, and a calm and measured voice. Under his patient command, the NTSB began a thorough investigation of the crash site and the events leading up to the derailment.

The agency published the first investigation update to its website in March 2023. And then on June 22, Payan presented his preliminary results at a public meeting in East Palestine. (It was the first onsite NTSB meeting in six years.) Using security camera footage collected from homes and businesses adjacent to the tracks, Payan was able to present a detailed videography of the train’s final minutes. Between the towns of Sebring and East Palestine, more than a dozen surveillance cameras had captured the train in motion; in ten of those camera feeds, the train was plainly on fire. In true-color camera feeds, the lower axle of the twenty-third car glowed a dull orange color; in infrared camera feeds, it blazed an intense white, throwing visible sparks.

The first two cameras to show the fire were in Salem, Ohio, some 26 miles west of East Palestine. The train passed the first camera at 8:11 p.m., 44 minutes before the derailment. That camera, which overlooked an alley of snow-covered cars, caught the train in the far background, its axle glowing orange. The camera was located six miles in front of the Salem hotbox detector—the one that had sent an alert to Atlanta but did not stop the train.

How had the Salem hotbox detector missed the fire? The cameras clearly showed flames and sparks along the length of the bottom of the twenty-third car, but when that same car crossed the hotbox detector 10 minutes later, infrared sensors registered the bearing temperatures at only 103 degrees. This wasn’t a case of a sputtering fire that started and stopped, either—the cameras along the route showed a steady blaze. The NTSB declined to comment for this story, citing the pending results of the final investigation. Norfolk Southern declined to comment as well.

I put the question to David Farwick, a veteran engineer who commanded trains in Ohio for Norfolk Southern for nearly 40 years. He told me that Norfolk Southern’s systems were well maintained and up to date. “Those hotbox detectors, they’re pretty sensitive,” he said. “It’s not like we were working with 1960s stuff. They were pretty good.” The detectors are positioned among the crossties on the track and use infrared sensors to scan the undercarriage of the train. More than 6,000 are deployed across North America. The sensors on the hotbox detectors line up directly with the roller bearings. Farwick seemed flabbergasted that a flaming train had crossed a detector and not tripped an immediate brake alert. “It blows my mind,” he said.

Regulators have also grown concerned in recent years about how long the trains are getting. Farwick told me trains are growing so long that engineers have trouble seeing the backs of them, even on a curve. I asked him whether the train crew would have known they were carrying hazardous materials. “Absolutely,” he said. Farwick explained that the conductor on each train carries a bound paper manifest of the train’s cargo known as a “consist.” In the event of a derailment or crash, a hard copy of this consist is to be immediately delivered to first responders. But Drabick, when questioned by NTSB investigators, said his firefighters never received the consist directly from the Norfolk Southern train crew: “I do not believe that we had any contact with those individuals,” he said. Drabick was only fully informed of the train’s hazardous contents when he arrived on site hours later.

The other looming question about the crash involves the degree of environmental poisoning East Palestine has suffered. In the months following the vent and burn of vinyl chloride gas, Environmental Protection Agency personnel repeatedly visited the town and surrounding areas to take soil samples. Per the EPA’s website, “the sample results indicate that impacts from the smoke and soot were minimal.” The EPA has also monitored the health of the town’s waterways. In the aftermath of the disaster, the agency recorded more than 40,000 dead fish and aquatic animals in the Sulphur Run creek adjacent to the derailment and burn site. While the agency claims that the creek “has not shown any contaminants at levels that exceed health standards since May 1,” it continues to maintain “Keep Out” signs posted around Sulphur Run.

East Palestine is immediately downstream of the crash site, and many local residents believe the creek has delivered poison into their homes. Two days after the derailment, Wallace returned to her evacuated residence to pick up some medication. “As soon as I pulled into my driveway, it hit me in the face—I started coughing ... until, like, I can’t breathe,” she said. “I look over because I know it’s the creek. I look over, and I see these chemicals free-floating down.”

Wallace told me water from the creek regularly seeps into the basement of her residence, and that she has since relocated. She has pushed for the EPA to start indoor monitoring in East Palestine homes; so far, the agency has declined. In any case, the damages Norfolk Southern owes the town are substantial. In June, Norfolk Southern announced that cleanup costs and injury compensation settlements related to East Palestine would cost the company nearly $1 billion, though it anticipated that much of that cost would be covered by insurance.

In a statement a couple of weeks after the crash, Jennifer Homendy, the chair of the NTSB, described the accident as “100 percent preventable,” but didn’t offer specifics. She was likely referring to the “hot axle” phenomenon. Train axles use ring-shaped bearings that keep the axle secure while permitting it and the wheels to rotate. A skateboard’s wheels rotate using lubricated ball bearings inside the wheels. Train cars instead use cylindrical roller bearings, which make contact with the axle, permitting easy rotation.

As of December 2023, the NTSB has not yet made a final determination, but multiple experts I talked with told me that they believed a failed roller bearing was the most likely cause of the East Palestine derailment. About two dozen trains derail this way in North America every year. Bearings can fail for any number of reasons, including insufficient lubrication, contamination, overloading, and, simply, age. Once a bearing fails, the axle begins to grind against the metal, and this friction causes a rapid rise in temperature; this was potentially the source of the fire. “Bearings do break down, but that’s the reason why you get these detectors, right?” Farwick said. “That’s exactly what these things are supposed to prevent.”

The roller bearings on train axles are sealed inside the wheel and can’t readily be accessed. A faulty one can easily escape visual detection. Hotbox detectors, by using infrared temperature sensors to monitor the bearings in motion, offer a second layer of protection. Generally speaking, they work. Since the early 1980s, train derailments in North America have fallen from more than 7,000 annually to just over 1,000, in part because of hotbox detectors.

The place to catch the failed roller bearing was not in East Palestine, but 20 miles west, in Salem, Ohio, where the train had crossed a detector 30 minutes before the derailment. That detector had recorded temperatures 93 degrees above the outside environment and sent a noncritical signal to Norfolk Southern central command in Atlanta. Whether dispatchers in Atlanta relayed this warning to the train crew remains unclear; the NTSB has yet to publish transcripts from the train’s black box recorder, and Norfolk Southern has refused to discuss the details of the accident.

Perhaps it is worth noting that in the days before the derailment, the East Palestine train had already been delayed twice by stops for unrelated mechanical issues.

In March, the NTSB opened a probe into Norfolk Southern’s safety culture. Regulators were concerned not only by the East Palestine derailment, but also two other Ohio derailments in the surrounding months, as well as separate incidents in which three railroad workers on Norfolk Southern lines were killed in a span of 16 months, starting in December of 2021. In a statement announcing the investigation, the NTSB urged Norfolk Southern “to take immediate action today to review and assess its safety practices.”

This October, Norfolk Southern unveiled a new layer of protection: giant metal sheds, festooned with cameras, that each train will pass through at various points on its journey. The shed is described as a “portal,” and its cameras take an average of 1,000 images per railcar, and send those images to an A.I. data center. Deep-learning algorithms are then employed to spot problems that track detectors and overworked railcar mechanics cannot.

Following the derailment, legislators introduced the bipartisan Railway Safety Act of 2023, which proposed decreasing the required distance between hotbox detectors to 15 miles, from an average of 25 miles today. The legislation is well intended, but it’s not clear if it would have prevented the East Palestine derailment: On that track, the hotbox detectors were an average of 16.7 miles apart. Closing the distance to 15 miles wouldn’t necessarily help.

The most striking revelation from the NTSB’s preliminary findings was the sheer number of camera feeds that had captured the train car on fire. It costs about $200,000 to install a hotbox detector, and critics have estimated the cost of compliance for the Railway Safety Act at up to $2 billion. Perhaps wireless video cameras could permit dispatchers and AI to regularly monitor the status of the cars, and would give engineers better visibility to the back of the trains.

Finally, there’s still the problem of the toxic derailment site. It remains a hazard zone, and the nearby State Line Tavern remains closed. Under the guidance of the EPA, much of the topsoil near ground zero was excavated. The soil was supposed to be shipped to a hazardous waste facility in Oklahoma, but that state’s governor, Kevin Stitt, blocked the plan in March. Similarly, the contaminated water from Sulphur Run was drained. The water was supposed to be sent to a treatment facility in Baltimore, but that fell through too.

For a while, the poisoned water and soil remained at the derailment site. “They have these big Shamu tanks,” Wallace said. “They each hold, like, 100 million gallons of water.” Wallace said a neighbor had flown a drone over the tanks, and seen the chemical sheen on top. Nearby, the toxic dirt was piled into giant mounds, and covered with tarps.

However, as of January 2026, the EPA reported that personnel had completed a “site-wide cleanup and restoration,” in which crews cleaned the remaining oily sheens from nearby waterways such as Leslie and Sulphur Runs, and removed more than 38 million gallons of wastewater. They also removed any remaining contaminated soil and debris for treatment or disposal, and completed the derailment site excavation. The EPA is now sampling groundwater, surface water, and drinking water quarterly and will continue monitoring the area. Comprehensive updates of the work are available at the EPA’s website.

#6398. Which came first: black holes or galaxies?

Astronomers once assumed galaxies were born before black holes, but giant black holes spotted in the early universe are forcing them to rethink their order of events.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Nearly every large galaxy is thought to have a supermassive black hole at its center. The Milky Way's black hole, known as Sagittarius A*, is enormous, weighing over 4 million times as much as the sun. But which came first: the black holes or the galaxies around them?

Astronomers told Live Science that they thought they knew, but new observations mean they're no longer sure.

For decades, the prevailing idea was that galaxies came first: Dying massive stars leave behind black holes that can merge and feed until they swell to millions of times the sun's mass, said Joseph Silk, an astrophysicist and professor at Johns Hopkins University.

Then, in recent years, the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) began peering back at the early universe. "Recent observations are challenging this picture, or at least showing us that it cannot be the whole story," Roberto Maiolino, a professor of astrophysics at the University of Cambridge, told Live Science in an email. "We are finding extremely massive black holes just a few hundred million years after the Big Bang."

The galaxy GHZ2 (white box) contains the oldest known supermassive black hole. Discovered by the James Webb Space Telescope in 2022, its light had to travel some 13.4 billion years to reach Earth.

Stranger still, some of these black holes look too big for their hosts. In nearby galaxies, a central black hole is typically about a thousand times less massive than its galaxy, Maiolino said, but some early ones "appear to be almost as massive as the stars in their host galaxies." In a study in the journal Nature, Maiolino and colleagues measured one such black hole's mass directly in an object called Abell2744-QSO1 and found that it holds most of the object's mass.

So where could such giants come from? Maiolino outlined several possibilities, and more than one may be correct. Some supermassive black holes may be ordinary stellar remnants that grew much faster than usual. Others may have been "born big," forming from the direct collapses of enormous gas clouds, which "would give the black hole a head start in its growth," Maiolino explained. Another idea is that these monsters were seeded by primordial black holes that formed "shortly after the Big Bang, before the first stars and galaxies existed."

Further complicating the question is that black holes and galaxies also push and pull on each other. A growing black hole can release an enormous amount of energy that heats or expels gas, which, in turn, curbs or shuts down star formation, Maiolino said.

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

However, it can also compress gas and potentially trigger new stars. "Black holes and galaxies influence one another throughout their evolution, and neither can be understood entirely in isolation," he said.

A black hole spewing jets inside the elliptical galaxy Centaurus A.

Silk said the balance varies. In giant, elliptical galaxies, black holes weighing billions of suns can have "histories of extreme violence" that helped limit their hosts' growth, while in spirals like the Milky Way, feedback from stars tends to dominate.

So which came first? Answering that question will take far more data from JWST. Right now, "we have samples of tens of objects, maybe 20, 30, 40," Silk said, and astronomers need far more data to tell whether oversize black holes are typical.

If black holes outweigh their galaxies the farther back astronomers look, that would strongly suggest black holes formed first, Silk said; if stars dominate, it would point the other way.

Maiolino suggested the question itself may need rethinking. "Asking which came first may be too simplistic," he said. "The more interesting question may be how black holes and galaxies formed, grew and influenced one another at different stages of cosmic history."

There may be no single sequence. "Different black holes, in different environments and at different cosmic epochs, may have formed and evolved through different pathways," Maiolino added.

For now, the cosmic chicken-and-egg puzzle remains open. As Maiolino put it, astronomers are "beginning to explore a period of cosmic history for which we still have many unanswered questions."

Olivia Maule is a former Live Science intern and science journalist whose beats include space, biotechnology and the environment. She holds a B.A. in biology and a B.S. in anthropology from the University of Florida and completed a master's degree in science communication at U.C. Santa Cruz. A 2025 AAAS Mass Media Fellow, she wrote stories and produced videos during a summer at El Nuevo Día, Puerto Rico's largest newspaper, and has written for Eos, Mongabay, Science magazine and Stanford Report. Olivia is a native Spanish and English speaker.

#6397. Crowded Proteins Can Change How Enzymes Work

Laboratory research suggests that nearby proteins can reshape enzymes, offering clues to how the physical environment inside our cells may help regulate the chemistry of life.

In laboratory droplets designed to mimic conditions inside cells, enzymes worked faster as the liquid became more crowded with proteins, up to a point. Active enzymes also helped nearby molecules move more freely through the liquid.

Many of the chemical reactions that keep cells alive occur in the cytoplasm, where proteins and other molecules can gather into compartments without an enclosing membrane. Researchers from the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology (OIST), in collaboration with the Max Planck Institute for Dynamics and Self-Organization (MPI-DS) and RIKEN, studied how enzymes interact with these crowded environments.

“What’s fascinating is that we can connect interactions between individual atoms to the movement of molecules across an entire droplet. Events at the smallest scales can shape, and be shaped by, the physical behavior of a much larger system,” says senior author Professor Paola Laurino, who leads the Protein Engineering and Evolution Unit at OIST.

The OIST researchers prepared tiny droplets containing different concentrations of a protein called bovine serum albumin (BSA). In separate experiments, they introduced two enzymes, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH), along with their substrates, the molecules upon which the enzymes act.

Enzyme activity increased as more BSA was added to the droplets. Only at very high protein concentrations did crowding begin to interfere with the reactions.

“This initial increase in enzymatic activity seemed counter-intuitive, as you’d typically expect any level of crowding to impair movement of the enzymes and substrates and increase the liquid’s viscosity, therefore slowing down the reaction from the start,” explains Laurino.

Laurino and her team also used fluorescent tracers to examine how enzyme activity affected the movement of molecules within the droplets. Both BSA proteins and fluorescent nanoparticles moved more freely in the presence of active enzymes. Droplets containing modified, inactive enzymes were more viscous, and molecules moved more slowly through them.

“Similarly, we found that higher concentrations of the enzymes or their substrates in the droplets also increased mobility,” says Professor Ramin Golestanian, director of the Department of Living Matter Physics at MPI-DS.

The researchers used fluorescent markers to track the movement of nanoparticles in the droplet. Credit: Dindo et al., 2026, 10.1038/s41467-026-77666-y.

Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations conducted by researchers at RIKEN suggested that crowding helped accelerate reactions by changing the shape of the enzymes. The simulations showed that the active site, the region where substrates bind and react, was open under dilute conditions and closed as the concentration of surrounding proteins increased.

“When closed, the energy barrier required was much lower, allowing the reaction to happen more readily,” explains Laurino. “To detect such a change in these simulations by MD was really surprising to us.”

Researchers at MPI-DS developed a theoretical model to explain the increased movement within the droplets. They proposed that enzyme activity creates differences in chemical concentrations throughout the liquid, generating tiny flows.

“These flows allow the molecules to move more freely and mix within the droplet, highlighting how enzyme activity can potentially lead to physical effects across larger scales,” says Golestanian.

Laurino plans to investigate whether these interactions also occur in complexes where several enzymes operate in close proximity. Her team will also conduct experiments in living bacterial cells to determine whether the findings hold under more complex biological conditions.

Reference: “Enzymes can activate and mobilize dense biomolecular condensates across scales” by Mirco Dindo, Jakob Metson, Weitong Ren, Michalis Chatzittofi, Kiyoshi Yagi, Alessandro Bevilacqua, Erika Fukuhara, Yuji Sugita, Ramin Golestanian and Paola Laurino, 30 October 2026, Nature Communications. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-77666-y

Funding: Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology Graduate University, Japan Society for the Promotion of Science, Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology Japan, RIKEN

#6395. Another bill to release Epstein files headed to House floor

Massie will force another vote on releasing files in the Jeffrey Epstein case. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo)

As Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., enters his final weeks in Congress, he is one step closer to another vote on legislation related to the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

A discharge petition led by Massie aimed at extracting more files from the Justice Department has now received enough support to force a vote on the House floor.

Rep. John Garamendi, D-Calif., was the decisive 218th signature on the discharge petition, a procedural tool allowing rank-and-file House members to register their support for a piece of legislation and circumvent leadership to force a vote. Massie and other supporters of the effort say the bill is a bid for transparency.

Earlier this week, Massie said his pitch to his colleagues was simple.

“They could be a hero if they sign it,” he said, as he chased down the final two signatures as the House returned from recess on Monday. Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., signed just before Garamendi.

Massie’s time left in office is ticking down after a challenger backed by President Donald Trump ousted him in his GOP primary earlier this year.

The petition marks the second push led by Massie to require the release of the Epstein files. Last fall, Massie and Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., led a discharge petition on a bill dubbed the Epstein Files Transparency Act, which directed the Justice Department to publicly release documents in its possession related to Epstein and his associate Ghislaine Maxwell.

The bill passed the House by a vote of 427-1 last November, and in the Senate a few days later. Trump signed the measure shortly afterward.

In a statement this summer, Massie said he believes the Justice Department is still withholding more than 3 million files that it is required to release under the November 2025 law and is “maintaining heavy redactions” on others.

The new bill would allow state attorneys general, local prosecutors and victims to sue the federal government for withholding such documents. It would also allow victims to privately view unredacted versions of any records that mention them.

Now that the new petition has reached 218 signatures, it must sit for seven legislative days before being called up by anyone who signed it. Last time around, Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., scheduled a House vote on the initial Epstein bill before that ripening period was over, saying it was a foregone conclusion that the legislation would reach the floor.

Other Republicans who have signed on to the petition this year include Reps. Nancy Mace, R-S.C.; Ralph Norman, R-S.C., and Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Pa., none of whom will be returning next Congress. Rep. Lauren Boebert, R-Colo., backed the initial effort last fall, but her name did not appear on the petition this time.

Allies of the issue in Congress have faced pushback from Trump. While the president suggested during his 2024 reelection campaign that he was open to declassifying some Epstein documents, Trump then shifted gears, calling them a “hoax.”

“Once you get to 218, you can never sign it," Massie said. "There's nobody left, no spots left. It goes straight to the floor, and then you can vote for it. But you were never part of the group that actually got it to the floor."

#6394. Physicists Crack a 44-Year-Old Nuclear Fusion Mystery

Scientists have found a way to predict the heating requirements of future fusion machines, offering valuable insight into one of the biggest challenges of harnessing the energy that powers the Sun.

In 1982, scientists studying nuclear fusion discovered something unexpected. Once the heating power inside an experimental fusion machine reached a certain level, the fuel suddenly became much better at retaining heat. This discovery offered a way to overcome one of the biggest challenges in fusion research. More than four decades later, predicting how much power is needed to trigger this change remains a difficult problem.

Nuclear fusion releases energy when light atomic nuclei combine, the same process that powers the Sun. Recreating this process on Earth requires heating a gas to extreme temperatures, turning it into plasma, a state of matter made up of electrically charged particles.

Machines called tokamaks use powerful magnetic fields to confine this plasma inside a doughnut-shaped chamber. However, keeping the plasma in place does not necessarily keep it hot. Turbulent motion within the plasma can carry heat away, making it difficult to maintain the conditions needed for fusion.

The phenomenon discovered in 1982 occurs when heating power crosses a critical threshold, causing turbulence near the outer edge of the plasma to drop sharply. Scientists call this the transition from low confinement (L-mode) to high confinement (H-mode), a state in which the plasma retains energy much more efficiently.

Achieving H-mode is essential for future fusion reactors. The difficulty is that the amount of heating power required depends on several factors, including how densely packed the plasma particles are and the direction of the magnetic field. Existing theories have struggled to explain both effects together.

In a study published in Physical Review Letters, researchers led by Brenno De Lucca, a doctoral assistant at EPFL’s Swiss Plasma Center (SPC), developed a theory that explains these effects within a single physical framework.

Using computer simulations, the researchers recreated the behavior of plasma inside a tokamak as heating power increased. They identified the physical processes responsible for the transition, developed a mathematical model to describe them, and compared its predictions with experimental measurements from existing tokamaks.

Their results showed that turbulence generates flows within the plasma that move at different speeds across its outer region. As neighboring layers move past one another at different speeds, they help disrupt the turbulent motion that created them in the first place. This reduces heat loss, allowing the plasma to retain more energy.

The researchers also found that the direction of the magnetic field, the movement of the plasma, and collisions between particles work together to make H-mode easier to reach in one magnetic field configuration than in the other.

Plasma density presents another complication. Increasing the density can reduce the amount of heating power needed in one range and increase it in another. The researchers derived equations describing these changes and other operating conditions, explaining why there is a particular density at which the heating requirement is lowest.

The model could help researchers determine whether future fusion machines will have sufficient heating power to achieve H-mode. For ITER, the world’s largest international fusion project, currently under construction in France, the researchers predicted a minimum requirement of 43 megawatts, comfortably below its planned heating capacity of 73 megawatts.

The outlook is tighter for SPARC, a compact tokamak that uses powerful magnetic fields and is being developed by the U.S. company Commonwealth Fusion Systems. Its predicted minimum heating requirement is 26 megawatts, slightly above its planned capacity of 25 megawatts, leaving considerably less room for uncertainty.

Reference: “Theory for the Power Threshold of the L−H Transition in Tokamaks” by B. De Lucca, P. Ricci, B. Labit, D. Mancini, L. N. Stenger and Z. Tecchiolli, 13 November 2026, Physical Review Letters. DOI: 10.1103/rw25-wy15

Funding: EUROfusion Consortium, European Union Euratom Research and Training Programme (Grant Agreement No. 101052200), Swiss State Secretariat for Education, Research and Innovation (SERI), Swiss National Science Foundation (SNSF), and Swiss National Supercomputing Center (CSCS)

#6393. Scientists Watch Electrons Make an Impossible-Looking Quantum Leap

Experiments with graphene have revealed how remarkably effectively light can control electrons, offering a possible route toward a new generation of high-speed electronics.

Imagine riding an elevator whose floor indicator climbs from 1 to 2 to 3 before suddenly jumping to 20. You arrive at the twentieth floor without ever passing through the floors in between. In the quantum world, electrons can make a comparable leap in energy, and physicists have now found a way to watch it happen in slow motion.

Researchers from the University of Regensburg, Philipps-Universität Marburg, and Forschungszentrum Jülich combined laser technology with electron microscopy to capture this unusual behavior in graphene, a material made of atomically thin layers of carbon. Their findings, published in Nature, could help lay the groundwork for future high-speed electronics that use light to control the movement of electrons.

In semiconductors and related materials, electrons can occupy only certain ranges of energy, known as energy bands. Separating these bands are gaps containing energies that electrons are not allowed to occupy. Electrons normally remain within their respective bands, though under certain conditions, they can jump from one band to another without occupying the forbidden energies in between. Physicists call this process a Landau-Zener-Majorana transition.

The researchers used the electric field of an intense light pulse to accelerate electrons in graphene, observing how they switched between energy bands as they moved. Under these conditions, the probability of electrons crossing the gap through a quantum process known as tunneling reached as high as 100 percent.

Even when energy states are well separated, electrons can have a high probability of making the jump. What matters is how quickly they approach the energy gap. This makes the process fundamentally different from conventional quantum tunneling, in which a particle passes through an energy barrier in space.

Capturing these fleeting transitions required the researchers to observe large numbers of electrons simultaneously.

“If you want to know who has won a race, you have watch all participants,” explains Vincent Eggers, first author of the study. “Likewise, we must observe as many electrons as possible at one time to catch those that undergo a quantum mechanical transition while moving.”

To do this, the team used an instrument called a photoemission momentum microscope. Rather than producing magnified pictures of objects, the microscope measures the energies and states of motion of electrons, creating a map of how they are distributed. The challenge was combining these measurements with powerful, rapidly oscillating light fields that could drive electrons in a controlled manner.

“Our team worked on this experiment for many years. Now, we can track electrons moving across the entire energy landscape of a solid in real time,” says Rupert Huber.

The experiment also depended on exceptionally pure graphene samples specially produced at Forschungszentrum Jülich.

Ulrich Höfer, Huber’s research partner and one of the pioneers of ultrafast electron spectroscopy, recalls, “Being able to observe such a fundamental quantum mechanical process during our first measurement campaign was a very special moment for us—it was also made possible by the samples we used.”

“These precision experiments require material that is nearly perfect at the atomic level. This ensures that impurities do not obscure the delicate quantum dynamics of the electrons. Another important factor for the study was the use of “rotated” graphene, a specialty from Jülich, which allows the quantum dynamics to emerge particularly clearly,” emphasizes Stefan Tautz from Forschungszentrum Jülich.

Beyond capturing quantum transitions, the new technique allows researchers to investigate what prevents electrons from moving in a controlled way. The graphene experiments already revealed how interactions with the crystal lattice, the repeating arrangement of atoms within the material, disrupt the initially orderly motion of electrons.

Understanding these disturbances could become increasingly important as researchers explore technologies that use the extremely rapid oscillations of light to control electrons directly, rather than relying solely on electrical voltages.

“Our experiment opens a panoramic window into the quantum world. Now, we can follow in real time how electrons move through the energy landscape of a material. And this is just the beginning. Our method can be applied to many other quantum materials, opening up completely new possibilities for controlling their electronic properties selectively with light,” says Giacomo Inzani from the University of Regensburg.

Reference: “Subcycle videography of Landau–Zener–Majorana transitions in graphene” by V. Eggers, G. Inzani, M. Meierhofer, L. Münster, J. Helml, R. Wallauer, S. Zajusch, S. Ito, L. Machtl, H. Yin, C. Kumpf, F. C. Bocquet, C. Bao, J. Güdde, F. S. Tautz, R. Huber and U. Höfer, 28 October 2026, Nature. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11214-y

This work is supported by the Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft (DFG, German Research Foundation) through SFB 1083, project-ID 223848855, SFB 1277, project-ID 314695032, research grant HO 2295/9, research grant HU1598/8, GRK 2905, project-ID 502572516, DFG major instrumentation INST 89/520, project ID 445487514 and by the European Research Council (ERC) Synergy Grant, project-ID 101071259.

A stunning new image from the Gemini North telescope captures two spiral galaxies caught in each other's gravity, helping to trigger the birth of new stars.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

What it is: NGC 7253 (also called Arp 278), a pair of interacting spiral galaxies

Where it is: 200 million light-years away, in the constellation Pegasus

Picture a spiral galaxy, and you'll probably imagine a swirl of stars. But some galaxies appear to be the complete opposite. One is NGC 7253, which looks more like a bizarre balloon animal than a cosmic coil. In reality, it's two spiral galaxies caught in each other's gravity. As shown in this recent image from the Gemini North telescope on Mauna Kea in Hawaii, the galaxies' once-ordered shapes are being disturbed and disrupted as their mutual gravitational pull stretches and distorts their spiral arms into a tangled arrangement of stars, gas and dust. It sounds and looks chaotic and destructive, but encounters between galaxies don't mean stars are physically colliding; the distances between individual stars are too great. Instead, something extraordinarily productive can happen.

Spiral galaxies contain huge clouds of cold gas and dust, particularly within their arms. When galaxies interact, gravitational forces can disturb and compress those clouds. If enough material is squeezed together and becomes dense enough to collapse under its own gravity, it can produce bursts of new star formation.

Evidence of just that can be seen in this image. Scattered through the galaxies are concentrations of bright pink light. These are H II regions — enormous clouds of hydrogen gas energized by intense ultraviolet radiation from hot, young stars.

The gravitational encounter is rearranging two structures containing billions of stars while simultaneously helping to create new ones. These interactions radically alter the shapes of the galaxies involved and, in time, can ultimately cause them to merge into a single galaxy. For now, NGC 7253 is listed as Arp 278 in the Atlas of Peculiar Galaxies, a catalog of galaxies that are neither perfectly symmetrical spirals nor smooth, spherical ellipticals.

The new image has another story much closer to Earth. It's just been given the Hawaiian name Nā 'Uhane Māhoe Huki Pū i ke Ola, meaning "The Twin Spirits Pulling Together Creating Life." Hawaii high school students participating in the 2026 Project Hōkūlani internship program chose the name. One reason was its position within Ka Lupe o Kawelo, the Hawaiian constellation corresponding to Pegasus.

The "twin spirits" represent both the two galaxies and the twin telescopes of the Gemini Observatory — one in Hawaii and the other in Chile.
