#6391. The Maya People Loved the Color Red. Scientists Say It May Have Helped Bring Them Down.

The reddish pigment cinnabar was so popular that it seeped into the water supply around Maya settlements, setting off a disastrous downstream effect.

The Maya people had a toxic relationship with the color red—quite literally, according to fresh research. The new analysis of the Yucatán Peninsula during the Maya era identified astronomically spiked levels of mercury, which might have contributed to the collapse of Maya culture.

“The mercury data was crazy,” Matt Waters, an environmental sciences professor and paleolimnologist at Auburn University, said in a university statement about the unexpected discovery on the peninsula. “Off the charts. These mercury levels aren’t normal.”

Matt Waters led a study published in Science Advances that explored sediment samples collected at two lakes—Lago Coba and Cenote Xcach—showing the intense spike in mercury (Hg) levels ranging from around 40 C.E. to 800 C.E.

“We show that Classic Period Hg concentrations in sediment cores from two lakes on the Yucatán Peninsula exceeded modern sediment Hg toxicity thresholds by orders of magnitude for centuries during ancient Maya occupation,” the authors wrote, adding that the heightened pollution coincides with aquatic food collapse, “confirming that Hg toxicity was an additional environmental stressor for Classic Maya populations.”

While Waters isn’t saying mercury caused the collapse of the Maya civilization, he also doesn’t want to ignore its impact. “It’s been confirmed that drought was an issue, deforestation was an issue, erosion was an issue, overpopulation was an issue, and feeding the population was probably an issue,” he said. “This study adds the impact of water quality. Let’s put that in the list. That’s what our study does. It establishes that list and moves it forward.”

The study actually began as part of a National Science Foundation project focused on harmful algal blooms, but a then-graduate student and study co-author, Savanna Wooten, suggested also testing for heavy metals. Sediment coring from the lake bottoms pulled up mud from thousands of years ago that contained the intense mercury spikes during the Classic Maya Period, which were then followed by an abrupt decline.

The powerfully high mercury concentration lasted for hundreds of years, and Waters believes the sudden change at the base level likely moved up the food web, impacting fish and other larger creatures. Not only would eating fish or drinking water have exposed humans to the toxic levels, but there may have even been fewer fish to catch. “They would have seen a strange color change in the water,” Waters told Live Science, “and a drop in its productivity, such as fish for protein.”

Waters linked to a study he’d worked on with a team from the University of Florida in the late 1990s that found a gap in ostracod shells during a specific period from Coba, correlating the missing shell timing to the rise in mercury. Further investigation into the cores found that declines in biological markers occurred throughout. “The algae was killed,” he said. “The cyanobacteria, they tanked. Purple sulfur bacteria, vanished. The biological community completely changed.”

The people “experienced this for decades and, in one case, for centuries.”

The source of that mercury was cinnabar, they believe, a vibrant red mineral made up of 86 percent mercury that Maya culture viewed as a sacred pigment. “This was not like mercury raining down from the sky,” Waters said. “This was not a regional thing. It was concentrated.”

Maya loved cinnabar, using the bright red in pottery, murals, temple walls, and burials. To keep up with demand, they heavily imported it, especially around Coba and Xcach. “It’s common knowledge that there was trade in obsidian, in jade, and beautiful stones, and weaponry,” Waters said. “I think this could start a conversation that cinnabar could have been a major trade commodity.”

It may also show a highly toxic love affair that contributed to Maya struggles.

#6390. Caltech Scientists Make Billions of Atoms Flash in Perfect Quantum Harmony

Caltech scientists aimed a laser at a crystal and watched billions of atoms fall into step, firing bursts of microwaves and infrared light in perfect sync.

In early 2024, researchers in Andrei Faraon’s Caltech lab discovered that a laser could make billions of atoms inside a crystal emit regularly spaced pulses of light. A tiny superconducting circuit trapped the microwaves the atoms emitted, creating a shared field that brought the atoms into sync.

“Remarkably, the atoms were flashing in two very different kinds of light at once, microwaves and infrared light, in perfect step with each other. That had not been observed before,” says Andrei Faraon (BS ’04), Caltech’s William L. Valentine Professor of Applied Physics and Electrical Engineering and the Fletcher Jones Foundation Director of the Kavli Nanoscience Institute.

Faraon’s team and Stanford University researchers led by Joonhee Choi traced the rhythm to a quantum phenomenon called superradiance. They used it to create a frequency comb, a light source with evenly spaced frequencies that serve as the ticks on a ruler. Frequency combs help atomic clocks keep precise time, let scientists measure distances and track ultrafast events, and identify chemicals by the light they absorb. The new comb generates both microwave and optical signals, a combination that could help connect quantum devices.

The team embedded billions of ytterbium ions, or charged atoms, in a yttrium orthovanadate crystal beneath a thin layer of superconducting material that trapped microwaves. A laser energized the ions, and the microwave field they generated enabled them to influence one another and synchronize. At first, they emitted microwaves steadily. Once the laser power crossed a threshold, the steady emission gave way to regularly spaced pulses.

Scientists have known about superradiance for more than 50 years. In this process, a shared electromagnetic field synchronizes atoms so they emit light together. Earlier experiments had produced a single flash or a steady beam. In the crystal, the ions settled into a rhythm and flashed repeatedly.

“Imagine a crowd suddenly starting to clap in perfect rhythm without anyone leading them. That’s essentially what these atoms are doing when they produce repeated flashes of light, and it’s remarkable that they can organize themselves this way,” says Choi, a Stanford assistant professor and former Caltech postdoctoral scholar.

In a conventional laser, light bouncing between mirrors prompts excited atoms to release energy in step with the passing light. The spacing between the mirrors helps set the frequency, so even a tiny shift can change it. With superradiance, the atoms themselves can set the emission frequency.

“Other mode-locked frequency combs depend on bouncing light off mirrors in a cavity, and those cavity lengths can fluctuate due to things like temperature,” says Tian Xie (PhD ’25), lead author of the Nature paper. “Because superradiance comes from atom–atom interference, it’s absolutely frequency-stable, and therefore it can, in principle, be a much better platform than previous frequency combs.” Xie completed the work as a graduate student in Faraon’s lab and is now a postdoctoral researcher at Stanford.

The team wants to use the laser to control how the ions pulse, “so that the atoms become a kind of programmable light source,” Faraon says. “Being able to tune each emission strength, pulse separation, and emission format would be very useful to suit each specific application,” he says.

Superconducting quantum computers use microwave signals, which easily lose their quantum information outside the ultracold conditions near absolute zero (about minus 460 degrees Fahrenheit). Infrared light can carry information over long distances through fiber optic cables. For a superconducting circuit to use that connection, its microwave signals would need to be converted into optical signals.

Ytterbium ions can interact with both. Each ion has three energy levels relevant to the experiment. The smaller gap between a pair of levels matches the energy of a microwave photon, while a larger gap matches the energy of an infrared photon.

“Whenever these ions generate a microwave field, there is a process that naturally generates a corresponding optical field at the same time,” Xie says. “That’s why in the experiment, you send a laser light to pump the atoms, and you see two emissions coming out at very different frequencies.” The paired emissions suggest the ions could one day link superconducting circuits to optical fibers.

Reference: “Observation of tunable superradiant frequency combs” by Tian Xie, Rikuto Fukumori, Wai-Keong Mok, Jiahui Li, Joonhee Choi and Andrei Faraon, 18 November 2026, Nature. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11289-7

The work was primarily funded by the Office of Naval Research with additional support from the Institute of Quantum Information and Matter (IQIM), the US Department of Energy, the Co-design Center for Quantum Advantage, and the Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation Experimental Physics Investigators. Individual researchers were supported by the Air Force Office of Scientific Research, the Terman Faculty Fellowship at Stanford University, the Quad Fellowship, and the Eddleman Fellowship.

#6389. Rand Paul chooses ranking member slot at Senate HELP

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., leaves the Senate Republicans’ lunch in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., announced Wednesday he plans to serve as the top Republican on the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee when Democrats take control of Congress next year.

The move clears the way for Senate Ethics Chairman James Lankford, R-Okla., to use his seniority to ascend to ranking Republican on the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which Paul currently chairs, and touches off several other shifts at the top of other committees.

The move fit in with Sen. Lisa Murkowski’s bid to use her seniority to succeed Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, as top Republican on the Appropriations panel. If Paul did not go to the top spot on HELP, Murkowski, R-Alaska, would be next in line for that committee in the next Congress.

Murkowski is second in seniority on Appropriations to Collins, who was defeated for reelection. But she faces a potential challenge from Sen. Jerry Moran, R-Kan., who is next in line behind her.

Paul said in a press release that he plans to bring the same approach to the HELP Committee as he did as chairman of Homeland, where he said he “challenged entrenched bureaucracies, forced federal officials to answer for their actions, and pulled back the curtain on what Washington tried to keep hidden.”

He cited calling Dr. Anthony Fauci before the committee to probe the former federal health official’s role in pandemic-related shutdowns and the origin of the COVID-19 virus, and releasing thousands of pages of pandemic-related documents. The panel voted in August to hold Fauci in criminal contempt of Congress for declining to answer questions about the pandemic during a highly charged hearing.

Related: Fauci could face criminal contempt charge following panel vote

Paul, an ophthalmologist, said at HELP he will “stand against efforts to put Washington between Americans and their doctors, their children’s schools, and their paychecks.” He predicted “a rush toward socialism unlike anything we have seen” when the Democrat-controlled Congress convenes in January.

Lankford, in a separate statement, confirmed his interest in becoming the ranking member of the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee. In many areas, he said, the panel can work in a bipartisan manner, and over the past decade he “worked across the aisle to improve emergency communications in federal buildings, strengthen the United States Postal Service, increase federal cybersecurity preparedness, government transparency, and the use of artificial intelligence.”

But he added that his job also would be to “push back on a [Democratic] majority that goes too far . . . Oversight is responsible, but obstruction is unacceptable.”

Lankford said he would work together with the likely committee chair, Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., “when we can agree and be a fierce opposition if there is an attempt to undercut our nation’s security.”

#6388. The Government Tested How Dangerous AI Could Get—Then Four ChatBots Helped Plan a Terrorist Attack

The Government Accountability Office secretly tested ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Grok and found that all four would help make plans when prompted.

The dawn of artificial intelligence brings with it both rewards and risks. With the ability to sift through unfathomably large data sets, AI could help detect cancers in their infancy, unlock some of the most enduring mysteries of mathematics, and even help contain the beating nuclear heart of future fusion reactors.

Unfortunately, the risks of this technology are far from minuscule, including its impact on human education, the environment, and potentially the survival of the human race (an all-too-plausible scenario put forward by AI tech CEOs). Even the everyday LLMs that now litter our digital lives—Claude, Gemini, ChatGPT, and Grok—can aid and abet some of the most dangerous actors on the planet.

At least, that’s the latest conclusion by the Government Accountability Office (GAO), a nonpartisan watchdog housed in the legislative branch of the U.S. government. Typically, GAO turns its investigative gaze on efforts to limit fraud and wasteful spending in the government itself, but in a new tactic at the urging of U.S. Senator Maggie Hassan (D-NH), the office instead performed real-world tests on the platform to see if these four popular AI models would aid in planning a terrorist attack.

“A terrorist can log onto an AI platform and in less than 12 hours walk away with a concrete playbook for how to carry out a deadly attack,” Hassan, incoming Chair of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, said in a press statement. “Today’s new report makes it clear that the AI public safety threat is no longer theoretical.”

GAO conducted this test in the spring this year, and earlier this week reported some disturbing results. Two of the platforms, according to an official GAO release, provided guidance on building and detonating an improvised explosion device, or IED, and two other AI models showing differing methods for targeting the electrical grid. Within 12 hours, all four models also gamed through potential locations and methods for carrying out such an attack.

Although these violent lines of questioning triggered each platform’s safeguards, GAO got around them using common safeguard-bypassing techniques. Additionally, they confirmed the validity of the information provided with experts. The results of this investigation were published in a 61-page report that will be central to future senate hearings on AI safety.

“We set out to do two different types of evil,” GAO director Kevin Walsh said in an interview posted on YouTube. “The first type is we wanted to create a bomb. And we didn’t just want to know how to create a bomb, we wanted it to help pick out a target, a location, and a time, and to give us instructions all the way…Evil scenario two, we wanted to do a bunch of economic damage, and in both cases that ended up being targeting the electrical grid.”

In one case, Walsh reports that one AI model would refuse to answer questions or divert the user to more safe behaviors but said that “it wasn’t always successful.” Walsh says that companies theoretically call law enforcement when suspicious activity is detected, but whether that occurs and at what frequency is uncertain.

“As AI capabilities evolve, AI providers will continue to refine their safeguards,” the report concludes. “However, in its current state, this technology can potentially be dangerous and its misuse represents a growing risk to national and economic security.”

The GAO officially released these terrorist-abetting findings on November 18, 2026, the same day Anthropic, creators of Claude, went public on the stock exchange. Despite the company’s own admission of AI being an existential threat to humanity, its IPO at one point reached a meteoric a $2 trillion valuation before dipping back down to a (measly) $1.6 trillion.

#6387. Quitting statins after age 70 initially appeared to be safe, yet heart attacks, strokes, and deaths increased after four years off those meds

A trial of adults aged 70 and older without cardiovascular disease found that stopping preventive statins may carry greater long-term risks.

When adults aged 70 and older stopped taking statins for preventing a first heart attack or stroke, they did not see a significant jump in heart attacks, strokes, or deaths two years later.

A research team followed participants for a median of 103 weeks, and up to four years for some.

During that time, 12.7 percent of the group that stopped taking statins suffered a heart attack, a stroke, or death. That compares with 9.2 percent of the group that continued taking them.

The results were presented on Nov. 7, 2026, at the American Heart Association (AHA) Scientific Sessions in Chicago and published the same day.

Named STREAM, the trial enrolled 1,880 adults aged 70 or older with no known cardiovascular disease. The name stands for statin discontinuation as prevention among the elderly and multimorbid.

Every participant was taking a statin to lower cholesterol as primary prevention. That term means the drug is meant to head off a first such event, not a second one.

Each also had at least two chronic conditions, such as a past cancer or lung disease. The average age was 77, and 47 percent of the group were women.

Of those enrolled, 938 were randomly assigned to stop the drug and 942 to carry on.

STREAM ran from November 2021 to April 2026 at 24 clinical centers in Switzerland, France and the Netherlands. Hospitals in Bern, Lausanne, Geneva, Zurich and Basel were among the Swiss sites.

The main outcome combined three events: a nonfatal heart attack, a nonfatal ischemic stroke, or death from any cause.

During the first two years, 100 people in the group that stopped and 77 in the group that continued had one of them. That works out to 10.7 percent against 8.2 percent.

STREAM was built as a noninferiority trial, a design that asks whether stopping is not meaningfully worse than continuing. The two-year difference stayed within the limit set in advance.

Outcomes were judged by reviewers who did not know which group a patient belonged to, according to the University of Bern, which led the project.

Patients and their doctors knew the assignment, because STREAM was run open-label.

Its rationale was that the value of these drugs is uncertain after age 70 in people with no heart disease. Side effects and risky combinations of drugs are also common in that age group.

Across the full follow-up, 119 events occurred among those who had stopped, against 87 among those who had continued. The counts come from the AHA’s late-breaking science report.

The design centered on the two-year comparison.

Nicolas Rodondi led the work. He is professor of primary care and internal medicine and director of the Institute of Primary Health Care at the University of Bern.

He estimated that over two years, one additional major cardiovascular event or death would occur for every 40 people who stopped their statin.

The association’s report notes that the estimate requires further investigation.

A second set of measures looked at how people felt. Pain, quality of life, fall risk and muscle weakness showed no difference between the two groups.

Sarcopenia, the loss of muscle mass and strength that comes with age, was also no more common in one group than the other. Reports of muscle pain were no different either.

Roughly 14 percent of participants crossed over along the way. Some who had stopped restarted, and some who had continued quit.

Extra analyses that took those switches into account did not change the result.

“Our findings provide information for shared decision-making about cautious statin discontinuation when statins are used for primary prevention only,” Rodondi said.

The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) advises a statin for some adults aged 40 to 75. They must have at least one risk factor and a 10-year cardiovascular risk of 10 percent or more.

When that risk falls between 7.5 percent and 10 percent, it tells clinicians to offer the drug selectively, because the likely benefit is smaller.

For adults 76 and older, the task force concluded that the evidence is insufficient to weigh the benefits and harms of starting one. The recommendation dates from August 2022 and replaced a 2016 version.

Its advice turns on a patient’s overall risk, not on LDL cholesterol alone, and it addresses starting a statin. STREAM tested the opposite question: what happens when older adults already on a statin stop.

“Although deprescribing inappropriate drugs in older adults appears to be safe, the results of our trial suggest that additional randomized trials of discontinuation are needed for specific drugs,” Rodondi said.

The study was published in the journal The New England Journal of Medicine.

Astrophysicists have dared to ask a cosmological question never asked before: Do black holes "wear pants"? New research shows how fast-spinning black holes may split apart.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Black holes are known to collide and combine in monstrously violent merger events, but new research suggests these celestial stalwarts can also fragment into smaller bodies, like a cosmic pair of pants splitting down the middle.

In a paper published Oct. 22 in the journal Physical Review D, researchers used several mathematical modeling methods to propose a "pair-of-pants" topology for black holes. The hypothesis suggests that under extremely specific conditions, these dark behemoths could fragment into numerous less-massive black holes.

"Understanding precisely what is forbidden, what is merely unlikely, and what becomes possible once the assumptions are relaxed is the central goal of this work," the researchers wrote in the paper.

Black hole fragmentation could play into other cosmic mysteries. For example, it could help to explain black holes with masses that are too small to be formed through conventional astrophysical processes. These hypothesized black hole "morsels" would be so small that astronomers could see them evaporating before their eyes on observational timescales.

In the new paper, the researchers explored whether black holes' event horizons — the boundaries beyond which nothing, not even light, can escape — could split under various cosmological conditions. These situations included classical four-dimensional general relativity (Einstein's description of our large-scale universe as we currently understand it) as well as cosmologically esoteric frameworks such as higher-dimensional space-time and modified gravity scenarios.

But modeling black hole dynamics, especially the split of an event horizon, is messy work. So the researchers simplified it by comparing discrete slices of space-time, effectively condensing the fragmentation process into static snapshots from before and after the split.

In our classical cosmos, it seems mostly impossible for black holes to split, the researchers found, but they did identify a loophole that might allow it to happen.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The "pair-of-pants" topology for the fragmentation of a black hole.

The first impediment is entropy, the possible arrangements of an isolated system's energy, which cannot spontaneously decrease but only stay the same or increase. This has been theorized by Stephen Hawking and recently demonstrated through detections of ripples in space-time called gravitational waves, suggesting that a black hole's surface area cannot decrease.

For these reasons, splitting a static Schwarzschild black hole — the simplest type of black hole in our four-dimensional general relativity — would be strictly forbidden because it would violate the second law of thermodynamics.

The second impediment is kinematics, the motion of orbital dynamics, which precludes the possibility of a permanent split because the black hole fragments would recombine into a single body incredibly quickly.

But there is a loophole: A rapidly rotating black hole could literally spin itself apart.

"This is why, in four-dimensional general relativity, an isolated black hole in empty space could only split if it spins very close to the maximum rate the theory allows, what we call a near-extremal black hole," study co-author Manuel Del Piano, a theoretical physicist at the University of Southern Denmark, told Live Science via email. "Loosely speaking, the equator of the horizon is then dragged around at nearly the speed of light."

Through this theoretical process, the two resultant black hole fragments could be gravitationally slingshotted away from each other before they could recombine. So under conventional space-time conditions, it seems "black holes do not wear pants."

Then, the researchers mathematically modeled black hole fragmentation in versions of space-time with more than four dimensions.

In models of higher-dimension space-times, a black hole's rotational velocity is no longer limited because gravity weakens with increasing dimensionality. Therefore, any such ultrafast spinning black holes could theoretically fragment, the researchers explained in the paper.

A diagram from the new study illustrating the theoretical pants-splitting method.

In the "black string" model, a normally spherical black hole would become cylindrical or string-like, stretching across any extra dimensions. It could then pinch off to fragment into multiple smaller bodies, akin to "beads on a string."

Additionally, the researchers calculated that black hole fragmentation may be entropically favored in space-time models with modified gravity, which alter the gravitational interactions in extremely warped environments near the black hole.

"The fragments are tiny, though: in one of our benchmarks, a black hole of ten solar masses would favour fragments … a few times the mass of the Great Pyramid of Giza squeezed into a region smaller than a proton, and the heavier the parent, the smaller the fragments," Del Piano explained.

Fragmentation also may be more likely if there is a "bumpy horizon" around black holes, akin to a dense blanket or shroud of exotic matter that acts as a singular-but-gigantic quantum entity. The superfluid qualities of this matter could create strange vortices that eventually cause a black hole to fragment into multiple smaller bodies.

Scientists might see a black hole decrease in size, an actual fragmentation, or simply an indirect gravitational signature, depending on the dimensions and whether it intersects the viewer's "brane," or slice of dimensionality.

The researchers expect that smaller objects — like the hypothesized, miniature primordial back holes that may have formed shortly after the Big Bang — are more likely to split, compared with much more massive astrophysical black holes such as those at the centers of galaxies.

"Overall, we expect small black holes, such as primordial ones from the early universe, to be the most prone to splitting," Del Piano told Live Science.

Gamma-ray telescopes or gravitational wave observatories may one day offer evidence of a signal associated with the supposed split of a small black hole, but the specifics, including whether this actually occurs, are uncertain.

"One important caveat: our analysis shows when splitting is allowed by entropy and conservation laws, not that it actually happens," Del Piano noted. "As we put it in the paper, a shattered glass has more entropy than an intact one, yet glasses don't shatter on their own. Settling the question requires full dynamical simulations, which is the natural next step."

Cacciapaglia, G., Del Piano, M., Sannino, F., & Vellucci, V. (2026). When black holes admit pair-of-pants topologies. Physical Review. D/Physical Review. D., 114(8). https://doi.org/10.1103/cx69-t466

#6385. Astronauts could turn everyday trash and moon dust into something surprisingly useful

Researchers have combined paper fibers and simulated lunar dust to develop lightweight insulation that could be manufactured on the moon.

Trash on the International Space Station is bagged by astronauts and loaded onto a cargo ship.

The ship then either returns it to Earth or burns up in the atmosphere. On the moon, part of that waste might be put to use as insulation.

Paper fibers have now been ground together with imitation moon dust by a team of chemists.

The mixture was dried into an aerogel, an ultralight solid made mostly of empty space. Very little heat passes through such a material.

According to the results, some insulation for a lunar base could be made on site. Two ingredients would be needed, and both should be plentiful there: waste paper and the ground outside.

The recipe was developed by Alexander Wei, a chemistry professor at Purdue University, and graduate researcher Jacob Staker. Their colleagues included researchers at NASA’s Glenn Research Center in Cleveland.

Wei said a lunar settlement will generate waste rich in cellulose, the plant fiber found in paper and cardboard packaging.

“And I can guarantee that astronauts on the moon will never run out of moon dust,” Wei added.

For now, the aerogels exist only as samples made on Earth. A manufactured stand-in was used for lunar soil, and the paper was clean laboratory filter paper.

The final drying step relied on a method the team considers less practical on the moon than freeze-drying.

Between 60% and 70% of wastepaper by weight is cellulose. When cellulose is torn into much finer threads, it can strengthen a material in ways the original fibers cannot.

A stand-in for lunar soil, or regolith, has already been mixed with recycled plastic by other engineers. Wei’s team paired the dust with paper instead and used it as a grinding aid.

Filter paper was first shredded in a food blender. The team then loaded it into a mill together with water, ceramic cylinders, and a powder called Lunar Highlands Simulant.

This powder is made from Earth rock to match soil from the moon’s highlands.

For two hours, the jars were spun at an acceleration about 60 times that of Earth’s gravity.

The team expects a mill of this kind to work in the moon’s weak gravity.

The paper fibers were thinned by the ceramic cylinders alone. Once dust was added, they became much thinner still.

The most common fiber width fell to about 4 millionths of an inch (0.1 micrometers).

Fibers milled with dust were eight times thinner than those milled without it. They were also at least 30 times thinner than the original paper fibers.

The milled mixture was frozen in small molds, and its water was replaced with alcohol.

The team then removed the alcohol with pressurized carbon dioxide, which is a standard way of drying aerogels.

“Imagine an aerogel as a high-tech thermos for a lunar base,” Staker said. “Most of it consists of empty space that insulates the interior, helping it maintain the temperature of what’s inside.”

Empty space accounted for 79.3% to 98.6% of the volume in these samples.

In total, 18 batches were made, and the recipe was varied between them. Cellulose made up 1% to 9% of the wet mixture by weight. Dust made up 25% to 75% of the finished aerogel.

Insulation is rated by its thermal conductivity, which describes how easily heat passes through a material. A lower value is better.

The batches scored between 30 and 45 milliwatts per meter-kelvin when measured in air.

An earlier attempt had produced a freeze-dried aerogel of imitation regolith and natural polymers. Its lowest reported figure was 70 in the same units.

The best new batches therefore had less than half the thermal conductivity of the earlier material.

The best insulation came from the batches with the least cellulose. Among the 18, the lightest batch was made from a mixture with 1% cellulose. Its conductivity of 30.9 was the lowest in that group.

When exposed to the moon’s near-vacuum environment, the pores would contain virtually no gas.

The team expects the aerogels to insulate better under those conditions. Several times less heat is conducted by other aerospace aerogels in a near-vacuum than in air.

Temperatures on the lunar surface can reach 266°F (130°C). That heat is a problem for many of the organic materials used in aerogels.

A sample heated in nitrogen did not start to break down until about 653°F (345°C).

Insulation and stiffness responded to the recipe in opposite ways. Heat was generally blocked best by the low-cellulose batches.

However, those batches were also soft, and they shrank the most during drying.

A batch made with 1% cellulose came out 52% narrower than its mold. Only 3.2% shrinkage was seen in a batch made with 9% cellulose.

The stiffest batch was also made with 9% cellulose. Under compression, it was nearly 300 times stiffer than the softest batch.

“Rather than trying to make the world’s best aerogel, we’re looking for the sweet spot where we can get the properties we need with the limited resources we have available,” Wei said.

To look for that balance, the team fitted a statistical model to the 18 batches. Three recipes suggested by the model were then made and tested.

Dust would be far more plentiful on the moon than waste paper. For that reason, one recipe was required to be at least 60% dust by weight.

A figure of 61.2% was suggested by the model. The resulting aerogel had a conductivity of 30.5, which was the lowest in the study.

The same aerogel shrank by about half. It also did not meet the standards for the strength test.

A second recipe was balanced across six measured properties. It insulated nearly as well, at 30.8, and shrank by 18.5%. This aerogel was stiff enough to be tested, but only 25% of it was dust.

The aerogels have not yet been made the way a lunar crew would make them. The team wrote that freeze-drying would be far more practical on the moon than the carbon dioxide method.

According to Wei, the lunar surface offers a natural vacuum and subfreezing temperatures at night. Wei said the water removed from the aerogel could also be recovered and reused.

However, this kind of material can be damaged by freezing. Growing ice crystals pack the fibers and dust together.

That packing is known to lower the quality of cellulose aerogels. To slow the growth of the crystals, the team proposed adding simple alcohols or sugars.

Only one kind of imitation dust was used, and the paper was not real trash. Every heat-flow measurement was taken at 73°F (23°C) in air.

For the weakest recipes, additives known to strengthen cellulose aerogels should be tested, the team suggested.

Freeze-drying is now being studied by the team for its next batches. Those tests should show whether a freeze-dried aerogel can insulate as well as the samples made so far.

The full study was published in the journal ACS Sustainable Chemistry & Engineering.

#6384. Flying squirrels have an unusual habit that may shape entire forests

Flying squirrels in China may influence where young trees grow by storing nuts in branches instead of underground.

Squirrels help oak forests grow by burying acorns and forgetting about them. But two species of flying squirrel in southern China have a different way of storing food.

Instead of burying nuts, they tuck them between small branches. A new study suggests that this habit may affect where young trees grow.

Researchers found fewer seedlings a short distance from parent trees. But their numbers increased again about 66 feet (20 meters) away, where squirrels often store their nuts.

Scientists have usually linked this pattern to tree diseases. The new study suggests that squirrels may also play a role.

The work was carried out by Xuelian Tan, Han Xu and their colleagues at the Research Institute of Tropical Forestry. This institute is part of the Chinese Academy of Forestry in Guangzhou.

The study was a field survey of two tree species in a single forest. It therefore shows a match between stored nuts and seedlings rather than proof that the squirrels planted them.

The research took place in Jianfengling, a forest within the Hainan Tropical Rainforest National Park on Hainan Island.

The forest averages about 67°F (19.7°C), and about 97 inches (2,461 millimeters) of rain falls there each year. In total, 992 species of free-standing trees and shrubs have been recorded in the forest.

Two of these trees are Cyclobalanopsis edithiae and Cyclobalanopsis patelliformis, which are close relatives of oaks. Their nuts are smooth and are not covered by the small cup at their base.

Many animals feed on these nuts. Their slick surfaces make them difficult to hold in place on a branch, however.

The flying squirrels solve this problem by gnawing grooves into the nuts, allowing them to wedge their food between branches.

The grooves differ between the two kinds of nut. Oval C. edithiae nuts usually receive one zigzag groove around the middle. Flatter C. patelliformis nuts, on the other hand, may carry up to 20 grooves on the underside.

Most stored nuts sat 33 to 82 feet (10 to 25 meters) from the nearest possible parent tree. Photographs in the new study show squirrels returning to collect their nuts.

Another image shows a gnawed nut that had fallen to the forest floor and begun to sprout.

The importance of this behavior is linked to an older idea about how tropical forests work. During the early 1970s, the ecologists Daniel Janzen and Joseph Connell observed a pattern among tree seedlings.

Young trees, they noticed, were seldom found close to adults of their own species. The pair put this down to disease and pests.

Fungi and plant-eating insects that target one tree species spread from an adult tree to the seedlings around it.

Seedlings close to the parent are therefore more likely to die. Most seeds, however, land near the parent tree in the first place.

When both effects are combined, most surviving seedlings would be expected at a middle distance from the parent.

Ecologists refer to this process as conspecific negative density dependence. In simpler terms, plants tend to do poorly when they are surrounded by their own species.

This effect helps prevent any single species from dominating a forest. It is one reason why a rainforest can support so many different kinds of trees.

An earlier study in one of the Jianfengling plots detected the effect in 89% of tree species.

Where a seedling ends up hinges on two separate events. A seed has to land somewhere, and the young plant has to survive in that spot.

Seed-carrying animals can shift the first of these. Whether they could mimic the disease pattern on their own had gone largely untested.

Twenty parent trees anchored the survey. On ten of them, squirrels had lodged nuts in at least one direction.

The other ten were bare on all four sides. Each of the first ten trees got two survey lines.

One pointed toward the stashed nuts, and the second ran off where no nuts hung. A single line from each bare tree, comparable in trunk size, formed a second point of comparison.

Markers went down every 16 feet (5 meters), stopping at roughly 100 feet (30 meters). Beside each marker lay three plots about a yard (1 meter) square. Every seedling inside those plots was tallied.

Seedlings along the test lines were most plentiful beside the parent tree. Their numbers, however, fell away at 16 and 33 feet (5 and 10 meters).

At 49 and 66 feet (15 and 20 meters), on the other hand, the counts climbed once more. Farther out they declined again, and the comparison lines showed no second rise at all.

The 66-foot mark stood out in particular. There, the test lines held more seedlings than both comparison groups. The difference was statistically significant.

This is, notably, the very band of distances in which the squirrels hang their nuts. Beside the trunk itself, the test lines also held more seedlings, though only relative to the second group.

The authors offered a simple explanation, namely that trees ignored by squirrels may produce fewer nuts. Fewer nuts would mean fewer seedlings and, in turn, fewer squirrel visits.

Comparisons on two sides of the same tree therefore mattered, since seedling numbers vary widely from tree to tree.

Disease, for its part, ought to leave more damage on saplings close to the parent. Fine roots from 33 young trees were therefore examined, 15 of one species and 18 of the other.

The trees grew at different distances from adults. Each sapling’s root samples were inspected at 100 points under a microscope for lesions, which can indicate infection.

The level of damage, however, showed no clear trend with distance.

Fungi are not cleared by this result. Root lesions, the authors wrote, may not reflect the full pressure that pathogens place on seedlings.

They also wrote that “our results do not imply that pathogens are unimportant.”

Squirrels that move nuts are, in their account, one more possible influence on where seedlings take root.

Tan and Xu’s team has not confirmed whether squirrels directly help new trees grow. Other animals and local growing conditions may also play a role.

Changing how squirrels store nuts could provide stronger evidence, but such experiments are difficult in the wild.

The researchers suggest tracking seedlings over several years to see whether the nuts grow into healthy trees. Future studies could also examine other animals and forests.

The full study was published in the journal Forest Ecosystems.

#6383. This Company Wants to Make Fuel From Carbon Dioxide—Using the Power of a Nuclear Reactor

AIRCO hopes to make a carbon-neutral fuel from captured CO2 and hydrogen. Some sustainability experts are skeptical.

The fossil fuel industry is the largest contributor to climate change, and it’s not even close. According to the United Nations, the industry is responsible for 68 percent of all greenhouse gas emissions and an incredible 90 percent of all carbon dioxide emissions. Stick a stake in the vampiric heart of fossil fuels, and beating back the worst effects of global warming becomes suddenly much more possible. But as the recent climate summit at Antalya, Türkiye, this month displayed, the industry shows no interest in giving up its polluting ways, leading some countries to say the world is now “held hostage by the oil mafia.”

Despite this unwillingness to change, some companies are trying to find ways to make some good out of a bad situation. One of those companies AIRCO (originally named Air Company), based out of New Britain, Pennsylvania, did just that by developing a technology that creates jet fuel of a thin “air”—well, kind of.

Instead of making fuel at a massive refinery and transporting it long distances, the system is designed to produce fully formulated synthetic jet or diesel fuel closer to where it will be used,” Nick Steinke, the company’s director of programs, government and defense, said in a recent interview with Waste360. “It takes captured CO₂ and hydrogen and integrates the conversion process into a modular, containerized system.”

Instead of relying on centralized fuel producers, the idea is that synthetic fuels could be created on-site where they’ll be used directly, circumventing the climate impacts of transporting the fuel entirely. Also the ingredients AIRCO uses also aims to come from green sources by leveraging carbon capture technologies for the required CO2 and using electrolysis to supply hydrogen from water.

Chemical & Engineering News reported earlier this year the company hopes to supply the U.S. military with a complete reactor system by 2027 that will be powered on a government site using a small nuclear reactor (SMR), and supply a sufficient flow of energy required for both carbon capture and electrolysis to provide the volumes of ingredients needed to make these mobile, fuel-creating systems viable. It’s a task that at least one expert says sounds easier said than done.

“The technology seems like it holds a lot of promise, especially on the fuel-conversion side, but the part that I have a lot of questions about is, where are you getting the carbon from?” Sarah Gleeson, a materials scientist at Project Drawdown, told WHYY, a local radio station. “Because if they’re saying that there’s some kind of direct air capture functionality in this really mobile device, I would be skeptical at the capacity and efficiency of it.”

Carbon capture is central to the company’s promise of its technology’s carbon-neutral nature with the company’s CEO telling WHYY that “using more CO2 in our production process to make the fuel than we are putting out in the entire process.” Carbon capture, as a broad technology category, still remains unproved even as some climate models rely on its implementation (and the fact that the oil industry likes the technology is concerning to say the least).

If humanity hopes to secure a healthy planet for future generations, ending its reliance on fossil fuels is priority number one. But step one in the process is first limiting—and eventually eliminating— new fuel from being extracted from the ground in the first place while the advancements in green chemistry try to put to work the carbon dioxide that’s already here.

#6382. Standard fertility tests may be missing an important clue about sperm health

Retained mitochondrial DNA in mature sperm has been linked to longer times to pregnancy, even among men with normal semen test results.

Men in couples who struggle to conceive are usually sent for a semen analysis. The test measures sperm count, concentration, shape and movement. Normal results do not guarantee a quick pregnancy.

A study of 327 men with normal semen results has now pointed to one extra factor. Some of their mature sperm still carried mitochondrial DNA.

This DNA belongs to the mitochondria, the parts of a cell that make energy. Couples needed more time to conceive when the man’s sperm held more of it.

The study was carried out at the Wayne State University School of Medicine in Detroit. It was observational, so a link was found but a cause was not established.

The senior author was J. Richard Pilsner, a professor at Wayne State’s C.S. Mott Center for Human Growth and Development.

“These findings provide an important new window into the male contribution to reproductive success,” Pilsner said.

Almost every cell in the body contains mitochondria. Energy for the cell is generated within these small compartments.

Mitochondria contain their own circular DNA, which carries 37 genes. In humans, it is passed on through the mother.

R. E. Giles and colleagues reported this maternal pattern in PNAS in 1980. Defects in these genes underlie several inherited diseases, and mitochondrial donation has been used to prevent their transmission.

Mitochondria are retained by the egg. According to a separate study, women’s egg cells keep this DNA largely free of age-related damage.

In sperm, a different process is assumed. Most paternal mitochondrial DNA is thought to be eliminated during sperm production.

That assumption sat awkwardly beside earlier data. Higher sperm mitochondrial DNA had been associated with lower semen quality and with longer times to pregnancy.

Two sources were proposed for the excess DNA. Ordinary body cells may have contaminated the samples, or immature sperm cells may have been present.

Purified, frozen sperm from the LIFE Study were analyzed by the Wayne State team. Couples in that cohort had been enrolled before conception and followed while they attempted pregnancy.

Female partners kept daily journals. Time to pregnancy was then calculated in menstrual cycles.

Inclusion was restricted to men who met the 2010 WHO criteria for sperm count, concentration and shape. Of these, 327 were analyzed.

Mitochondrial DNA was quantified by digital PCR, a method that detects and counts individual copies of a target sequence.

Values ranged from 0.5 copies at the lower end to 49.0 copies at the upper end.

Bulk measurements cannot indicate which cells contain the DNA. Imaging of individual sperm was therefore required.

Samples from 18 men were selected at random, six from each of the low, moderate and high groups. Fluorescence in situ hybridization, which labels a chosen DNA sequence with a glowing tag, was adapted for sperm.

Image scoring was performed blind to group. A total of 50 sperm per participant were assessed.

Signal was located in the midpiece, a segment between the head and the tail. Mitochondria are arranged in a sheath around this segment.

Distinct spots were resolved around the midpiece in three-dimensional microscope images. Signal was not localized to the head or tail.

Jeffrey Mann, the study’s first author, is a postdoctoral fellow at Wayne State. He described the meaning of the images.

“Directly visualizing mitochondrial DNA within the sperm midpiece provides compelling evidence that the mitochondrial DNA detected by polymerase chain reaction reflects DNA retained within mature sperm,” Mann said.

Men with higher DNA levels had a larger share of glowing sperm. The correlation between the two measures was 0.87, where 1 would be a perfect match.

In men with moderate or high mitochondrial DNA levels, the glowing signals covered a larger area of the sperm midpiece than in men with low levels.

Sperm within a single sample differed from one another. In high-group samples, glowing sperm were found beside sperm with no signal.

A high reading appears to reflect a mixed population. Some sperm kept their mitochondrial DNA, while others removed it as expected.

DNA levels were then compared with the time each couple took to conceive. Higher levels were linked to a lower chance of pregnancy per menstrual cycle.

The team reported a fecundability odds ratio of 0.79. Values below 1 indicate lower odds of pregnancy per cycle as levels rise.

Differences between the low, moderate and high groups were unlikely to be due to chance. The link remained after adjustment for both partners’ age, body mass index and smoking.

Pilsner linked the imaging and pregnancy results.

“For the first time, we directly visualized mitochondrial DNA retained within mature sperm and showed that this feature is associated with lower likelihood of achieving pregnancy, even among men with normal semen parameters,” Pilsner said.

The team views the measure as a possible addition to routine semen analysis. A separate study found that body fat can lower sperm counts in men of normal weight.

“These findings suggest that conventional semen analysis may miss molecular signatures within sperm that provide important information about couples’ ability to conceive,” Pilsner said.

The study did not prove that retained DNA slows pregnancy. Only an association was shown.

Men with abnormal semen results were excluded. This limited the influence of other sperm problems on the findings.

The results cannot yet be extended to men with abnormal semen or diagnosed infertility.

Some factors were not measured. These included how often couples had sex, which also affects time to pregnancy.

The probe detects specific DNA sequences. Whether each spot represents a complete mitochondrial genome or a fragment is still unknown.

Imaging was performed on only 18 men. The microscope images have been posted online for other researchers.

Future studies could test a link with TFAM, a protein that packages mitochondrial DNA. Retention in men with abnormal semen results could also be examined.

“This finding opens new questions about the molecular mechanisms that allow some sperm to retain mitochondrial DNA,” Mann said.

Normal semen results may not give a complete picture of male fertility. Leftover mitochondrial DNA in sperm could be worth measuring alongside the standard tests.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

Archaeologists discovered a stash of Celtic coins ahead of a construction project for an electrical substation in Hungary.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists in Hungary have discovered a stash of more than 200 Celtic silver coins that are over 2,000 years old. It's one of the largest hoards found there in decades.

Researchers unearthed the coins during excavations ahead of construction for an electrical substation in western Hungary between 2023 and 2025, according to a translated statement from the power company E.ON. The hoard dates to sometime between the late second century B.C. and the early first century B.C.

The coin cache weighs roughly 4.4 pounds (2 kilograms). In today's market, it's worth more than $2,000 as raw silver alone, but its rarity and historical value effectively make it priceless, the statement said.

The site was once part of a farm, and plowing there had unearthed several individual coins in recent decades, the statement said.

During the latest excavations, archaeologists initially found a few coins and then searched the area with metal detectors, which led them to the coin hoard. The treasure had been packed inside a small ceramic vessel and sat about 16 inches (40 centimeters) below ground.

"This is a rarity in Europe," Eszter Kreiter, an archaeologist at Hungary's National Archaeological Institute, said at a news conference, according to local news outlets. She added that the last similar find was made in Hungary in the late 1960s.

The hoard's silver coins are modeled on Greek tetradrachms — a very early type of large silver coin that was introduced in the late sixth century B.C.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The newfound Celtic tetradrachm copies are a type known as "Velem," which are named after Velem-Szent Vid, a fortified Celtic hilltop settlement, or oppidum. Similar coins have been found at that site, which is located about 10 miles (15 kilometers) to the west.

Each coin has a stylized head on one side that probably depicts the Greek god Apollo, and portrays a helmeted rider and horse on the other side.

Artifacts from more than 7,000 years of occupation have been found at the site, including a glass bead (bottom, center) thought to be about 2,500 years old.

The excavations have revealed evidence of more than 7,000 years of occupation at the site, officials wrote in the statement. The artifacts include a nearly 7,000-year-old polished stone chisel used for woodworking and a glass bead with a peacock's eye pattern that seems to have been part of jewelry from the sixth or seventh century B.C.

A Roman-era villa was built at the same site in later centuries, without disturbing the hoard of buried silver, Kreiter said at the news conference.

The site in Hungary's western Szombathely region was excavated between 2023 and 2025 ahead of the construction of an electricity substation.

The villa has long since been demolished, but the excavations enabled the archaeological team to reconstruct its floor plan, including its underfloor heating system, she said. They also found a Roman-era brick with a dog's paw print.

The artifacts from the site will become part of a museum exhibition.

According to Museum Wales, the Celts were loosely related Iron Age peoples descended from Proto-Indo-European speakers. Emerging in Central Europe, Celtic groups occupied much of Central and Western Europe from about the 10th to the first century B.C. The Celtic Gauls were finally defeated by the Romans, led by Julius Caesar at Alesia, now in eastern France, in 52 B.C. The Britons were also Celtic, though most people of Celtic descent would not have recognized that name.

Several modern ethnic groups, including the native Irish and the Bretons of coastal France, trace their descent to the Celts. Regions with strong Celtic origins are sometimes called the "Celtic fringe" of Western Europe.

Writing in the Journal of Roman Studies, the British coin expert Christopher Howgego, an honorary curator and professor emeritus of Greek and Roman numismatics at the University of Oxford, stated that Celtic tribes in the Carpathian Basin, now in Hungary and Romania, started minting their own silver coins after Celtic mercenaries had seen them when serving with Hellenistic armies in Greece and Macedonia.

Howgego has written that the Greek-inspired Celtic coins included adaptations of classical Greek portraits, as well as distinctive Celtic designs. These copycat tetradrachms held very high value for their makers, so they were rarely used for everyday purchases. Instead, they were often hoarded as wealth or buried as ritual offerings.

Tom Metcalfe is a freelance journalist and regular Live Science contributor who is based in London in the United Kingdom. Tom writes mainly about science, space, archaeology, the Earth and the oceans. He has also written for the BBC, NBC News, National Geographic, Scientific American, Air & Space, and many others.

#6380. The prickly pear cactus has a surprising trick for surviving in the desert

Scientists have discovered that tiny, short-lived leaves help prickly pear cacti capture carbon during the day and accelerate growth.

Cacti are usually described as plants that replaced their leaves with spines and thick green stems.

When rain finally reaches the desert, though, the prickly pear sprouts small green leaves on each new pad. Within a few weeks, these are shed again.

A team in Israel found that these leaflets behave like the leaves of a common garden plant. Carbon dioxide is taken in by them during the day.

The researchers estimate that they supply about a fifth of the carbon a young pad needs for growth.

So the cactus has two ways of gathering carbon rather than one. Older pads collect it after sunset, and the leaflets add to the supply once the sun is up.

The research was conducted by scientists at Ben-Gurion University of the Negev (BGU) in Israel. They worked with researchers from the Gilat Research Center of the Volcani Institute.

Potted plants of Opuntia ficus-indica were grown for the experiments. This is the prickly pear species that is cultivated on farms.

The plants were kept in a net house on BGU’s desert campus at Sde Boker. They were watered every day for a year.

Ilya Gelfand is a professor at BGU’s Jacob Blaustein Institutes for Desert Research and a co-author of the study.

“The cactus effectively has two gears,” said Gelfand. “Most of the year it runs in saving mode and breathes at night to hold on to every drop.”

“When water arrives, it switches on a second, faster gear: temporary leaves that work by day like a regular plant. When the good times end, it simply drops them.”

In most plants the tiny pores on the leaves are opened during the day.

Carbon dioxide enters through them and is used by the plant to build sugars. Water is lost through the same openings, and that loss becomes costly in hot desert conditions.

Cacti, agave and many other succulents get by on less water because their pores open at night instead. The carbon dioxide is stored as an acid until the following morning.

The pores then close, and carbon dioxide released from the stored acid is used to make sugars with the help of sunlight.

This strategy is known as crassulacean acid metabolism or CAM. Mature prickly pear pads rely on it so heavily that scientists classify the species as a full-time CAM plant.

The prickly pear is also an important crop that is grown on about 6.4 million acres (2.6 million hectares) worldwide.

Much of this area lies in drought-prone parts of Africa and South America. In these regions the plant is used for food and livestock feed and for slowing desertification.

Until this project, nobody had examined the leaflets as working organs. Each one measures only about 0.4 inch (10 millimeters) in length.

Around 150 of them can be carried by a single new pad, and they fall off after about six weeks.

The study was led by Patrick Mdemba, who is a doctoral student at BGU. Pores were the first thing he and his colleagues examined.

Clear nail polish was brushed onto pads and leaflets at five different times of the day. After the polish had dried it was peeled away and examined under a microscope. Each thin film preserved an impression of the pore openings.

The older pads opened their pores at night, which was the expected result for a CAM plant. The leaflets showed the opposite pattern. Their pores were opened in the morning and closed after dark, as in a typical leafy plant.

Young pads that were two weeks old did not follow either pattern. Their pores were found to be open at every time the team checked.

Acid build-up between dusk and dawn was then measured in each tissue. A large amount was stored overnight in the older pads.

The young pads stored more acid as they grew older. In the leaflets no significant difference was seen between the dawn and dusk readings.

Mdemba’s team also looked at the carbon inside the leaflets. Carbon in nature comes in a lighter form and a heavier form. Cactus pads that feed at night build up more of the heavier one.

In week-old leaflets the carbon looked much like the carbon in the pads. The mother pad had probably supplied it. Five weeks later the leaflets held noticeably more of the lighter form that daytime leaves collect.

For a second test the researchers sealed whole plants in a clear box almost 4 feet wide. They filled it with carbon dioxide made from the heavier form. One run lasted from 10 a.m. until noon, after the pads had closed their pores.

The marked carbon was found in the leaflets. The pads on those same plants gained no significant amount.

Next came leaflets with no pad at all. Mdemba cut them from pads less than a week old and kept them in sealed jars on a sugar-free gel.

In sunlight the carbon dioxide in each jar went down. Under aluminum foil it went back up. The cut leaflets also grew heavier until about day 15.

Mature pads in an earlier study took in carbon dioxide about twice as fast per square inch as the leaflets.

Mature pads in an earlier study took in carbon dioxide about twice as fast per square inch.

The team then worked out a carbon budget. A pad with about 150 leaflets gets roughly 0.12 grams of carbon a day from them. A 1998 study put a growing pad’s daily need near 0.6 grams. So the leaflets supply about 20% of it.

The leaflets covered their own growth first. What was left over went to the young pad.

Mdemba then took the leaflets away. All of them were cut off some young pads. On other pads they were left on but painted with clear nail polish, which sealed their pores.

Pad size was checked every five days. By day 25 both groups were about a third smaller in area than normal pads. Pads with no leaflets also weighed about 38% less at three weeks.

Without working leaflets, then, a new pad grew more slowly.

“That lets the cactus grow quickly whenever the desert briefly allows it, without giving up its ability to survive drought,” said Gelfand.

Desert rain tends to arrive in short bursts. For desert plants the timing of that water can matter a great deal.

Some desert shrubs drop their leaves when life gets hard. The prickly pear makes its leaflets in the wet weeks and drops them within about two months.

Every plant in the study got water daily. That may have made the leaflets look more important than they would be in a dry field. Well-watered pads may rely less on their night feeding.

The authors listed other limits too. They did not measure the two enzymes that capture carbon in each system. Gas exchange was not followed over a full 24 hours. Their conclusions come from pores, acid and carbon tracers instead.

They recommend measuring those enzymes in leaflets and young pads, along with gas readings around the clock.

Plants under drought stress should be tested as well. That work could show how much the leaflets matter when a wet spell is short.

The full study was published in the Journal of Experimental Botany.

#6379. Older adults don’t need to lift heavy weights to build strength

Strength training with lighter weights may help older adults build strength and maintain muscle mass without heavy lifting.

Strength training is recommended for older adults to help maintain muscle, balance and independence. Heavy loads are commonly used in these programs.

Earlier research has reported that pain and high physical demands can lead older adults to drop out. The authors note that those who drop out often have traits associated with frailty.

A pilot trial in Perth, Western Australia, compared heavy training with lighter training in 40 adults over 55. Strength increased in both groups over 12 weeks.

Neither group showed a measurable change in muscle mass.

The study was led by Brett Buist of the School of Human Sciences at the University of Western Australia. Training intensity was chosen by the participants rather than assigned at random.

“Both high- and lower-intensity resistance exercise appears equally effective at improving muscle strength while maintaining muscle mass and quality of life in older adults,” Buist said.

Frailty has been linked to falls, hospital admissions, disability and death. Low physical activity and the loss of muscle mass and strength are listed among its common contributors.

The condition is not always permanent. Ohio State University’s guide to frailty states that it can often be slowed or improved with support.

Low strength is reflected in poorer walking and balance. These changes are known to raise the risk of a fall in older adults.

World Health Organization figures cited in the paper put the share of people over 60 at 12% in 2015. That share is projected to reach 22% by 2050.

Lifting weights appears on the National Institute on Aging’s list of strength exercises. The Perth study examined how heavy those weights need to be.

Of the 40 recruits, 33 were women. All participants were living independently in the community.

Sessions were held twice a week at the university under the supervision of exercise physiologists or physiotherapists. Every session included a leg press, a deadlift and a bench press.

Drop jumps from a low box were also performed in each session. The box was about 4 inches (10 centimeters) high, and each landing delivered a firm impact through both feet.

A four-week introductory phase at low-to-moderate intensity was completed by all participants. From week five each person could either move to the heavy program or continue at the lighter level.

In both groups the sets were ended while two to five more repetitions could still have been completed.

The number of sets multiplied by repetitions was matched closely between the two programs. In this way the load on the bar remained the main difference.

To be classified as a heavy lifter, a participant had to leg press more than 80% of their estimated maximum. That level had to be reached in at least three out of every four sessions.

Twelve participants met this standard and 14 trained at the lighter level.

By the end of the trial both groups were able to press more weight with their chests and legs. Strength was assessed using the one-repetition maximum, which is the heaviest weight a person can lift once.

Increases in chest press, leg press and leg press relative to body weight were found in each group. Substantial loads were still handled by the lighter group.

Leg press loads in that group averaged about 71% of maximum. Deadlift effort was rated at a median of 5 on a 10-point scale.

Earlier reviews of research in older adults have generally favored heavy lifting for building strength. In some of the studies behind them, heavy training was compared with loads as low as 20% of maximum.

According to Buist’s team, loads that low were probably insufficient to increase strength. Unequal amounts of total work have also complicated earlier comparisons.

Leg press strength relative to body weight was the only outcome that differed significantly between the groups. However, the authors advised caution when interpreting this result.

“Clinicians can target factors that contribute to frailty using resistance exercise with intensity tailored to individual preferences without compromising outcomes,” said Buist.

Neither group showed a measurable gain in muscle. Lean mass measured by whole-body X-ray scans stayed close to baseline in both programs.

This stability was viewed by the researchers as a useful result because lean mass usually declines with age.

Lean tissue already accounted for about 64% of the volunteers’ body weight at the start. This proportion was higher than in a comparison study cited by the authors.

No protein supplements were provided during the trial. The training volume was modest as well, with 12 working sets in each session. Some studies that did produce muscle growth used as many as 39 sets.

A small reduction in body fat as a share of total weight was observed in the lighter group. Higher general health scores on the SF-36 survey were reported by the heavy group.

Other scores on the questionnaire changed very little in either group. Most volunteers began between the 50th and 75th percentiles for Australians of their age and sex.

Postural sway was measured on a force plate during standing trials of 30 seconds each. After training the recorded sway path was longer under some of the test conditions.

A longer sway path is normally taken as a sign of poorer balance. However, scores on the 14-item Berg Balance Scale did not decline and balance confidence was maintained.

The authors suggest that participants may have been exploring their limits of stability. Resistance training is known to extend those limits.

The participants who completed the trial were not the group of greatest concern. Of the 39 people tested at baseline, 12 withdrew for reasons including joint pain and holidays.

An average baseline weight of about 162 pounds (73.7 kilograms) was recorded for those who withdrew. Participants who stayed averaged 133 pounds (60.4 kilograms) and had greater leg strength relative to body weight.

Heavier and weaker adults are of particular concern in frailty research, and they were overrepresented among the dropouts.

The final analysis included only 26 people, so small differences between the groups may have been missed. Physical activity outside the supervised sessions was not recorded.

Bonnie Furzer, a co-author from the University of Western Australia, presented the findings as guidance for those who prescribe exercise.

“For older adults who are not tolerating high-intensity resistance and impact training, lowering exercise intensity should be considered to assist adherence whilst maintaining benefits,” said Furzer.

Longer trials and studies in frail adults have been recommended by the authors.

Until that evidence is available, a weight that people continue to lift may matter more than the heaviest one possible.

The full study was published in the journal Translational Exercise Biomedicine.

#6378. Scott Colom elected Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction

Mississippi Democrat Scott Colom, here at a news conference in Jackson on Nov. 4, has defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. (Rogelio V. Solis/Getty Images)

Democrat Scott Colom has unseated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith to become Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction.

The result is a stunning flip for Democrats in a deep-red state where they last won a Senate election in 1982, and it brings the Senate Democratic Caucus to at least 55 seats in the next Congress.

Colom was leading Hyde-Smith 49.2 percent to 48.7 percent — or by just over 4,600 votes out of more than 960,000 cast — when The Associated Press called the race Wednesday, a little over a week after Election Day. Ty Pinkins, the 2024 Democratic Senate nominee who ran as an independent this year, had 2 percent.

In recent days, as absentee and provisional ballots were counted, Colom had all but declared victory, repeatedly saying that Hyde-Smith had no path to victory.

“I'll work every day in the U.S. Senate to build a future that generations of Mississippians can be just as proud to call home,” he posted Monday on social media.

With his victory, Colom joins several other Democrats who flipped seats in deep-red states, including Texas’ James Talarico, Kansas’ Adam Hamilton and South Carolina’s Annie Andrews. Democrats have so far flipped eight Senate seats to win control of the chamber, overcoming a difficult Senate map and giving them their largest majority in the chamber since 2011.

That majority could expand further if Democrats flip the Senate seat in Alaska, where former Rep. Mary Peltola narrowly leads Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan.

Republicans have dominated Senate elections in Mississippi in recent decades. The last Democrat to be elected senator in the Magnolia State was John C. Stennis, who won his sixth full and final term in 1982. Colom will be the third Black man to serve as a Mississippi senator after Republicans Hiram Revels and Blanche Bruce during Reconstruction.

While Revels and Bruce, who left office in 1881, were elected by the state Legislature, Colom will be the first Black senator elected directly by voters.

Colom has served as a district attorney for four counties in northeast Mississippi since 2016. President Joe Biden nominated him for a federal district judgeship in 2022, but Hyde-Smith effectively blocked his nomination by not returning a so-called blue slip, a Senate Judiciary Committee tradition that lets senators derail district judge nominees in their home states.

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer said last week that he’d had Colom in his sights for several years as a potential Senate candidate, including for a race against the state’s senior senator, Republican Roger Wicker.

“I had Scott Colom and his father come to my house, and I served them a nice little brunch or something. I said, ‘You got to run,’” the New York Democrat recalled to MS NOW. “They were smarter than me. This was four years ago. They said, ‘We don’t want to run this time, but we know that Hyde-[Smith], the incumbent, is so weak, we could beat her.’”

Still, the Mississippi race didn’t capture as much national attention as other Senate contests until the closing weeks of the campaign. A trio of Black senators, Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland, Lisa Blunt Rochester of Delaware and Cory Booker of New Jersey, all campaigned with Colom throughout the summer and fall. Key national figures, including former President Bill Clinton, former Vice President Kamala Harris and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, also stumped for him in October.

Colom’s campaign engaged voters with quirky ads and unconventional forms of outreach, including meeting with people lining up to attend a Trump rally. One ad that went viral played on Hyde Smith saying earlier this year that people had “so many proteins to choose from” when asked about rising beef prices.

“Pick another protein?” says a man in the ad. “I’d rather pick another senator instead.”

Major Democratic outside groups made a late play in the state, with WinSenate, which is affiliated with Senate Democrats’ top super PAC, investing $2.2 million. The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee spent $500,000 on a coordinated ad buy late last month.

The pro-Republican Senate Leadership Fund dropped $1.7 million on the race, and Trump headlined a rally for Hyde-Smith on Oct. 26.
