#6376. Birdsong has more in common with human speech than scientists expected

A comparison of 367 bird species and 52 human languages reveals unexpected similarities in the rhythms and patterns of vocal communication.

Birds and humans share some surprisingly similar patterns when they make sounds. Even birds that never learn their songs naturally produce rhythms much like those found in human speech and music.

The finding comes from a comparison of the songs of 367 bird species with people speaking and singing in 52 languages.

Three patterns of human speech and music appeared across the birds, in those that learn their songs and in those that don’t.

The authors interpret that as a sign that the patterns come from the shared mechanics of making sound rather than from learning alone.

Logan James of McGill University and the University of Texas at Austin led the work with Jon Sakata of McGill. Several co-authors work at McGill’s Centre for Research on Brain, Language and Music.

In an interview with Earth.com, James noted that the shared patterns were what excited the team most.

“These results highlight that, despite the tremendous diversity across human languages and hundreds of species of birds, there are still fundamental shared sequencing patterns,” he said.

The recordings came from xeno-canto, where birders around the world upload recordings. The team kept only recordings the recordist had rated top quality and labeled as song rather than calls.

No second species could be in the background, no playback could have been used to provoke the bird, and the singer had to have been seen.

Software then split each song into its separate sounds, and experienced annotators checked every sound. That work produced more than 74,500 individual sounds from about 5,900 songs.

The researchers paired each group of vocal learners with closely related birds that do not learn their songs: songbirds with suboscines, and hummingbirds with nightjars.

On the human side, the team used recordings of people speaking and singing in 52 languages, made for an earlier project.

In human speech and song, the pitch rarely leaps far from one syllable to the next. The team measured the pitch at the end of each bird sound and the start of the next.

Across the birds, the jumps were smaller than chance would produce.

Human voices also keep a beat, with sounds spaced evenly in time.

Birdsong showed the same pattern more often than would be expected by chance.

And people generally stretch the last sound of a phrase, the way a singer holds a final note.

Birds did that too. Their songs also tended to grow louder through the middle of a phrase and fade at the end, as human music does.

Songbirds have been the usual comparison for human speech because they, like us, learn their songs by listening. This study could set them against close relatives that don’t.

Sakata told Earth.com that the team expected birds that learn their songs to show greater similarities to human speech, since people also learn to speak.

“What surprised us was that the songs of birds that do not learn their songs (e.g., suboscines, nightjars) actually had comparable patterns to us relative to the vocal-learning birds,” he said.

Where vocal learning did make a difference, it did not act the same way in songbirds as in hummingbirds. The authors counted that as no consistent effect.

The matches were not perfect. Unlike human voices, which tended to become quieter throughout a phrase, birdsong tended to grow louder in the middle before fading at the end.

The authors suspect breathing explains part of it.

A person usually speaks or sings a whole phrase on one breath, and they suggest that is why the volume drops toward the end. Birds take tiny breaths between the sounds in a song.

Lung size may matter too. Across the birds, bigger species stretched their final sounds more, and a human has much bigger lungs than any of them.

But nightjars, among the largest birds in the study, stretched their final sounds even more than people do, so size can’t explain all of it.

The team also ran a broader measurement of how pitch and rhythm change together across a whole phrase, the same one that separates speech from song in human recordings.

By that measure, bird songs as a group were closer to human speech than to human singing. Hummingbirds and suboscines came out nearest to both, closer than the songbirds.

James said no large group of birds was closest to human patterns overall.

A few species were, on that combined measure, among them the scaled antbird, the blackhead antbird and the rufous-tailed hummingbird.

Songbirds and suboscines did keep a steadier beat than hummingbirds and nightjars, so they are the better birds to study for the roots of human rhythm.

In a commentary published alongside the study, Kazuo Okanoya of Teikyo University wrote that the work gives researchers a basis for testing the mechanisms behind the shared patterns.

“Linguistic concepts can guide such tests but should not be used in place of experimental data,” he added.

The study was based entirely on recordings, so the researchers could not confirm whether similarities in how birds and humans produce sound explain the shared patterns.

It also remains unclear whether listeners’ preferences help shape these patterns.

Sakata said very little is known about the shape of the voice box in many of these species, and that mapping that variety is a next step.

James said earlier work by the group found that people tend to like the same male courtship sounds that females of that species like.

“So we are also curious to examine how much birds (and humans) like the sound of patterns that conform to these universal patterns,” James said.

Other features of human music, such as distinct notes and nested layers of structure, have not been checked in birds yet. The authors wrote that those are the next measurements to take.

The full study was published in the journal Science.

November’s full moon, known as the "Beaver Moon," will rise in the east at dusk tonight (Nov. 24), marking the first of three consecutive supermoons.

It will be the third and final full moon of fall in the Northern Hemisphere and the first in a series of unusually close full moons that includes December's spectacular Christmas supermoon — the closest full moon since 2018. These bright moons are just some of the many winter skywatching highlights headed our way in the coming months.

The Beaver Moon gets its name from the time of year when nocturnal beavers in North America traditionally build dams and prepare for winter under the full moon, according to TimeandDate. Other nicknames include the Frost Moon and Snow Moon, and the Anishinaabeg people in North America call it Baashkaakodin Giizis — the Freezing Moon — according to the Center for Native American Studies.

The moon will reach its full phase at 9:53 a.m. ET on Tuesday, when it will be below the horizon in North America. The best time to see the Beaver Moon is at moonrise that evening, as it rises in the east around the same time the sun sets in the west. That's when the moon will appear against a relatively bright twilight sky, making it easier to appreciate its size and color.

The moon will appear full on Monday and Wednesday as well, but Tuesday offers the best opportunity to see it rise during twilight.

The Beaver Moon will be the first of three consecutive supermoons, according to EarthSky. A supermoon occurs when a full moon coincides with the moon being relatively close to Earth in its elliptical orbit. The moon's distance from Earth changes throughout the month. On average, the moon is 238,900 miles (384,472 kilometers) from Earth. When a full moon occurs near perigee, or its closest point during its orbit, it appears slightly larger and brighter than usual. #6374. Premature birth may change the brain’s biological clock

Brain scans and donated tissue show that premature birth sets the cerebellum on its own track, leaving it out of step at the due date.

Premature birth interrupts a critical period of brain development.

Now, researchers have found that even by their original due dates, babies born prematurely show signs of altered development in a key region of the brain.

The cerebellum of a baby born early matures on a different track. At the due date, its cells are in a different state from a full-term baby’s, according to a new study of brain scans, developmental checkups and donated tissue.

Georgios Sanidas and Gabriele Simonti of Children’s National Hospital in Washington, D.C., led the work.

The study’s senior authors were Panagiotis Kratimenos of Children’s National and the George Washington University School of Medicine and Vittorio Gallo of Seattle Children’s Research Institute.

The tissue came from infants who had died and whose families consented to autopsy, and the authors thank those families in the paper.

In an interview with Earth.com, Kratimenos noted that the work offers parents of preterm babies relief as well as hope.

“Our work shows that premature birth does not break the brain, nor does it simply pause it,” Kratimenos said.

Between 24 and 40 weeks of pregnancy, the cerebellum grows about fivefold in volume, faster than any other part of the brain.

It handles movement and balance, and it is wired into thinking and language as well.

For a baby born at 26 weeks, much of that growth takes place in a neonatal intensive care unit.

Doctors have known that early birth changes how the cerebellum grows and how a child develops.

What they didn’t know was what happens to the cells inside it, because that can only be studied in human tissue.

The team followed 176 infants born early, none of whom had major brain injury, through scans and checkups.

At the due date, each extra week of pregnancy before birth was worth about 230 cubic millimeters of cerebellum, in proportion to the rest of the brain.

Ultrasound showed the size gap already in place at 28 weeks. The babies born earliest then grew at the same rate as the rest, so they had not closed it by the due date.

Later checkups showed the same pattern. Between nine months and three years of age, the babies born at the lowest gestational ages were more likely to have motor, thinking and language delays.

A smaller cerebellum went with motor and thinking delays in particular. Lung disease and the other complications of intensive care shaped the numbers, but they didn’t explain them.

To see the cells, the team turned to cerebellar tissue from 83 infants who had died, born anywhere from very early to full term. In 11 of them, the researchers mapped which genes were switched on where.

Three patterns of gene activity tracked how early a baby had been born.

The cerebellum’s most numerous neurons, the small granule cells, were still running an immature program in the babies born earliest.

In babies born closer to term, that program had given way to one built for forming and firing connections.

Under a standard microscope, the granule cells in the earliest-born babies look finished, because they have already reached their adult position.

“Even though those granule cells had reached the right neighborhood, they were still carrying the genetic features of immature cells,” Gallo said.

The large neurons that carry the cerebellum’s output, the Purkinje cells, were different again.

In the earliest-born infants their genes were tuned to building cell material, with signs of stress, rather than to settling into a mature circuit.

“Being born early forces those same cells to prioritize immediate survival over wiring, leaving them in an unfinished state even months later,” Kratimenos told Earth.com.

Under the microscope, in 77 of the brains, the differences were structural too. A temporary outer layer of brain cell precursors that normally disappears after birth lingered longer in preterm infants.

In full-term infants the density of Purkinje cells fell with age, the normal trimming that refines a circuit. In preterm infants it stayed flat.

The layer that holds the Purkinje cells’ branches grew at the same rate in both groups.

The preterm cerebellum continued to grow without showing the same signs of cellular maturation.

It kept its overall architecture while its development went a different way, which is why a scan that measures size alone may miss it.

Preterm babies are assessed, monitored and enrolled in trials by postmenstrual age, the weeks since the mother’s last period. The authors argue that this number measures time, not biological maturity.

Two babies at the same postmenstrual age can be at different developmental stages.

Treatments given around a premature birth, such as magnesium sulfate before delivery and caffeine after it, may therefore act on tissue that differs from one baby to the next.

“To time treatments properly, we have to match our therapies to the biological clock of a baby’s brain cells, rather than their age on the calendar,” Gallo said.

Gallo suggests that therapies designed to promote brain wiring may be less effective before the cells reach the appropriate stage of development.

In a commentary on the paper, Molly Kelly-Goss and Elizabeth Crouch wrote that a preterm infant may follow two calendars.

One is the cerebellum’s physical growth, and the other is the maturation of its cells and molecules.

In their words, “neither captures the true complexity of brain health at the time, nor what it means for the child years later.”

The study can’t separate the timing of birth from everything that comes with it. Inflammation, low oxygen and the stress of life outside the womb all arrive together.

The tissue and the scans also came from different infants, since the cerebellum can’t be sampled in a living baby’s brain, and each infant had one MRI scan.

Whether the gap persists, shrinks or is made up later in childhood is not known.

The authors wrote that the same slow maturation that leaves the preterm cerebellum vulnerable may also leave its development open to change for longer.

Gallo said the team’s gene signatures for each stage could guide treatment in two steps.

The first would protect a baby from inflammation and stress in intensive care, and the second would bring in therapies that boost brain wiring once the cells are ready.

Testing that will take studies that time treatments to a baby’s biological stage.

The full study was published in the journal Science.

#6373. The 9 Robot Toys for Kids That Make STEM Learning Fun

Get them working on those science and engineering chops out of the classroom.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

STEM-based schoolwork is a key part of your kid’s curriculum, but encouraging genuine enthusiasm for science, technology, engineering, and math that extends beyond the classroom requires more than a good teacher. For the right kid at the right age, a robotics kit may be a perfect fit. It can give a budding inventor the chance to learn about science in a practical way, on their own terms, and allows them to get creative. It also shows that science can be fun, and more than just a subject at school.

A good robotics kit balances out learning and problem solving with play. Not all of them do that effectively, though: Choosing the right one for the child in your life may not be so straightforward—particularly if you’re unfamiliar with the basics that robotics kits teach. To help you find a STEM gift this holiday season that's both fun and educational, we’ve compiled a lineup of editor-approved robotics kits. Whether you're getting ahead of shopping season or looking for a great last-minute holiday gift, these toys are both fun and give your child's mind a chance to grow.

During our research, we drew from our collective experience covering STEM toys and equipment for kids, including topics like the best microscopes and the best graphing calculators. We also read through studies on the importance of STEM education.

To make our selections, we looked for kits from reputable companies within the robotics space, such as Learning Resources and Wonder Workshop. We also took a look at toys and items that parents on the staff have bought for their own kids, making special note of any that ended up as household favorites.

While evaluating each kit, we gauged value for the price (especially because some kits cost upwards of $100), the STEM topics it covers, as well as how intuitive and (just as importantly) fun it is to use, according to parents’ reviews. Furthermore, we considered a wide variety of toys to account for different kids’ interests, ages, and skill levels.

If you’re on the search for a robot kit with a variety of play options that isn't too expensive, this is it. The solar robot toy from Sillbird includes the pieces necessary to build 12 different robot designs, so your kid will never run out of new ways to play.

The robotics kit offers two levels of difficulty, with half of the builds being simpler to assemble while the other half are more complex. So, once your kid masters the easier builds, they can move on to more challenging designs, all without ever needing a new toy.

A unique feature of this robot in particular is its power source. Instead of burning through heaps of batteries like other robot toys, it relies exclusively on an integrated solar panel that sits on the robot’s head. Whenever it slows down, simply place it in some sunshine and wait for it to recharge.

You can always count on Lego to be fun and engaging, but this kit throws in some coding and robotics to the classic building experience. This 1,177-piece set includes three Lego Star Wars droids—R2-D2, a Gonk Droid, and a Mouse Droid. Each of the droids looks like a standard Lego creation, but is designed to hold color and distance sensors, as well as an interactive motor.

Once they're built, kids can use the free Lego Boost smartphone app to program their droids and give them 40 different coding missions. Lego Boost is available on iOS, Android, Kindle, and Windows 10 devices.

With additional pieces included in the kit, kids can build and attach tools and weapons directly onto the droid for extra fun as they play.

This 77-piece activity set is reasonably priced and is perfect for beginners to coding and robotics. Botley the Coding Robot comes to life with an easy-to-use remote, so there are no apps to download (and no screen time involved). All coding is done directly on the remote control and Botley can be programmed to follow up to 120 steps in a row.

The kit includes coding activity sheets to help beginners learn the basics and get the most out of their robot. The kit also comes with several fun accessories, including black line pieces that Botley can follow on its own like a track, as well as several cubes and rods you can use to build obstacle courses.

For parents who want to introduce young kids to coding or build confidence in their new skills, Wonder Workshop’s Dash is a smart choice for young enthusiasts. Where many kits require extensive building before they’re up and running, Dash comes fully assembled and ready for about five hours of playtime before it needs a charge.

Each Dash is programmed to respond to external stimuli, so it can recognize and respond to dancing, singing, and the sound of your voice.

This coding toy is compatible with Lego, allowing kids to use it as a base for making their own Lego creations. There are also five free apps to download that give kids fun coding project ideas, from beginner concepts to more advanced ones as they gradually get the hang of programming.

Makeblock’s mBot is an excellent toy for young programmers looking to challenge their knowledge and electronics skills in practical application. The small robot takes about 15 minutes to build using an easy-to-follow guide and step-by-step instructions in 3D.

Kids learn to code in Scratch, a graphic programming language, with free included software. There’s also an app with game-based tasks to challenge kids and help them advance their skills.

The robot itself also has several features that expand its range of capabilities, such as the line follower sensor, the infrared sensor for the remote control, and the Bluetooth chip for controlling the bot from your phone. The toy is compatible with Lego bricks and has four expansion ports where you can add additional parts later on.

There’s a lot to like about this very cute little robot ball. It’s reasonably priced for what it offers, has a super-cool LED matrix that shows off characters and vector graphics, and boasts a top speed of 4.5 mph. The Sphero also has built-in sensors that detect light, cardinal directions, gyroscopic direction, and speed.

What makes this robot special is how it allows users to grow along with it. Once basic skills are mastered, young coders can move on to learning JavaScript, Scratch, and Swift.

Another plus is this robot toy’s durability. It’s waterproof and scratch-proof, so young explorers can take it outside through ponds and over rocks.

Robotics toys are, at their core, building toys. This kit from KiwiCo comes with internal motor pieces, external body parts, and blank robot skins so kids can design their own robot.

The finished product uses springs and a spinning mechanism to help the robot jump forward and rotate its arms. The key reason we like this kit so much is how well it focuses on hands-on application.

Unlike other options that are based in coding and higher-level thinking, this helps kids work with their hands and see how each individual piece interacts with the other.

Coding and basic electrical engineering are the focuses of this rover from Snap Circuits. Kids are challenged to build a full circuit board piece by piece, with over 30 parts to snap together, and then attach the board to the wheeled base.

Once the rover is built, kids code commands and directions for their “missions,” including patterns of flashing lights and sounds to get into the action.

One of the great things about this robot toy is that it takes kids from beginner to intermediate as their skills improve. After kids get a grasp of how to code through the app, they can create more advanced commands on their own using Blockly.

The robot also functions as a fun remote-control car that kids can drive in real time through the app.

This kit encourages kids to build and rebuild the robots, cars, and creatures of their dreams. It’s perfect for the budding inventor who likes to tinker with things around the house. There’s even a game element—10 playing cards that challenge kids to build various creations on the spot.

Protective goggles and a screwdriver accompany the included wooden pieces, electric motors and batteries, and hardware and tools. All the wooden pieces fit together easily and are designed with multiple purposes in mind.

While there is no coding element to the toy, its main focus is on helping kids build creative solutions to prompts and bolster their engineering and problem-solving skills.

Studies show that in addition to STEM literacy, robotics can help develop core skills like hands-on creativity, problem solving, communication, and teamwork. So teaching robotics isn’t just about setting up your kid to have a career as a computer programmer or engineer—it equips them with tech know-how and critical thinking they’ll need for virtually any type of education or work.

Choose toys that allow your kid to use their imagination and play out multiple different situations, both real and made up. Furthermore, make sure even if you want the toy to help them learn STEM skills, it still fits their interests and passions. A toy that gets played with often will help them learn a lot more than a more educational one that collects dust.

While you may think robotics clubs are only for middle and high schoolers, research has shown that children are also able to master basic robotics and programming skills when they’re introduced in pre-K to second grade.

Many of these kits are appropriate for children as young as 3 years old, while some are more advanced with an age suggestion of 8 and up. Before you buy, check the recommended age range listed by the company or on the box to make sure you’re choosing a robotics kit that challenges your kid while still being accessible to them.

You don’t have to shell out hundreds of dollars right away on a robot, especially if your kids are still learning what they like. There are plenty of robotics kits that run under $50 if you aren’t sure your kids are going to enjoy this kind of play and learning. Pricier options over $100 offer more complexity and can often grow with the kids, since they’re customizable to continue challenging them as they get older and gain experience.

#6372. Power shutoffs meant to prevent wildfires may carry unexpected health risks

Planned power shutoffs in California were linked to more respiratory-related hospital visits, particularly when wildfire smoke was also present.

When the wind picks up on a hot, dry day in fire country, the power company may switch off the electricity on purpose. A line with no current in it can’t start a fire when it drops into dry brush.

A planned shutoff has a cost of its own, though. In California, on days when a large shutoff reached a neighborhood, people there were more likely to turn up at an emergency room with a breathing problem.

The rise was largest among people with chronic lung disease, and wildfire smoke in the air at the same time made it larger still.

Lauren Blair Wilner, an epidemiologist at the University of Washington, led the analysis with colleagues at Scripps Institution of Oceanography and Columbia University.

Utilities call these planned outages public safety power shutoffs, or PSPS, and no study before this one had measured what they do to hospital traffic.

In an interview with Earth.com, Wilner pointed to the days when the two overlapped.

“Surprisingly, the effects of a PSPS event and wildfire smoke co-occurring were not simply additive – we found evidence that their effects on health were multiplicative,” she said.

Three major California utilities serve 88% of the state’s electric customers. They have run these power shutoffs since 2012 and report each one to the California Public Utilities Commission.

The research group PSE Healthy Energy compiled those reports.

Wilner’s team matched the reports for 2013 through 2019, by zip code, against every emergency room visit and unplanned hospital admission by adults across 1,504 California zip codes.

Those records came from the California Department of Health Care Access and Information and included more than 6.6 million visits for breathing problems.

Each visit day was compared with the other days of the same weekday that month, so every patient served as their own comparison.

A large shutoff meant more than 593 customers in a zip code without power.

On those days, the odds of an emergency room visit or admission for a breathing problem were about 6% higher. Smaller power shutoffs made no measurable difference.

Shutoffs and smoke arrive together more often than not. Of the 11,293 zip-code days with a shutoff, 7,656 also had wildfire smoke in the air.

Asked by Earth.com what else the study showed, Wilner came back to those overlapping days. “Co-occurrence is what we really need to think about here,” she said.

Because days with both outnumbered days with a shutoff alone, she added, shutoffs should be studied together with the fires they are meant to prevent.

Picture a day with a large shutoff and 10 micrograms of smoke particles in each cubic meter of air. The odds of a breathing-related visit that day were 16% higher than on a day with neither.

The shutoff alone added about 6% and that much smoke alone about 1%, so the pair did more than add up.

The pattern was strongest among people with COPD, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, a long-term illness that narrows the airways and makes breathing hard work.

On days with a large shutoff, the odds of a COPD visit were 29% higher. With smoke on top, they were 37% higher.

Many people with COPD rely on an oxygen concentrator, a machine that pulls oxygen out of room air.

It runs on electricity, and its battery typically lasts three to four hours. A typical shutoff in this study lasted 86 hours, more than three days.

Wilner said planners should take simultaneous outages into account as they prepare for wildfires and expand healthcare capacity.

“It is essential to put measures in place to ensure that people relying on electricity dependent medical equipment have access to power and can readily access healthcare, if needed,” she said.

Visits for heart problems didn’t rise during shutoffs, with or without smoke, and neither did visits for mental health crises.

Earlier studies of blackouts in New York State and Florida largely agree, suggesting that outages may be more strongly associated with respiratory problems than heart problems.

How long a shutoff lasted also mattered less than how many people it reached.

When the team counted total hours without power over the previous week instead, they found no link between duration alone and hospital visits.

Each additional 1,000 customers without power, on the other hand, was linked to about 2% higher odds of a breathing-related visit. For COPD visits, the figure was 6%.

Utilities report outages by circuit, so the team can’t say who inside a zip code lost power.

The researchers assumed customers were spread evenly along each circuit, which means some people counted as exposed weren’t.

Nor can the records show whether a patient was home during a shutoff. People may travel to a place that still has power, and breathe more smoke on the way.

Only adults 20 and older who reached a hospital are counted, so anyone who got sick at home and stayed there is missing.

The study covered 2013 to 2019, when planned power shutoffs were less common than they are today.

Since 2022, utilities in Washington, Oregon, Idaho, and Hawaii have used shutoffs too. California requires utilities to warn customers first and to open centers where people can charge devices.

Wilner’s team didn’t test whether those centers keep anyone out of the emergency room.

Wilner’s team is turning to what happens after a wildfire or other disaster, when outages and evacuations overlap.

“There are not complete datasets on historical evacuations and power outages after disasters, making it impossible to study the ways in which these things play out and affect health after an event,” she told Earth.com.

Those records, she said, would show what affected communities need and how to reach them.

For now, seven years of California records offer valuable insight into the potential health consequences of planned power shutoffs.

The full study was published in the journal PLOS Medicine.

#6371. Some of the most effective treatments for back pain are also the most affordable

A review involving nearly 15,000 people suggests that several drug-free treatments for lower back pain can improve health outcomes and reduce overall costs.

Treatments such as yoga, acupuncture, and cognitive therapy might seem like added expenses for people with lower back pain.

However, a new review suggests that these approaches can improve health outcomes while reducing overall costs.

Researchers reached that conclusion after reviewing 20 papers covering 24 studies and 14,884 people.

Eight treatments that use no drugs and no surgery were both more effective and less costly than usual care in at least one way of counting the costs.

The authors wrote that these treatments are still far from routine in most countries.

Manuela Ferreira, a professor at the George Institute for Global Health in Sydney, was the senior author. Her team included researchers at the University of Sydney and the University of Warwick in England.

“Low back pain is the world’s leading cause of disability, but many effective treatments can also save healthcare dollars,” Ferreira said.

“Our review found that approaches such as exercise, yoga, acupuncture and psychological support can help people recover while providing good value for money.”

Pain in the lower back is the leading cause of disability worldwide, and treating it costs a lot. In Australia, back problems accounted for about 2.2% of all health spending in the 2020 to 2021 financial year.

The team searched ten research databases for studies that compared what a treatment cost with what it achieved. They kept only treatments backed by at least one of three major guidelines.

Those come from the World Health Organization, the United Kingdom’s National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, known as NICE, and the North American Spine Society.

Benefit was measured in a unit that combines how long a person lives with how well they live during that time. Health economists call it a quality-adjusted life year.

The team converted every cost to 2024 British pounds and used the same cutoff NICE uses. A treatment counted as worth paying for if each extra year of healthy life cost less than £20,000.

Twenty papers published between 2005 and 2026 met those criteria.

They covered 24 studies, 55 comparisons with usual care, and 14,884 people in nine high-income countries, most often the United Kingdom.

Usual care in these trials meant ordinary first-contact care: a doctor’s advice, a booklet, some medication, and sometimes a referral to a physical therapist.

Six single treatments came out both more effective and less costly than that.

They were yoga, acupuncture, cognitive therapy, support for people managing their own pain, education aimed at reducing fear of the pain, and mindfulness-based stress reduction.

Two combinations did the same: workplace advice paired with a gradual return to activity, and a program of diet and physical activity.

In an interview with Earth.com, Ferreira was asked what someone with back pain should ask a doctor first. She suggested two questions.

“Is there anything more serious causing my back pain? If not, which is the case for most people, can you teach me or refer me to someone who can teach me how to manage my own symptoms?” she said.

In health economics, a treatment that is both more effective and less costly is described as dominant.

In the whole review, only one comparison went the other way, and that was a British massage program.

Massage cost about £324 more per person than usual care in 2024 money, and it gained no extra healthy time at all.

Whether a treatment saves money depends on whose bills get counted.

The review sorted every result three ways: the health system’s costs, an insurer’s or employer’s costs, and society’s costs, which add in lost wages and missed work.

A British yoga trial shows why that matters. In it, 313 people with chronic or recurring back pain were offered 12 weekly group classes.

Counting only health care, the classes added about £715 per person, and each extra year of healthy life cost about £19,300, just under the £20,000 bar.

Counting lost workdays too, the yoga group cost society about £293 less per person than the usual-care group. And the yoga group still gained more healthy time.

The biggest saving in the review came from a Dutch program for workers on sick leave with chronic back pain.

It paired workplace advice with a gradual return to activity, and it cut society’s costs by about £7,315 per person compared with usual care. An Australian cognitive therapy program cut them by about £2,671.

Savings like those count only when lost work is part of the sum.

A treatment did not have to save money to be considered cost-effective.

Counting the health system’s costs, 14 of 18 comparisons passed, including exercise alone, spinal manipulation, and exercise paired with cognitive therapy.

Counting society’s costs, 15 of 19 passed, and counting an insurer’s or employer’s, 11 of 14 did. Passing was the rule, but confidence in each pass varied.

Where a study reported how likely its treatment was to be good value, the figure ran from 50% to 99.6%.

One of the clearest savings came from an enhanced course of acupuncture in the United States, with extra sessions added to a standard 12-week course. It cut health care costs by about £396 per person.

Acupuncture and massage were tested in many of the studies, and their results were inconsistent.

The authors wrote that this points to context, who is paying, and how the treatment is delivered. A Belgian modeling study found osteopathy was dominant from a payer’s perspective.

The three modeling studies in the review met far fewer items on their quality checklist than the trials met on theirs, though. The weakest of them met two of 57 items.

A review in 2011 of 26 studies reached a similar verdict on some of these treatments, including exercise, acupuncture, and cognitive behavioral therapy.

Nine new economic evaluations have come out since the most recent review of the topic, in 2019.

The authors wrote that theirs is the first to cover every treatment the current guidelines recommend, measured against usual care.

Ferreira’s team wrote that yoga, acupuncture, cognitive behavioral therapy, and treatments aimed at reducing fear and stress still aren’t routinely offered or paid for in most countries.

Working out why, the team wrote, should be the next focus.

Asked what surprised her most, Ferreira said it was that these treatments are not always available to patients.

“I was pleased to see so many options can benefit both patients and society,” Ferreira noted.

“The good news for people with back pain is that some of the most effective treatments are also among the most cost-effective.”

“Investing in evidence-based care such as exercise, physical therapies and psychological support could help more people get better while reducing pressure on health systems.”

Every one of the 24 studies came from a high-income country, so the authors wrote that their findings are unlikely to carry over to lower-income settings.

Ferreira said testing them in poorer countries would take new trials and studies with local patients, clinicians, and policymakers.

Those would check that the treatments are safe, suited to local conditions, and acceptable.

Costs are tied to the health system that recorded them, and the studies measured them too differently to pool into one estimate.

Some people were left out by design. Studies of sciatica, where the pain runs down the leg, weren’t included, and neither were people who had back surgery in the past year.

Out-of-pocket costs, community services, and lost work were reported less often than the treatment’s price.

The larger gap is in what the review had nothing to compare. Not one of the studies that met its criteria tested a drug, an injection, or an operation for chronic pain in the back. Those treatments are paid for all over the world.

“We have not found studies on guideline endorsed pharmacological or surgical interventions for low back pain and therefore highlight the urgent need for those as well,” Ferreira told Earth.com.

The authors wrote that future studies should count lost work and community costs too.

The full study was published in the journal PLOS Medicine.

#6369. One of Russia’s most active volcanoes rises above a sea of clouds

A striking Landsat 9 image reveals the snow-covered summit and active lava dome of Shivelyuch volcano on Russia’s Kamchatka Peninsula.

Today’s Image of the Day features one of Russia’s most active volcanoes rising above a blanket of clouds on the Kamchatka Peninsula.

Snow covers the upper slopes of Shivelyuch, while a dark formation near the summit offers a glimpse of the volcanic activity taking place within the mountain.

The image was captured on November 8, 2026, by the Operational Land Imager aboard Landsat 9. Although clouds concealed much of the surrounding landscape, the volcano’s summit remained visible from space.

The contrast between the snowy mountainside and the exposed volcanic rock offers a striking portrait of a landscape that is continually being rebuilt from within.

Shivelyuch, also known as Shiveluch, is among the largest and most active volcanoes on the Kamchatka Peninsula in Russia’s Far East.

The mountain has a complex geological history. Its older structure, known as Stary Shiveluch, dates back roughly 65,000 years.

A younger volcanic complex, Molodoy Shiveluch, subsequently developed within the remains of the older mountain.

The Smithsonian Institution’s Global Volcanism Program has documented at least 60 major eruptions at Shivelyuch during the Holocene, the geological epoch that began approximately 11,700 years ago.

Successive eruptions and collapses have left extensive deposits of volcanic material across the surrounding terrain. These deposits preserve a record of the mountain’s turbulent past.

One of the most intriguing features of Shivelyuch is its enormous caldera, a depression measuring approximately 5.6 miles (nine kilometers) across.

Within this depression, a lava dome has developed as magma reaches the surface. The dome stands out against the snow in the satellite image.

Unlike the fluid lava commonly associated with Hawaiian volcanoes, the thick lava that builds volcanic domes does not travel easily across the landscape.

Instead, it accumulates around the opening from which it emerges.

As more material reaches the surface, the dome can expand, develop fractures, and become increasingly unstable.

Sections of these domes sometimes collapse. Such events can unleash pyroclastic flows – rapidly moving mixtures of scorching gas, ash, and fragmented rock that sweep down a volcano’s slopes.

The process can dramatically alter the appearance of a mountain, sometimes within minutes.

Kamchatka’s extraordinary volcanic landscape owes its existence to the movement of enormous sections of Earth’s outer shell.

The peninsula sits along the Pacific Ring of Fire, a vast region of geological activity surrounding much of the Pacific Ocean.

Here, the Pacific tectonic plate descends beneath another plate in a process called subduction.

Water released from the descending plate promotes melting in the overlying mantle, generating magma that can eventually rise toward the surface.

Over millions of years, this process has created a remarkable concentration of volcanoes, along with hot springs, geysers, and other geothermal features.

Kamchatka provides scientists with an opportunity to observe some of the fundamental processes responsible for reshaping Earth’s surface.

The effects of volcanic activity at Shivelyuch can extend well beyond the peninsula.

Although volcanic ash resembles ordinary dust, it consists of tiny fragments of rock, minerals, and volcanic glass.

These abrasive particles can damage aircraft engines and other critical equipment.

High-altitude winds can carry ash clouds across international borders and oceans. In July 2026, ash from Shivelyuch reached Alaskan airspace after traveling across the Bering Sea, disrupting air travel.

Even between major explosions, previously deposited ash can become airborne again when strong winds sweep across the landscape.

This means that an ash plume does not necessarily indicate that a new explosive eruption has occurred.

Volcanic activity at Shivelyuch had persisted for several months when Landsat 9 acquired this image.

Monitoring a remote volcano surrounded by unpredictable weather presents considerable challenges.

Satellites offer scientists an invaluable perspective on places where direct observations are difficult.

In addition to capturing changes in the appearance of volcanic landscapes, instruments aboard some satellites can detect infrared radiation associated with unusually hot surfaces.

These measurements help researchers identify areas of elevated temperature that may be associated with freshly exposed lava or other volcanic activity.

By comparing observations collected over extended periods, scientists can also track the growth and destruction of lava domes, map volcanic deposits, and document changes to the surrounding environment.

Weather clouds can interfere with many of these observations, making clear views of active volcanic features particularly valuable.

Seen from hundreds of miles above Earth, Shivelyuch appears almost serene. Its snow-covered slopes emerge from the clouds, revealing a rugged summit seemingly isolated from the world below.

Yet the mountain’s appearance belies the geological activity taking place beneath its surface.

The dark lava dome visible in today’s image represents the latest chapter in a history of destruction and renewal spanning thousands of years.

Long after the surrounding clouds have dispersed, the forces responsible for building Shivelyuch will continue to transform the mountain.

Image Credit: NASA Earth Observatory /Lauren Dauphin, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey

#6368. Some Democrats doubt Trump is serious about cutting deals in new Congress

President Donald Trump speaks with reporters on the South Lawn of the White House on Oct. 13 before leaving for a campaign rally in Alaska. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

President Donald Trump’s postelection statements about working with Democrats have presented the incoming majority with a kaleidoscope to decipher, but some Democratic lawmakers have their doubts.

On the one hand, the Republican president has contended that he can work with House and Senate Democrats after the new Congress is seated in January, even floating a bipartisan immigration bill. But on the other, he promoted his hard-line aide Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff, raising doubts about any cooling of the political environment.

At every stop along his October campaign rally blitz before Republicans suffered massive losses on Nov. 3, Trump railed against “Dumbocrats” and their “bad” policies. He mocked their candidates as too extreme, too corrupt and too beholden to the most progressive wing of their party. He even warned that, if voters handed them control of the House and Senate, it would set off “a 1929-style economic depression.”

Voters ignored him. They handed House Democrats over 250 seats at least come January, and the party will have at least 54 seats in the Senate.

Trump was asked during a “60 Minutes” interview taped Friday afternoon at the White House if he could resist insulting Democratic lawmakers for six months if that’s how long it took to reach a deal on major legislation. “Very easily,” he responded.

But several Democrats are so sure about getting to a “Kumbaya” moment with Trump during his final two years.

Virginia Sen. Tim Kaine said it was hard to take the president at his word because he is “so unpredictable.”

“But I'm certainly telling my colleagues we should try to put as many bills as we can on his desk that do good things for the American public, and then see how he behaves,” he said Tuesday.

"We're gonna put bills in front of the president on affordability starting Day One,” California Rep. Robert Garcia, the likely incoming House Oversight and Government Reform chair, said Tuesday. “We'll have to see if he's serious, but I don't trust Donald Trump for a second.”

The White House on Monday sent Garcia a letter, obtained by CQ Roll Call, warning House Democrats that their anticipated spate of probes "may cross the line into blatant criminality."

Rep. Jim McGovern, a Massachusetts Democrat who is in line to chair the Rules Committee in the new Congress, said on the floor Tuesday that he does not see a GOP that is ready to heed the election's lessons and come to the bargaining table.

“Instead of taking the hint or listening to the overwhelming majority of Americans who told them to change course, Republicans are doubling down on the same tactics and messaging they've been jamming down our throats these last two years, and it's a perfect example of why they lost in the first place,” he said. “They do not listen.

“Then to double down even further, the failed lame-duck president appointed Stephen Miller, the architect of all the cruel policies that most people hate, as his new White House chief of staff,” McGovern added, referring to the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. “What planet are these people living on?”

Kaine said congressional Democrats might not notice that much of a change from the White House with Miller moving into the chief’s suite near the Oval Office.

“Stephen Miller was calling a lot of the shots, even if he wasn't chief of staff,” the Virginia Democrat said. “So I view that as a kind of a change of the face, but not of the character of the administration.”

House Republicans’ Tuesday vote to make hard-line conservative Jim Jordan of Ohio their next leader is another red flag for Democrats.

“White House Chief of staff Stephen Miller and House Minority Leader Jim Jordan,” Brendan Duke, a former senior Democratic Senate aide now with the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, wrote on X. “Where is the pivot to the center after a historic election loss?”

Getting to the center is what retiring Nebraska Rep. Don Bacon says his fellow Republicans and Trump should be doing after the election massacre.

"I do wish we could get to the point where we could solve big problems, instead of just beating the other side,” said Bacon, who has floated a 2028 presidential bid. “We can’t do this Republican-only or Democrat-only. And I would say this to the president, too: We’ve got to start working across the aisle to solve these problems.”

Despite his postelection talk of working with Democrats, Trump has sought to blame them for an up-and-down U.S. stock market.

“Right after the election it went down $3 trillion,” he said Monday during an unplanned White House press briefing. “That was because of the result of the election, because the stock market does not want to see Democrats. And your 401(k)s have gone way down because of the ridiculous result.”

He's also returned this week to questioning the midterm results: “It's not even a result. It's almost hard to believe. Now, I wasn't on the ballot.”

Members of House Republicans’ new leadership team on Tuesday sounded dug in and ready for a partisan brawl over Democrats’ promised investigations into the president, many of his top aides and Trump family members. Jordan's election as GOP leader shows that “we are ready to dig in for the fight,” outgoing Speaker Mike Johnson told reporters Tuesday.

Michigan Rep. Lisa McClain, who was reelected House GOP conference chair, pointed to Garcia's two-word statement on Election Day: "Lawyer up."

“Tell me how ‘lawyering up’ helps anybody with affordability?" she said. “They're going to be focused on going after President Trump. We are going to be focused on improving the quality of life for every American.”

To that end, retiring Maryland Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, a former No. 2 House Democrat, said Republicans should heed one big takeaway from the election: “Trump lost.”

Scientists are perplexed at discovering the world's deepest explosive volcanic eruption at Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A submersible mission to the deepest ocean trench on Earth has made a shocking discovery: the deepest pyroclastic volcanic flow ever found on the planet, in a place geologists didn't expect to see any volcanic activity.

This evidence of a violent undersea eruption was found 20,000 feet (6,000 meters) below the ocean surface on the walls of the Challenger Deep, the deepest point of the Mariana Trench and the deepest part of the ocean. It was a "complete surprise," said Robert Stern, a professor emeritus of geosciences at the University of Texas at Dallas and first author of a new study describing the discovery.

Typically, volcanic activity doesn't occur that close to an ocean trench, Stern told Live Science. And given the site's extreme depth, the lava that made the flow must have had some very strange chemistry. Normally, the intense pressure of seawater at these depths would prevent an explosive eruption, instead favoring a goopier, seeping type of flow. But the flows seen on the edge of the Challenger Deep were similar to the explosive, roiling gases that coated Pompeii in ash in A.D. 79.

"It's not something that as a geoscientist I would have said would be predicted," said Sune Nielsen, a geochemist at the University of Lorraine in France who was not involved in the study. "Very far from it."

A fish in the genus Pseudoliparis in an image taken during during a dive by the Jason/Medea ROV at 20,659 feet (6,297 m).

The Challenger Deep is in the remote western Pacific at the southern end of the Mariana Trench. There, the Pacific oceanic plate pushes under the Mariana oceanic plate in a process called subduction. At the trench where the two plates meet, the ocean floor plunges down 6.8 miles (10.9 kilometers). Mount Everest could fit in the chasm, with room to spare.

Geoscientists aren't sure why the trench is so dizzyingly deep, but they have turned up some clues. For instance, there is a tear in the Pacific Plate that allows one narrow strip of the plate to subduct particularly rapidly. The curvature of the plate is also very steep, perhaps because the rocks of the Mariana and Pacific plates aren't very strongly connected to each other, allowing the Pacific Plate to dive steeply and flex freely.

The new findings, reported Monday (Nov. 23) in the journal Frontiers in Earth Science, suggest that volcanism and magma also may play a role, Stern said. The researchers were exploring a segment of the Challenger Deep's forearc, a roughly 120-mile-wide (200 km) expanse that sits between the trench itself and the volcanic arc created by the subduction zone. These volcanic arcs are standard subduction zone features; for example, Mount St. Helens and Mount Rainier are part of the volcanic arc of the Cascadia subduction zone in the Pacific Northwest.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

But though there are some volcanoes north of Challenger Deep along the Mariana Trench, the Challenger Deep segment of the trench is odd in that there is not an organized volcanic arc there. Instead, there's an ocean ridge. Regardless, the space between this ridge and the trench was expected to be volcanically quiet because there is not usually enough heat in that region of a subduction zone to melt magma.

Nevertheless, the cameras on the deep-diving remotely operated vehicle Jason/Medea, which went to the site in 2014, caught strange, pancake-like rock features at three different spots in a 60-mile (100 km) stretch of the trench. Samples brought on board the ship revealed rock embedded with volcanic glass and a pyroclastic flow texture.

A sea cucumber in an image from the Jason/Medea dive at 12,726 feet (3879 m).

The researchers are currently getting the rock dated, but volcanic glass usually erodes quickly in the ocean, Stern said, so the presence of glass suggests the eruptions were fairly recent. "They're not yesterday," he said, "but I don't think they're a million years old."

The pressure of the water at the depths of the flows is equivalent to 592 atmospheres of Earth stacked on top of one another. Typically, that kind of pressure keeps a lid on the dissolved water and carbon dioxide in magma that expands rapidly to cause explosive eruptions. Thus, Stern said, the eruptions by the Challenger Deep may have been driven by a supercritical fluid ‪—‬ a weird state sort of in between a gas and a liquid.

"We just don’t know how those magmas will behave at those water depths," said Stephen Self, a volcanologist at the University of California, Berkeley, who was not involved in the study.

The mission's observations also suggest that the crust of this region is extending, or stretching, in two different ways. To the east, the stretch is caused by a mechanical pulling apart of the crust. To the west, volcanic eruptions are stretching the crust. It's a perplexing finding, Nielsen said, without a clear explanation.

Stern and his colleagues suspect that the two plates are starting a new subduction zone in this western part. That would be an exciting finding; subduction zones move around over tens of millions of years, and researchers don't know much about how new ones start. The geochemical studies of the rocks that Stern and his team pulled up could answer questions about where the lava that made the pyroclastic flows came from and why this bizarre region can generate magma where none should be.

"This region is really, really unusual for our planet, and there is quite a bit of, 'What, really? Wait, how is that? OK, yeah, I guess maybe.'" Nielsen said. "So obviously, I find it super interesting."

Stern, R. J., Pujana, I., Anderson, M. K., Chin, E., Dygert, N., Harigane, Y., Le Roux, V., Leybourne, M., Ohara, Y., Okumura, T., Segee-Wright, G., & Etheridge, E. (n.d.). ROVing in the deep: Tectonic and magmatic complexities of the challenger deep forearc segment, southern mariana convergent margin. #6366. Narwhals may have a hidden vulnerability as the Arctic warms

Narwhals and seals rely on the same Arctic fish, but warming waters could leave narwhals with fewer options.

A narwhal and a seal do not appear to have much in common. The narwhal is a whale with a long spiral tusk. It can also dive much deeper than most seals.

In one Arctic fjord, however, the summer diets of these animals share a great deal.

Four marine mammals share those waters each summer. A new study found that narwhals, ringed seals and harp seals all lean heavily on one small fish, polar cod.

Of the group, narwhals had the narrowest diet. That could leave them with the least room to adjust if warming changes the fjord’s prey.

Monica Ogawa led the research. She’s a specially appointed assistant professor at Japan’s National Institute of Polar Research. She is also affiliated with the Arctic Research Center at Hokkaido University.

“Our findings provide further insights into potential changes in the Arctic marine ecosystem associated with climate change,” Ogawa said.

The fjord is called Inglefield Bredning, or Kangerlussuaq in Greenlandic. It lies in northwest Greenland. About 700 Inuit live in three settlements along its shores: Qaanaaq, Qeqertat and Siorapaluk.

Hunting marine mammals is how people there make a living. These animals are hard to watch while they feed underwater. So the team checked what they had already eaten.

Stomachs were collected over three summers, from 2022 to 2024. They came from animals taken in regular subsistence hunts, within existing rules and quotas. Local hunters and biologists did the collecting.

In all, 126 stomachs were gathered. Ringed seals supplied 54, harp seals 17, bearded seals 23 and narwhals 32. Each stomach’s contents were washed through a series of sieves, and every item was identified.

How big were the fish? To find out, the team measured tiny ear stones found inside fish heads.

“The collection of a large number of stomach samples would not have been possible without the cooperation of local Inuit hunters,” Ogawa said.

“Continued sample collection through collaboration with hunters will play an important role in the long-term monitoring of Arctic marine ecosystems.”

In total, 62 types of prey were identified in the stomachs. These included 27 species of fish and 19 species of shrimp. Clams and snails were also recorded, along with squid and tiny drifting animals.

Polar cod was found more often than any other prey. It was the main food of ringed seals, harp seals and narwhals.

Polar cod was present in 77.5% of ringed seal stomachs that contained food. By estimated weight it made up 82.1% of their diet.

The narwhal results were similar. Polar cod and one closely related fish accounted for 93% of the prey weight in narwhals. Squid or related animals were present in 88.9% of narwhal stomachs with food.

The diets were then compared between species. A meaningful overlap was found between ringed seals and harp seals. Harp seals and narwhals overlapped to a similar degree.

“The dietary niches of all species, excluding bearded seals, substantially overlapped, suggesting a high potential for interspecific competition,” Ogawa said.

The polar cod eaten by narwhals averaged about 4.7 inches (119 mm). Seals ate larger polar cod that averaged 6.4 to 7 inches (163 to 179 mm).

Narwhals also ate much more of a second fish. It is known as Arctic cod and is sometimes called ice cod. This fish is most often found between about 660 and 2,600 feet (200 and 800 meters) deep.

Narwhals can dive deeper than 2,600 feet. In this fjord they have repeatedly collided with research equipment moored at about 1,300 feet (400 meters).

This behavior suggests that narwhals may feed close to the seafloor. The authors propose that narwhals may use their diving ability to reach fish in deep water. In this way they could avoid competing with seals for the larger polar cod.

The diets of individual narwhals were also much more alike than those of individual seals. Narwhals were the only species in which this similarity was large enough to be considered ecologically meaningful.

Narwhals had already been ranked by earlier studies among the Arctic mammals most at risk from warming. Their limited range of prey is one reason for this.

Greater variation was found among seals, even within a single species. Seal pups ate smaller cod than older seals. Young ringed seals ate more tiny drifting animals and moved toward polar cod as they grew older.

The widest diet was recorded in bearded seals. A total of 52 types of prey were found in their stomachs. No meaningful overlap was found between their diet and those of the other three species.

Sculpins were the main prey of bearded seals. These are spiny fish that live on the seabed. Clams and snails were present in 70.6% of bearded seal stomachs with food. They were not found in any of the other species.

Most of the bearded seals were taken in shallow water where the seafloor can be reached easily. The shrimp they ate also lived on the bottom. In contrast, narwhals ate shrimp that live in open water in deeper areas.

Bearded seals are considered by the authors to be the most resilient of the four species. “Overall, dietary specialization and age structure emerge as key determinants of ecological resilience in marine mammals,” Ogawa said.

Something else turned up in the stomachs. It hints that the fjord itself may be changing.

Earlier studies were done here from 1938 to 1941 and again in 1998. Back then, the tiny drifting animal seals ate most was a cold-water crustacean called an amphipod.

The cold-water amphipod species recorded in earlier studies tends to avoid water warmer than about 36°F (2°C).

This time, krill were the most common drifting animal in ringed seal stomachs. Krill had never been recorded before in marine mammal stomachs from Inglefield Bredning.

The krill species found here can handle warmer conditions. They’re spreading north as Arctic seas heat up.

Redfish turned up too, in bearded seals. This fish comes from more southern waters and is moving north. It hadn’t been recorded as prey in this area before.

No such change was seen in narwhals or harp seals, compared with older studies. That difference may reflect how flexible each species’ diet is, the authors suggest.

A stomach shows only an animal’s last few meals. It can’t tell us how a narwhal eats across a whole year.

The fjord’s cast also changes with the seasons. Narwhals and harp seals leave in winter. Once sea ice returns, walruses arrive. So the study is really a summer snapshot from one fjord.

Harp seals may become important in this story. At present they visit the fjord only during summer. Warming is expected to push them farther north and keep them there for longer periods.

According to the authors, competition for the same cod could then develop among the three species.

How many cod live in the fjord, and where do they gather? The team doesn’t know yet. That information could help determine whether seals and narwhals actually compete for food.

Stomachs can’t show how deep each animal hunted, either. The authors called for tags that record each animal’s dives. A survey of the fish themselves is needed too.

“Building on the findings of this study, we hope to better understand how Arctic marine ecosystems will change in the future and how these changes may affect marine mammals and the local communities that depend on them,” Ogawa said.

Future studies could test whether narwhals would switch prey if polar cod and Arctic cod decline. That decline is expected as Atlantic fish move north.

The full study was published in the journal Marine Ecology Progress Series.

#6365. Surrounded by female cows, a bull named Achille chose to form a close bond with a male donkey named Patroclo that lasted for weeks, leaving scientists baffled

Achille the bull and Patroclo, a male donkey, mated and groomed each other for weeks in an Ethiopian pasture, forming a very unusual and mutual bond.

On a beautiful plateau in Ethiopia, a bull named Achille spent his days in a pasture full of female cows and other bulls. Yet over two weeks in March, researchers watched him ignore the females, and his own species, to mount a male donkey named Patroclo.

This happened not once, not twice, but at least 51 times.

Male cattle sometimes mount each other when no female cows are around, but Achille had plenty of them right beside him, and Patroclo never tried to get away.

The researchers concluded that the pair shared a selective, mutual bond, and that the mounting was part of it.

Elisabetta Palagi, an associate professor of biology at the University of Pisa in Italy, and her colleagues described the pair in a two-page report.

Martina Francesconi and André da Cruz, both PhD students at Pisa, are the lead authors. Da Cruz is also affiliated with CRIA, an anthropology research center in Lisbon.

Their report focuses on this one bull and one donkey, who they watched and studied very closely for eight days.

In an interview with Earth.com, Palagi said the team discovered the pair unexpectedly. They were in Ethiopia studying geladas, a kind of monkey, for a University of Pisa project called BRIDGES.

“It is a lovely reminder that careful field observation can reveal questions we had never thought to ask,” she said.

The pasture is in Debre Libanos, in Ethiopia’s Oromia region. Achille and Patroclo belonged to different owners. They met only during the day, when cattle and donkeys shared the pasture in mixed herds.

At night, Achille was housed with another adult bull, a cow, and a calf. Patroclo was housed with two other male donkeys.

Both animals had other possible partners in the same pasture. On any given day, there were three to six bulls and three to seven cows. There were also three male donkeys and two to seven female donkeys.

When the bull and the donkey kept interacting, Palagi said, the team began documenting the pair systematically.

The researchers recorded how Achille and Patroclo behaved toward each other and toward the rest of the herd. They kept recording even when nothing sexual was happening.

In all, the team saw the two together on four days and apart on four more.

Thirty-four of the 51 mounts included penetration. The researchers saw no avoidance and no aggression between the two animals.

Asked what surprised her most, Palagi named two things. One was how selective the two animals were about each other. The other was how actively Patroclo took part.

“What initially looked like an unusual encounter turned out to be a persistent pattern of preferential interaction,” Palagi told Earth.com.

Patroclo often presented his hindquarters to Achille and nipped him. Twice, another bull tried to come near Patroclo. Patroclo chased and bit him.

The two animals also licked, rubbed, and nuzzled each other. The team looked closely at the six seconds or so around each mount.

In about a quarter of the mounts, that friendly contact happened just before. In nearly three-quarters, it happened just after.

Contact before a mount isn’t a surprise, the authors wrote, because it may make mounting easier. Contact afterward is harder to explain. It appears to keep the social interaction going after sex is over.

Palagi said Achille and Patroclo had friendly contact with each other more often than with other animals, and it lasted longer.

The two also stayed close. When both were in the pasture, they spent more time near each other than apart.

Achille approached and mounted another male donkey only twice. That donkey avoided him and flattened its ears, a threatening expression.

When Achille tried to mount the other donkey, Patroclo moved toward Achille. Achille immediately stopped and directed his friendly behavior at Patroclo instead.

The researchers also analyzed Patroclo’s facial expressions using a coding system developed for horses. They compared four situations: Achille mounting him, Achille making friendly contact, Achille standing close by, and Patroclo alone.

Across all four, Patroclo’s face showed no detectable difference. To the team, that suggests Patroclo didn’t see Achille as a threat.

Achille courted cows the way bulls usually do, but he never tried to mount one. The other bulls nearby may have discouraged him, the researchers wrote.

After similar courtship with Patroclo, Achille did mount him.

The one time another bull tried to mount Achille, Achille rejected him. Among the rest of the herd, the team recorded no mounting between cattle and donkeys during the study.

Same-sex sexual behavior is widespread in animals. It has been documented in several species of the horse family.

But the team couldn’t find a published report of such behavior in donkeys. They also found no report of a lasting sexual relationship between domestic hoofed animals of two different species.

Classic explanations for same-sex sexual behavior include one animal forcing another, mistaken identity, and a shortage of opposite-sex partners.

The authors wrote that none of these seems to fully explain Achille and Patroclo. Their relationship was selective and mutual.

A bond like this must also come at a cost. The two spent time and energy on each other that could have gone into producing offspring. To the authors, the strength of the bond seems to outweigh that cost.

“Their relationship reminds us that sexual behavior can be part of a social bond beyond reproduction, and that these bonds can cross species boundaries,” Palagi said.

Nobody knows yet what the bond does for either animal. The behavior may benefit one or both of them directly. Or it may be a result of the way cattle and donkeys form social bonds.

Palagi said the team can’t tell whether sex helped keep the bond going or came out of an attachment the two animals already had.

Domestication may have played a part in the behavior too. The authors wrote that it changes animals’ social settings and their chances to interact with other species.

The next step, Palagi said, is to find out how often relationships like this one occur and to follow them over time.

She suggested comparing friendly behavior and signs of tension before and after sex. That could help test whether sex is linked to keeping a relationship going or to easing tension.

The team would also need to observe different pairs in different social settings to tell those two possibilities apart, she said.

The full study was published in the journal Current Biology.
